### Editorial Statement

The text of Jonathan Edwards is reproduced in this Edition as he wrote it in manuscript, or if he published it himself, as it was printed in the first edition. In order to present this text to modern readers as practically readable, several technical adjustments have been made. Those which can be addressed categorically are as follows:

1. All spelling is regularized and conformed to that of *Webster's Third New International Dictionary*, a step that does not involve much more than removing the "u" from "colour" or "k" from "publick" since Edwards was a good speller, used relatively modern spelling, and generally avoided "y" contractions. His orthographic contractions and abbreviations, such as ampersands, "call'd," and "thems." are spelled out, though pronounced contractions, such as "han't" and "ben't," are retained.

2. There is no regular punctuation in most of Edwards' manuscripts, and where it does exist, as in the earliest sermons, it tends to be highly erratic. Editors take into account Edwards' example in punctuation and related matters, but all punctuation is necessarily that of the editor, including paragraph divisions (especially in some notebooks such as the "Miscellanies") and the emphasizing devices of italics and capitalization. In reference to capitalization, it should be noted that pronouns referring to the deity are lowercase except in passages where Edwards confusingly mixes "he's" referring to God and man: here capitalization of pronouns referring to the deity sorts out the references for the reader.

3. Numbered heads designate important structures of argument in Edwards' sermons, notebooks, and treatises. Numbering, including spelled-out numbers, has been regularized and corrected where necessary. Particularly in the manuscript sermon texts, numbering has been clarified by the use of systematic schemes of heads and subheads in accordance with eighteenth-century homiletical form, a practice similar to modern analytical outline form. Thus the series of subordinated head number forms, 1, (1), *I*, a, (a), in the textual exegesis, and the series, I, *First*, 1, (1), *I*, a, (a), in Doctrine and Application divisions, make it possible to determine sermon head relationships at a glance.

<!-- p. x -->

4. Textual intervention to regularize Edwards' citation of Scripture includes the correction of erroneous citation, the regularizing of citation form (including the standardization of book abbreviations), and the completion of quotations which Edwards' textual markings indicate should be completed (as in preaching).

5. Omissions and lacunae in the manuscript text are filled by insertions in square brackets ([ ]); repeated phrases sometimes represented by Edwards with a long dash are inserted in curly brackets ({ }). In all cases of uncertain readings, annotation gives notice of the problem. Markings in the text designate whole word units even when only a few letters are at issue.

6. Minor slips of the pen or obvious typographical errors are corrected without annotation. Likewise, Edwards' corrections, deletions, and internal shifts of material are observed but not noted unless of substantive interest.

7. Quotations made by the editor from the Bible (AV) and other secondary sources are printed *verbatim ac literatim*. Edwards' quotations from such sources are often rather free but are not corrected and are not annotated as such unless significant omissions or distortions are involved.

Other conditions of textual preparation are related to differences of genre and factors unique to particular texts or manuscripts. For information on such matters please consult the note on the text in each volume or the first volume of each series within the Edition.

### Editor's Introduction

Jonathan Edwards was a person of his time and place, and no more so than in his understanding of the church and ministry. Native son of the "New England Way," he absorbed the conventions and constraints of the Congregational tradition. In the main this was the system articulated in 1648 in the Cambridge Platform, though for any minister in mid-eighteenth-century Hampshire County, Massachusetts, Congregationalism encompassed certain amendments relating to membership and the independence of each gathered church. Inheriting this system, Edwards was also heir to historic lines of tension. He indicated one of these when, late in life, he professed himself no admirer of congregational democracy.[^003-note1] Uneasy with the balance of power between lay members and the ministry, Edwards felt a similar disquiet with the relation between councils and individual congregations; here too the fruits of experience left him disenchanted. But the tension that especially figured in his ministry arose from the dual role of the church: functioning as an "instituted" means of grace to everyone and financed by a townwide system of taxation, the church in Northampton, like most others elsewhere in New England, was also a "gathered congregation" in which membership was restricted to "visible saints."

It was Edwards' fate to be caught up in circumstances that exacerbated these long-standing tensions. One of these circumstances was the drift of theological opinion away from orthodoxy. Alarmed by this drift, a majority of the Hampshire County ministers attempted in 1734 and 1735 to prevent First Church, Springfield, from choosing Robert Breck, an apparent "Arminian,"[^003-note2] as its minister. Another circumstance was the outbreak of revivals. Edwards led a revival in Northampton in 1734–35, and the town was shaken a second time

<!-- p. 2 -->

during the Great Awakening of 1740–42. Out of the Awakening emerged a movement of protest against any practices that compromised the gathered church. In his own way Edwards shared in this reaction. Hence in February 1749, he told the Northampton church that he had come to believe that persons requesting admission to the Lord's Supper must be "godly or gracious persons."[^003-note3] His dismissal followed in July 1750.

This volume in *The Works of Jonathan Edwards* contains one publication in which Edwards defended the actions of the group that tried to thwart the ordination of Robert Breck, two publications in which he defended his conception of the church, and a fourth in which he narrated the sequence of events in Northampton that culminated in his dismissal. Collectively, these texts bring home how much Edwards was engaged with issues that grew out of Congregationalism, the amendments to it known as Stoddardeanism, the revivals of the 1730s and 1740s, and religion as experienced by the laity of Northampton, or what we may term "popular religion."

The standard interpretation of the turmoil about church membership that led to Edwards' dismissal remains the one advanced early in the nineteenth century by his grandson and biographer, Sereno E. Dwight. Dwight's thesis may be reduced to the phrase, "Stoddardeanism (i.e. 'laxness') begat Arminianism." Writing as a committed Congregationalist and evangelical, Dwight connected two quite different processes and made one the cause of the other. The first of these was an easing of access to church membership that he traced back to the "half-way covenant" decision of the Synod of 1662 and that he saw as abetted by the Reverend Solomon Stoddard in *his* Northampton ministry, for Stoddard had allowed "unregenerate" persons to enter the church and participate in the sacrament of the Lord's Supper. According to Dwight, the easing of access to the church accelerated a second process, a weakening of doctrinal orthodoxy as "liberals" began to emphasize free will and human ability, a tendency that culminated in the rise of Unitarianism.[^003-note4]

<!-- p. 3 -->

Only recently has it become clear that Dwight, together with a host of nineteenth-century evangelical writers, misrepresented Stoddard and the consequences of Stoddardeanism in eighteenth-century New England.[^003-note5] The larger error has been to impose a framework of "declension" on the relation between orthodoxy and lay people, for the received tradition, which continues to be widely reiterated among twentieth-century historians of religion in New England, has it that sincerity gave way to hypocrisy among the third- and fourth-generation colonists.[^003-note6] That such failures of understanding should prevail for almost two centuries is perhaps a measure of how easily moral judgments—in this case, a contempt for "formalism" and, if I may say so, popular religion—have infiltrated the telling of the history of New England Congregationalism. The dismissal of Jonathan Edwards in 1750 has stirred up further bouts of special pleading.[^003-note7] The interpretive tradition includes yet another vein of speculation, the efforts some have made to discern themes from Edwards' philosophical theology or his fascination with the history of redemption in the controversy about admission to the Lord's Supper.[^003-note8]

<!-- p. 4 -->

The purpose of this introduction is to locate *An Humble Inquiry* and its companion, *Misrepresentations Corrected*, within more appropriate contexts: first and foremost, debates and decisions about the nature of the church that unfolded in English and American Puritanism in the seventeenth and early eighteenth centuries; second, popular religion as Edwards encountered it in Northampton; third, the thinking of Solomon Stoddard and the ministers who espoused a Stoddardean understanding of the church; and fourth, Edwards' place in the revival of the 1740s and his response to the more radical tendencies that emerged from that revival.

These four contexts were parts of a whole in which the social and the religious were commingled and inseparable, a whole that we may term a culture. Growing up within this culture, Jonathan Edwards was constrained by its boundaries in imagining (or reimagining) the nature of the church. He was constrained for another reason. Because this culture was a whole, any change in one of its parts reverberated in the others. The nature of the church was no narrowly religious or doctrinal matter, but a many-sided issue that quickly became charged with politics. In bringing popular religion into the forefront of my narrative, my purpose is to reveal more fully the politics of the Northampton controversy. Why did the townspeople explode when Edwards proposed to restrict their access to baptism and the Lord's Supper? The answer to this question has to do with the mingling of the social and the religious in eighteenth-century New England.

#### The Robert Breck Affair

The story of the entanglement that is known to us as the Breck Affair has been told before, and the full details need not be repeated here.[^003-note9] Daniel Brewer, the longtime minister of First Precinct, Springfield,

<!-- p. 5 -->

died in 1733. Seeking to replace him, the church attempted twice to recruit graduates of Yale. These efforts failing, it turned to Harvard and in May 1734 invited Robert Breck to preach with a view to settlement. Breck was installed and ordained in January 1736 despite the opposition of a majority of the ministers in Hampshire County.

Edwards was one of the Hampshire ministers who opposed Breck's settlement in Springfield. Fifteen years later, Edwards wrote to his congregation that "I had no hand at all in opposing these ministers [^003-note10] in anything they did; for all that was done of that nature, was done when I was not in New England, and when I was totally ignorant of anything that was done until all was over. My crime was merely defending what others had done, at their request." This retrospective judgment is contradicted by evidence that Edwards did indeed play a significant role in the controversy. As late as August 1735 he cosigned letters critical of Breck that the Hampshire Association sent to the Springfield church. During September and October he was out of New England, spending at least part of the time in New York City.[^003-note11] This absence explains why Edwards did not attend the council meeting that resulted in Breck's arrest, yet it did not hinder his being asked to write the defense of the Hampshire Association's actions. That defense was *A Letter to the Author of the Pamphlet* (1737), the final shot in a very public quarrel between certain Boston ministers who befriended Breck and those in Hampshire County who opposed him.[^003-note12]

<!-- p. 6 -->

Robert Breck arrived in Hampshire County with his reputation clouded by reports of how he had behaved as a student at Harvard and as a ministerial candidate in Windham County, Connecticut. Born in Marlborough, Massachusetts, in 1713, where his father of the same name was the town minister, he matriculated at Harvard in 1726. By his own admission young Breck "fell into bad Company" and had a lively time of it until his father withdrew him in May 1729. A year later the faculty agreed to let him graduate with the class of 1730 on the grounds that, in the interim, he had "followed those studies at home whch were proper for his College study," had "Confessed his former Miscarriage at college," and, as testified by proper witnesses, had demonstrated "studious blameless behavior." Breck returned to Harvard in 1732 and took his M.A. in 1733. He began to preach in December of that year as a candidate for the ministry of Third Parish, or Scotland District, in Windham. He quickly found himself in trouble, for the sermons that he preached, including a guest sermon from the pulpit of his neighbor Thomas Clap of First Parish, contained statements that ran contrary to the Westminster Confession. Breck seems to have asserted that persons who followed the "Light of Nature" could be saved with or without faith, that certain passages of Scripture were corrupt, and that predestination gave "no Encouragement to Duty."[^003-note13]

The winds of change were blowing in the intellectual universe of New England Calvinism, and Breck was shifting with them. As some who had heard him preach in Windham testified, he spoke admiringly of the English Arian Thomas Chubb. Breck conceded to his critics that, at the outset of his ministry, he was not "fully settled and established in" the "Point" of faith as "necessary to Salvation." In his own

<!-- p. 7 -->

defense he painted himself as someone still at bottom soundly orthodox, though liking to voice speculations from the pulpit. Hindsight tells us that, along with others in New England, he was moving toward a more rational theology that his contemporaries usually termed Arminianism. Yet he was willing to avow the Westminster Confession and to declare that he "hated the Name of an Arminian."[^003-note14]

His older neighbor and fellow Harvard graduate, Thomas Clap of First Parish, remained traditionally orthodox. Dismayed by the ideas Breck was voicing, Clap was also troubled by rumors of Breck's misdoings as an undergraduate. Had he been expelled from Harvard for stealing books? When Clap put this question to him, Breck denied the story and defended his opinions.[^003-note15] Third Parish gave him a vote of confidence by calling him to the pulpit. Even so, aware that Clap was not convinced of his merits, Breck decided to look elsewhere for a permanent position.[^003-note16]

The offer from First Precinct drew Breck to Springfield in May 1734. Word followed swiftly of his problems in eastern Connecticut. The main line of communication between Windham and Springfield ran through members of a clerical and civil elite, the Williamses. The controversy would eventually involve five members of this clan, all of them ministers and all committed to defending orthodoxy. In 1734 the family patriarch, the Reverend William Williams of Hatfield, Massachusetts, was the senior minister in Hampshire County and the man most likely to serve as "moderator" of meetings of the Hampshire ministers. One of his sons, Elisha, was rector (chief officer) of Yale College, and another (by a different wife), Solomon, was minister in Lebanon, Connecticut. A cousin of theirs, Stephen, was minister in Longmeadow, adjacent (on the south) to Springfield. Stephen's

<!-- p. 8 -->

brother Eliezer was minister in Mansfield, Connecticut, which adjoined Lebanon. Two other Hampshire ministers were or soon would be related to the Williamses. Jonathan Ashley of Deerfield married one of William Williams' daughters in 1736. And because William Williams had married, as his second wife, a daughter of Solomon Stoddard, he was Edwards' uncle. As clan and cousinage, the Williamses had been known to act forcefully in securing the appointment of ministers they favored and in blocking those they disliked.[^003-note17]

Hearing of his neighbor Thomas Clap's concerns, Eliezer Williams wrote in August 1734 to Stephen that Robert Breck was "not a sutable Person to be employ'd in the Ministry." Thus forewarned, the ministers in Hampshire County, acting in their organized capacity as the Hampshire Association and assuming a customary role as supervisors of an ordination, told Breck on September 4 that they wanted him to secure a "certificate of orthodoxy" from Thomas Clap and two other Windham County residents, the Reverend Daniel Kirtland of Norwich and a layman, Nathaniel Huntington, of Windham. But the rupture between Breck and Clap was not easily healed. In late August Breck had written Clap a letter in which he complained of what was being said about his preaching and his misdemeanors as an undergraduate. "I took you always to be a Gentleman," he told the older man, "& not only so, but a Christian." A visit he paid to Clap in September failed to produce "Satisfaction." Two months later, Breck was telling friends and members of the Springfield church that his Windham County critics did not speak the truth. Clap, unreconciled, communicated directly on October 7 to the Association about errors in Breck's preaching. In late November, six of its members, including Edwards, advised the parish not to proceed to his settlement.[^003-note18]

Settlement in Springfield seemed all the more unlikely since Breck had reached an impasse in negotiations over salary with the parish. But Breck returned from Cambridge early in the new year after the church members, having decided that he was without fault and resenting what they saw as interference from the Hampshire ministers, recalled him on January 1. Hoping all would work out for the best,

<!-- p. 9 -->

William Williams urged Breck to send Clap a "Confession," which he did. Breck presented this confession and a new "Vindication" to the members of the Association on April 8. In the latter he acknowledged having "tho't it not an unprofitable way of spending time in discoursing upon some of the controverted points in divinity." But he also insisted on his orthodoxy.[^003-note19] Thereupon three members of the Association, William Rand, Ebenezer Devotion,[^003-note20] and Isaac Chauncy, declared that they were willing to begin the ordination process. Six others, led by William Williams, voted for a full hearing of Breck's critics, to take place at a special session of the Association. From this point on, the majority clung to the condition that, before ordination could proceed, Breck should meet face-to-face with those who accused him of misbehavior.

On April 17 the Springfield church, ignoring a cautionary letter from William Williams, gave Breck a formal call. The vote was not unanimous, and the small handful in opposition—the "dissatisfied"—turned to the Association for advice and assistance. Their complaint was discussed at a meeting of the Association on August 14. But by this time Breck, armed with a certificate of orthodoxy signed by eight ministers from elsewhere, had accepted the call of the church, which in turn invited four of the Hampshire ministers—the three who voted in his favor in April, together with William Williams—to participate in the ordination council. William Williams declined the invitation. When he learned that Breck had also invited four ministers from outside Hampshire County, he wrote to one of them, the Reverend William Cooper of Fourth (Brattle Street) Church in Boston, suggesting that one or two of Breck's supporters in Boston join with their Hampshire colleagues to air all the issues. But the Boston clergy were embarked on a different course. Cooper and three others, Samuel Mather, William Welsted, and Joshua Gee, turned up in Springfield and convened an ordination council on October 7. Thomas Clap was on hand as principal complainant. In the midst of these sessions, which took place behind closed doors and extended into the next day, Breck was abruptly arrested, charged in civil court with preaching heresy,

<!-- p. 10 -->

and taken off to Connecticut, the site of the alleged offense. Released on bond, he returned to Springfield one day later in time to arrange for a reconvening of the council in January 1736. All was calm on this occasion; Cooper preached the ordination sermon, and Breck was formally installed and ordained.

Thereafter the controversy was fought out via pamphlets and letters to the press. Someone sympathetic to Breck fired the first shot, a letter in the *Boston Gazette* of October 10, 1735, mocking the literary style of "country" ministers, accusing them of meddling, and ridiculing another letter (itself not fully quoted) written by a person whose identity was partially concealed. As was later revealed, the author of this second letter was Elisha Williams, who had written to his cousin Stephen urging that the Hampshire ministers publicize "the Folly and wickedness" of the ordination council. Other letters followed, pro and con.[^003-note21] In December the Springfield church petitioned the Massachusetts House of Representatives to affirm that the council was in order. The House conducted an inquiry into the conduct of the three justices of the peace who had ordered Breck's arrest, and in January, by a close vote, officially rebuked them for having "interrupted that Church and Ecclesiastical Council."[^003-note22]

The Hampshire ministers fought back, telling their side of the story, with due emphasis on Breck's limitations as preacher and person, in *A Narrative of the Proceedings of Those Ministers of the County of Hampshire, Etc. that have Disapproved of the Late Measures Taken in Order to the Settlement of Mr. Robert Breck* (1736). A riposte was soon forthcoming, the anonymous *An Examination of and Some Answer to a Pamphlet, Entitled, A Narrative and Defense…With a Vindication of Those Ministers and Churches, that Approved of, and Acted in the Settlement of Said Mr. Breck* (1736). The series ended with the reply of the Hampshire majority, Edwards' *A Letter to the Author*.

The author of *An Examination* was almost certainly William Cooper and not Robert Breck, to whom it is attributed in certain older bibliographies.

<!-- p. 11 -->

Neither at this stage nor in his previous intervention was Cooper motivated by a personal relationship to Robert Breck. "As to Mr. Breck himself," he declared in a letter to William Williams, "tho' I heartily wish his Usefulness, and entertain good Hopes concerning him, yet I have no particular Interest in him, and know of nothing to give me an undue Byass towards him."[^003-note23] The truth of this statement is borne out by Edwards' silence on the matter. And Edwards could not accuse Cooper of defending a fellow liberal. The Boston minister spoke in favor of the Westminster doctrines in the sermon he preached at Breck's ordination.[^003-note24] When the Great Awakening erupted in the 1740s, he defended it against its critics and, more tellingly, signed three prefaces to as many books by Edwards in which the revival was presented as a "work of grace." His endorsement of Edwards extended back to 1731, when he lent his name to the preface of Edwards' first published sermon.

These circumstances force us to look elsewhere for the motives of the Boston ministers. Their rhetoric is at once revealing and concealing. From the outset of the controversy, these men described the Hampshire majority as "a set of ambitious, arbitrary, and unjust usurpers" intent on disrupting the "liberty" of local congregations to choose as they pleased. "And a fine Scheme it is," Cooper blustered, "to fetter and enslave the Churches; and have Things carried according to the Will…or arbitrary Disposition of a particular Set of Ministers." Cooper and his colleagues argued that associations like the one in Hampshire County were a violation of Congregational principles as articulated in the Cambridge Platform of 1648:

> And in a Word, We don't look upon them [^003-note25] to be any Part of the Constitution of these Churches…such an Association of Pastors…is an Usurpation upon the Liberties of Congregational Churches, and those Churches are servile indeed that tamely submit to them therein.

Local churches could decide for themselves whether to seek "Advice" from a ministerial association, and the authority of that advice was

<!-- p. 12 -->

contingent on the "free and voluntary" actions of the congregation. From this reasoning followed Cooper's case against the Hampshire ministers: they intervened in Springfield without ever being asked to do so by the church.[^003-note26]

Via such assertions, Cooper cast the friends of Breck as defenders of the rights of local congregations as enshrined in the Cambridge Platform, and his critics as "Presbyterian"-minded ministers. But let us look more closely at this rhetoric. We may do so, first, by returning to the Cambridge Platform, as Edwards and the Hampshire ministers did in their rebuttal. This description of Congregational church polity was the product of the founding generation of New England ministers, the immigrants from England who experimented with a system of church government that empowered individual congregations—hence the term "congregational" or its near synonym, "independent"—and entrusted the "power of the keys," or decision making in the congregation, to (male) full church members. In both respects the Congregational system curtailed the authority of the ministry as it was customarily sustained in the "presbyterian" or "classical" system of church government. The framers of the Platform modified the strict independence of each local congregation by urging a process of "communion" or consultation between churches and by affirming the legitimacy of "synods" as "necessary to the well-being of churches, for the establishment of truth, & peace therin." As defined in the Platform, synods were a relatively toothless instrument. Intervention from outside was proper when the church itself requested advice. Yet the Platform also recognized that situations could arise that would justify a "fuller act of brotherly communion," a process of "admonition" undertaken without prior invitation. And in chapter 8, which described the election of ministers as performed by individual congregations, the Platform urged that "neighbour-churches be advised withall, & their help made use of in the triall of church-officers, in order to their choyce."[^003-note27]

Much had happened between 1648 and 1735 to fill out these rules. The many episodes of conflict over issues like church membership and whom to elect to the ministry had prompted an increasing use of "councils," often though not always a small group of ministers, to mediate disputes. Experiences of this kind, together with the felt need

<!-- p. 13 -->

to affirm a stronger role for the ministry as a collective body, lay behind a resolution passed by the Synod of 1662 declaring that "Consociation of Churches" was scriptural and "expedient." Not until the 1690s, however, did the ministers in New England formalize the existence of "consociations" or "associations," groups that enrolled the clergy in a given region for the purpose of discussing issues of the day. An attempt in Massachusetts to give legal standing to these groups, the so-called Proposals of 1705, collapsed in the face of opposition from the civil government and from certain ministers. The clergy in Connecticut succeeded where their colleagues failed, securing in the Saybrook Platform of 1708 a state-recognized system of ministerial consociations. Yet their victory was but partial since many congregations in Connecticut refused to accept the Saybrook Platform.[^003-note28]

The Hampshire Association emerged in the wake of these events. Organized in 1714 and endeavoring to meet monthly, it undertook the same kinds of business that concerned the four or five associations already functioning in eastern Massachusetts. One role such groups expected to assume was the ordination of new ministers and, perforce, a review of each candidate's credentials. Ordination in New England was initially downplayed, even to the point of allowing laymen to perform the function. But the reemergence of a higher sense of clerical office, a process under way as early as the drafting of the Cambridge Platform, was accompanied by a new insistence on ordination as exclusively a function performed by the clergy.[^003-note29] Hence the expectation that Robert Breck would seek ordination from his Hampshire colleagues should the Springfield church vote to have him as its minister. That his colleagues could refuse this function and, by doing so, prevent the church from exercising its undoubted right of choosing someone for the ministry was implicit in the process. Indeed, precedents existed for refusing to ordain and for looking closely at a candidate's beliefs.[^003-note30]

<!-- p. 14 -->

These contexts accentuate the decision William Cooper made to raise the cry of usurpation and to pin the label "Presbyterian" on the Hampshire clergy. To do so was to invoke a well-worn rhetorical tradition that dated back to the seventeenth century, and one that lay opponents of the Saybrook Platform had recently revived. But as some of his contemporaries knew, Cooper was no populist at heart. The central task awaiting Edwards was to defuse the rhetoric of Breck's friends. He did so by exposing them as *critics* of the Cambridge Platform.

The longest section of *A Letter to the Author* has to do with issues growing out of the Cambridge Platform: on the one hand, the legitimacy of the council that ordained Breck, and on the other the legitimacy of the Hampshire ministers' intervention. Edwards saw the former as turning on the composition of the council. Repeating a line of attack pursued in *A Narrative*, he insisted that the phrase "neighbour-churches" in the Platform did not sanction bringing ministers from as far away as Boston to a Springfield ceremony.[^003-note31] And what of Cooper's protestations that the Boston ministers were the true friends of congregational liberties? Here Edwards' tactic was to quote from a short pamphlet, *Some Brief Remarks upon a Letter to a Gentleman Relating to the Office of Ruling Elder*, published in Boston in 1731. No name appeared on the title page, and no bibliographer has proposed an attribution.[^003-note32] But Edwards knew that its author was one of the Boston members of the ordaining council. Criticizing the campaign to restore ruling elders, an "office" described in the Platform, the author mocked the very rhetoric Cooper was employing. In one instance the Platform was embraced; in another, it was ridiculed. The exact passage follows as part of *A Letter*.

If the Cambridge Platform was not really the issue in 1736, what was? We may best explain the intervention of the Boston ministers by regarding the controversy as a local echo of disputes in the early eighteenth century among Nonconformist ministers in England and Presbyterians in Scotland and Ulster. These controversies originated in the demand by certain clergy—usually the more orthodox or evangelical—that their colleagues formally subscribe to the Westminster Confession. Among the London Nonconformist clergy a debate at Salter's Hall in 1719 found some ministers arguing in favor of freedom of

<!-- p. 15 -->

conscience. Hindsight tells us that the faction speaking on behalf of liberty of conscience, or the right of private judgment, was beginning to break with the doctrines of high Calvinism. The same "liberal" tendency was present in the Church of Scotland, where the issue of "subscription" was disputed over a much longer period and with schism as its lasting consequence. The situation in New England was different in two respects: each side included ministers of undoubted orthodoxy, and subscription was displaced by the ambiguities inhering in associations and their power to review a candidate's credentials. But the outcome was the same, to begin the process of relaxing the accountability of individual ministers to their peers. William Rand, the firmest of Breck's friends in Hampshire and himself becoming doubtful of the orthodox tradition, underlined this outcome in an ordination sermon he preached in late 1735. "Every person," Rand declared, "is to judge for himself in such cases, and not to submit his reason and conscience to any human determinations whatsoever, but to examine whether they be agreeable to the mind of Christ."[^003-note33]

The majority of the ministers in the Hampshire Association were of a different way of thinking. For them the greater danger lay not in "persecution" of dissent, but in allowing false opinions to corrupt the household of God.[^003-note34] Such was Edwards' frame of mind. Like others in New England he was alarmed by the signs of Arminian opinion at home and abroad. In 1734 he was preaching to his Northampton congregation on the doctrine of justification by faith and insisting in

<!-- p. 16 -->

these sermons on the Reformed principle of humankind's natural inability. Some years later, in *A Faithful Narrative of Surprising Conversions*, he recalled how a "great noise…about Arminianism" broke out in Hampshire County in the mid-1730s. Those who shared his sense of alarm were determined to keep a close watch over candidates for the ministry. Thomas Clap had written Stephen Hopkins in April 1735 that "it is of absolute Necessity and Importance, in order to preserve the Purity of Religion, in these dark Times of Error and Declension," that any suspicion of "any thing amiss, in the Principles or Morals, of Candidates for the Ministry," be aired to the fullest. Edwards agreed. In what is doubtless a veiled reference to the Breck affair, his biographer Samuel Hopkins reports him as feeling

> it of Importance that Ministers should be very critical in examining Candidates for the Ministry, with respect to their *Principles*, as well as their religious Dispositions and Morals.…His Opinion was, that an erroneous or unfaithful Minister was likely to do more hurt than good to the Church of Christ; and therefore he could not have any Hand in introducing a Man into the Ministry, unless he appeared sound in the Faith.

"On this account," Hopkins observed, Edwards "met with considerable difficulty and Opposition in some instances."[^003-note35] Agent though he may have been of his uncle, cousins, and the Hampshire majority in the Breck affair, Edwards was nonetheless a willing participant in the effort to prevent the young man's ordination. It is telling that, thereafter, the two ministers never became friends or were reconciled.

The general task of rebutting Cooper involved Edwards in a host of minor issues and details, most of them already covered in *A Narrative*. These issues included the role of Elisha Williams in the affair, the interception of the letter he had written to his cousin, the responsibility of the Hampshire ministers for the debacle of Breck's arrest (it seems likely that the plan—possibly instigated by the "dissatisfied" in Springfield church—was for the magistrates to arrest the ordaining council), the behavior of the "man on horseback" who read pro-Breck testimonies to the crowd in Springfield, the privacy of a letter sent to William Williams by Benjamin Colman, Williams' willingness to oppose Breck, the irregularity of the ordaining council, and letting

<!-- p. 17 -->

Breck choose four of its members. The most crucial matter was undoubtedly the accusation that the Hampshire ministers had never been invited by the Springfield church to intervene. Here Edwards had to reach to make his case, in part by making much of the "neighbour-churches" clause and the apparent irregularity of having Breck himself designate some of the churches that participated in his ordination. It is symptomatic of still-persisting tensions that Edwards raised anew the issue of Breck's orthodoxy, reiterating one more time the charge that he had preached false doctrine.

The significance of the Breck affair must not be exaggerated. Of little importance to Edwards' earliest biographers, the controversy dramatized the weakness of ministerial associations in an ecclesiastical system ill-suited to the task of preserving unanimity among the clergy. A new ethos of liberty of conscience, though but faintly present in New England in the 1730s, would in time become another obstacle to orthodoxy. But this is to anticipate. The war between liberalism and orthodoxy lay in the future. As it was, Robert Breck became friends with his neighbor Stephen Williams and in 1741 was admitted to the Hampshire Association. Not until another decade had passed, and in a wholly different setting, did Edwards raise the issue of qualifications for church membership.

#### Congregationalism and the Gathered Church

In February 1749, Edwards informed the Northampton congregation that he would admit to full communion only those he judged "in profession, and in the eye of the church's Christian judgment, godly or gracious persons."[^003-note36] This announcement touched off an emotional and political earthquake. Contemporaries described the church members as "transported into an uncommon Degree of Rage and Madness," and the man who was responsible for this reaction "perceived so great a ferment in the town" that he delayed preaching on the topic.[^003-note37] Moving quickly and acting almost as one, the church and the town told Edwards bluntly that, unless he recanted, he was betraying his ministry and would be asked to resign. Here is not the place to recount the

<!-- p. 18 -->

successive councils that met in Northampton or the prolonged negotiations that preceded them, most of which Edwards described in a text that follows.[^003-note38] The relevant events are these: after telling the church of his decision, Edwards wrote *An Humble Inquiry* in the spring of 1749; printed books reached Northampton in the fall. In February and March 1750, he explained his thinking in five public lectures. By a bare majority, a council of ministers and lay delegates that met in June concluded that Edwards and his congregation could not be reconciled. Thereupon the church members voted by an overwhelming majority (some two hundred for, twenty opposed) to dismiss him.[^003-note39] On July 2 he preached his *Farewell Sermon*.

All this while the townspeople had cast around for someone in the ministry to defend their position in writing. Solomon Williams, the minister of Lebanon, Connecticut, met their needs with *The True State of the Question*, published in May 1751. Edwards, who by this time was living in Stockbridge, replied in *Misrepresentations Corrected* (1752). He never spoke out again on the issue, but others did, in an exchange of publications that lasted into the nineteenth century.

The issue that aroused Edwards, the townspeople, and Solomon Williams in the middle of the eighteenth century had been of critical importance to the founders of the New England Way in the seventeenth century and almost as important to Protestant reformers in the century of the Reformation, especially those who came to be known as Puritans in England. Its genesis may be traced to Augustine and his controversy with the Donatists. But though Edwards knew something of these contexts, the one that really mattered to him was much closer in time and place. No less a person than his grandfather Solomon Stoddard, the man whom he succeeded in the ministry of Northampton, was the principal advocate in New England for a broadly inclusive definition of church membership. Point by point, the *Humble Inquiry* takes up Stoddard's reasoning and rejects it.

But as the townspeople complained, and as Edwards himself acknowledged,

<!-- p. 19 -->

he had followed "Mr. Stoddard's Way" for most of his ministry and had not given any signs of discomfort with the system. That is, Edwards had been a Stoddardean by choice. To understand where he started from and, in light of this position, where he ended up, we must therefore return to Stoddard and the evolution of his thinking about the church. Here at once the whole of the New England Way—both in theory, as elaborated in treatises of the early decades and in the Cambridge Platform, and in practice, as modified over time and by the Synod of 1662–becomes relevant. So do certain debates among English Nonconformists, for Edwards and Stoddard were responding to men like Thomas Blake and Richard Baxter as well as to writers within the New England tradition.

In general Puritans expected the church to consist of a body of true Christians. From the very outset of the Puritan movement in England, its leaders struggled to transform the state church into such a body. For them the existing Church of England was a "mixt multitude," an ungainly mass of people, many of whom ignored the "duties" of the moral life. "Discipline" would be the means of shaping this mixt multitude into a more vital and observant Christian community. Behind this program lay a complex symbolism taken from the Bible. As the historian John Coolidge has observed, Elizabethan Puritans drew on Paul's letter to the Ephesians in describing the church as a house of which Christ was the cornerstone. This symbolism enforced an exclusiveness: not everyone, but only those who participated in the life of the risen Christ and became "vital" or "living" stones, could be members of this "temple."[^003-note40]

The English reformers derived this vision of the church not only from Scripture, but also from Martin Bucer, John Calvin, and other leaders of the Rhineland reformation. Speaking of Calvin's understanding of the church, Ernst Troeltsch has remarked that "the Church is not merely an organ of salvation which provides the objective means of grace.…It ought rather at the same time to provide the means of sanctification; it ought to prove itself effective in the Christianizing of the community, by placing the whole range of life under the control of Christian regulations and Christian purposes." To make effective the element of sanctification, or the routinized pursuit of holiness, the Genevan reformer set up a system for reviewing

<!-- p. 20 -->

the moral conduct of persons who wished to participate in the sacrament of the Lord's Supper; under his system, the sacrament became "the occasion for the official inspection and purification of the congregation." He also emphasized the procedures of admonition and excommunication (that is, processes for rebuking and excluding the unworthy) as means of ridding the church of persons who seemed immoral or profane. Yet Calvin did not make personal or collective holiness a mark of the true church. Critical of the Anabaptists for their puristic zeal in seeking "a church besmirched with no blemish," he held fast to the Augustinian distinction between visible and invisible. Here on earth the church is unable to differentiate the elect from the reprobate; here "the church is at the same time mingled of good men and bad," as Christ indicated in the parable of the wheat and tares (Matthew 13:24-26). Imagining the visible church as a household in which believers progressed in faith, Calvin proposed that the preaching of the Word and the sacraments of baptism and the Lord's Supper had an objective status as means of grace to everyone. The Calvinist understanding of the church thus incorporated two distinctly different elements: the visible church as objectively constituted and comprehensive and as a special kind of ethical community.[^003-note41]

The clergy who became Puritans in Elizabethan England affirmed both parts of Calvin's doctrine, the church as means of grace to everyone and the church as disciplined community. But in the distinctive setting of a hierarchical and partially reformed Church of England, they gravitated toward a de facto voluntarism that worked against an inclusive, corporatist conception of the church. So it happened that zealous parish clergy fashioned special covenants between themselves and the "godly" who wished to withdraw from the mixt multitude. The many varieties of such local arrangements all had the same consequence,[^003-note42] namely, to increase the distance between the Reformed tradition and English Puritanism on the nature of the church. That distance is evident as early as the 1570s, when Thomas Cartwright, a

<!-- p. 21 -->

leading reformer, argued that although the state may require adults to attend the preaching of the Word, church membership itself was distinct from attendance and depended on demonstrating "profit" to a group of ministers. Those who passed this scrutiny would become regular members; those who failed could be dismissed. Cartwright also felt that no one should receive baptism or attend the Lord's Supper without satisfying the prior conditions of Christian knowledge and godly behavior. Meanwhile his contemporary John Field was describing the church as "a company or congregatione of the faythfull called and gathered out of the worlde by the preachinge of the Gospel." Only when we stop to ask why an English Presbyterian (as Field has traditionally been termed) sounded so much like a Congregationalist of the 1640s do we sense the drift into "voluntary" religion.[^003-note43]

This mixture of traditions—on the one hand, the Reformed system, on the other, the development of voluntarism—was conveyed to New England with the Puritan migration of the 1630s. By the end of that decade, the clergy and the more zealous of the colonists in New England had enhanced and formalized the voluntary aspects of the church. The New England Way began with the principle that the proper mode of church order was a system of congregations, each with an explicit covenant and a ministry elected by the male lay members, who shared the power of the keys to decide cases of church discipline. A more daring decision was to require adult candidates for church membership to describe in public their experience of the work of grace, the premise being that such a test would differentiate "visible saints" from counterfeits. In practice as in theory, the test of a "relation" worked to exclude a certain number of the colonists from church membership.[^003-note44]

We may regard the church history of New England for the next hundred years as a whole. During this century the clergy looked for ways of restoring a broader, more inclusive membership even as they continued to defend the principles of Congregationalism. Pressure for change had several sources. The Puritan community in England reacted at once, and for the most part critically, to the ecclesiology that

<!-- p. 22 -->

emerged in New England. English clergy warned that the insistence on explicit covenants implied that the Church of England was not a true church and that the test of a relation brought the colonists to the verge of abolishing the distinction between the visible and invisible churches. The Presbyterian Samuel Hudson was one of many critics in the mid-seventeenth century who insisted that "visible" was not to be confused with "actual" and who wondered if, in terming members of the church "visible saints," the colonists had merged these two categories.[^003-note45] Once the Civil War broke out in England and thrust Puritans into power, middle-of-the-road reformers were angered by the fact that Independents (some of whom had returned from New England) were organizing gathered congregations in their very midst. Writing in 1657, the minister Richard Baxter denounced the Independents who proposed that "it is only the Regenerate and such as shall be saved, that are to be added to the Church." In response, Baxter reasoned that "then we must admit none, becaus we know not one man to bee such." No group here on earth, Baxter affirmed, could differentiate the true saint from the apparent saint.[^003-note46]

Responsive to such critics, the New England clergy also had to deal with the divergence between practice and principle. From the side of practice the anomalies were mounting—of people left outside the gathered church and of baptized children who, once they reached adulthood, were having children of their own. What was the status of these baptized children turned adult? And did their children somehow come within the covenant? From the side of principle a barrage of English publications continually reminded the framers of the Cambridge Platform that the church was a means of grace to everyone. Baptists in England and New England, though few in number, spoke against this doctrine.

When the New England clergy met in Cambridge in 1646 and 1648 to draft a platform, they were seeking some way of acknowledging their critics but also of reaffirming the ideal of gathered congregations limited to godly people. Taking heed of contradictory signals, the Cambridge synod embarked on a process of accommodation that was resumed at the synods of 1662 and 1679. Debate among the clergy was not confined to these meetings. The Synod of 1662 and its decision

<!-- p. 23 -->

to affirm the halfway covenant prompted a cluster of publications.[^003-note47] So did the emergence of Baptists, who in 1665 organized a congregation linking Charlestown and Boston. At the end of the century the founding of the Brattle Street Church, which did without a covenant and laid aside the requirement of a relation of spiritual experience, stirred up further controversy. Certain clergy played a leading role in articulating a compromise that reaffirmed the "first principles" of New England while acknowledging important changes. One such person was Jonathan Mitchel, minister of the Cambridge church. The two Mathers, Increase and Cotton, took up where he left off.

The affirmations that emerged from synods and statements by these clergy were as follows:

1. Describing, in the Cambridge Platform, the matter of the visible gathered church as "*Saints* by calling" and insisting that prospective members "ought to be *examined & tryed* first," the framers of the Platform asserted that "a personall & publick *confession*, & declaring of Gods manner of working upon the soul, is both lawfull, expedient, & usefull." This language meant that gathered churches were entitled to ask candidates for membership to make a relation of the work of grace, or conversion, as well as offering a "confession" of doctrinal knowledge. Presumably, no one could enter as an adult without having experienced the work of grace.[^003-note48]

2. The Platform emphasized, however, that "the weakest *measure* of faith is to be accepted in those that desire to be admitted into the church: becaus weak christians if *sincere*, have the *substance* of that faith, repentance & holiness which is required…& such have most *need* of the ordinances for their confirmation & growth in grace." In the literature leading up to the Platform and in its aftermath, the ministers declared that in scrutinizing candidates they exercised the "judgment of charity," a phrase that enabled them to acknowledge uncertainty and to accept the appearance of faith. In the same breath the ministers acknowledged that their congregations included many who were "hypocrites."[^003-note49] Indeed, in a passage others after him sometimes quoted, John Cotton averred that "it were better to admit diverse

<!-- p. 24 -->

Hypocrites then to keep out one sincere Child of God from coming into the Church."[^003-note50]

3. The children of those admitted as members were to be included in the church covenant and baptized.[^003-note51]

4. Once these children became adults (or in the language of the time, children of the church), they were to remain as members even though they failed to make a relation of spiritual experience.

5. In turn the children of *these* members were considered to be in covenant and therefore entitled to its benefits, the sacrament of baptism and the "watch" of the church.

Propositions 4 and 5 were controversial. Defending them, Jonathan Mitchel, Richard Mather, Thomas Shepard (1605–49), and his son Thomas Shepard II (1635–77) reasoned that the scope of baptism under the New Testament duplicated the scope of circumcision under the Old. According to their reading of the Old Testament, an entire nation participated in the covenant even though "many of them were not sincerely godly" or "were never of the *invisible* church."[^003-note52] Proposing that baptism be as generously inclusive and that it not be based on prior evidence of repentance and faith, these clergy differentiated two kinds of holiness and two kinds of covenants: real holiness and the covenant of grace, on the one hand, and "federal holiness" and the "external covenant" on the other. The basis of *federal*- or *covenant-holiness* was, quite simply, the "covenant-relation" into which children entered through their parents. In effect, the ministers were arguing that God manifested the covenant of grace through an "external dispensation," the visible church and its covenant. To be sure, the parents who claimed the privilege of the external covenant for their children had to meet certain conditions: they must "understand the doctrine of Faith, publickly profess their assent thereto," and not be "scandalous

<!-- p. 25 -->

in life." By meeting these conditions the parents established themselves as "Confederate visible Believers, though but in the lowest degree such."[^003-note53] As here, so in succeeding passages the language of the Synod of 1662 was full of equivocations: the "parents…are confederate visible Believers, at least in some degree"; "this sort of persons showing nothing to the contrary, are in charity…visible Believers"; they had "Faith and Repentance" simply by virtue of being in the church, and as long as "they do not reject it." The reasoning was very nearly tautological: the external covenant produced benefits that qualified the halfway members and their children to remain within it.[^003-note54]

In response to the Baptists, who rejected the typological fusion of Old Testament and New, the clergy turned increasingly to another argument, that children of the church, although members only in external covenant, were more likely to be saved than if they remained unbaptized. To exclude them was to hasten their degeneracy. To include them was to make use of the church as a "school" or "garden" in which they were nurtured. Granting that all of those in outward covenant were not inwardly elect, Thomas Shepard the elder insisted nonetheless that those within this covenant were a "special people unto God":

> He will prune, and cutt, and dresse, and water them…; nay…he will take away this refuseing heart from among them indefinitely, so that though every one cannot assure himself, that he will do it particularly for this or that person, yet every one, through this promise, may hope, and pray for the communication of this grace, and so feel it in time.[^003-note55]

In yet another version of this argument, the ministers emphasized the many good qualities and advantages of children of the church—"the good Effects of a pious Education," the time they spent "under the Means of Grace," their "Profession of the Faith, not contradicted by any thing scandalous in their Life." Essentially, this was to reason that membership within the external covenant was a *positive* event, with benefits to follow; to those of this status, Increase Mather declared, God will "infallibly make them the offer of his covenant [^003-note56]." This way of thinking culminated in Mather's assertion that God had

<!-- p. 26 -->

"cast the line of Election" so that it ran in part "through the loyns of godly parents."[^003-note57]

6. But if the "seed" of the covenant could receive baptism and be subject to church discipline, the only persons admitted to the sacrament of the Lord's Supper were members in "full communion," or those who qualified in the old way. The ideal of purity was transposed, therefore, to this sacrament.

Since it was access to this sacrament that was ostensibly the issue in the Northampton controversy, it is important to review how the clergy who preceded Jonathan Edwards understood the Lord's Supper, and on what grounds they restricted full church membership to "saints by calling."

The meaning of the Lord's Supper within the Congregational tradition was consequent upon the doctrines of the church covenant and the covenant of grace. The sacrament had little independent meaning of its own, functioning instead as a sign or seal of prior actions—that is, of entering into each of these two covenants. In this regard the sacramental theology of the colonists allowed for little or no emphasis on the elements themselves or for the real presence.[^003-note58] Yet in writing about the sacrament in manuals of devotion, English reformers in the first half of the seventeenth century had more to say about spiritual preparation for the Lord's Supper than about any other aspect of personal and collective religion. At great length, these reformers made the point that the Lord's Supper was only for persons who, beforehand, engaged in stringent self-examination and repentance for sin. These writers warned that communicants must feel themselves to be truly of the faithful. The more elemental message was that no one could come to the Lord's Supper who was spiritually unclean. In support of this taboo, these clergy pointed to 1 Corinthians 11:27-29:

> Wherefore whosoever shall eat this bread, and drink this cup of the Lord, unworthily, shall be guilty of the body and blood of the Lord. But let a man examine himself, and so let him eat of that bread, and drink of that cup. For he that eateth and drinketh unworthily,

<!-- p. 27 -->

   eateth and drinketh damnation to himself, not discerning the Lord's body.

Citing these verses time and again, English writers assumed that their horrific message would protect the Lord's Supper from the mixt multitude that filled the Church of England. Who would dare participate except those assured of being spiritually renewed?[^003-note59]

The ministers who came to New England reiterated this understanding of the sacrament despite having put in place other means of excluding the unworthy from church membership. But in later years, as they moved toward more inclusive baptism, the sanctity of the Lord's Table took on a fresh importance. To this sacrament, they insisted, only those could come who knew the experience of the work of grace, had "actual" knowledge of Christ, and manifested their inward state in the "fruits" of the Spirit. The men and women who met these conditions were "full" church members, as contrasted with the children of the church who were limited to the sacrament of baptism. The Synod of 1662, which reaffirmed the legitimacy of these children, went on declare that the Lord's Supper remained closed to all but those who were visible saints.[^003-note60]

The thinking of Jonathan Mitchel of Cambridge, chief author of this "middle way" between "extreames," is revealed in a document that Cotton Mather included in his biography of Mitchel. Having brought himself to favor the halfway covenant, Mitchel felt it all the more important "to plead for the Holiness" of the gathered church "by Requiring further Degrees of Preparation, in those that they received unto the Supper of the Lord." Citing 1 Corinthians 11:28-29, he argued that "Worthy Receivers" must "Examine themselves, and Discern the Lord's Body." Though he used the word "charity" four times in a single sentence, the thrust of the conditions he outlined was that visible saints must in some manner manifest "a Work of grace." Echoing a long exegetical tradition, he cited the three thousand Peter baptized, on the condition of their "conversion" (Acts 2). And he warned of the "Formality and Deadness" that would follow should the churches admit persons to the Lord's Supper who had "only Doctrinal Knowledge, and Outward Blamelessness."[^003-note61]

<!-- p. 28 -->

Mitchel consciously positioned himself between strictness and laxity. So too he sought a compromise formation that encompassed both "grace" and "holiness" in the church—the former via a more generous policy of baptism, the latter via restricting the Lord's Supper to visible saints. Compromise imposed itself not only upon Mitchel but upon most of his fellow clergy. Valuing the purity of the gathered church and worried lest the profane enter it in such numbers as to gain control of church discipline, they also realized that to exclude everyone who could not meet the test of a relation would drastically diminish the size of their congregations.[^003-note62] Moreover, it would mean rejecting as not adequately Christian thousands of people who seemed decently behaved and who knew their catechisms. So it happened that, by the close of the seventeenth century, most of the clergy rationalized their situation.

Increase and Cotton Mather reaffirmed the legitimacy of this middle way in a series of books they wrote in response to its critics, chief among them Solomon Stoddard.[^003-note63] The arguments they used were much the same as those Mitchel had employed. The two Mathers were already on record as defenders of the halfway covenant. Yet they continued to insist that the visible church was a particular gathered body consisting of "Saints and true Believers" and that "none but such as are (so far as men exercising a due Charity are able to judge) Sincere Converts, or True Believers on Christ, ought to be received into the Churches." Citing the eunuch that Philip baptized after having heard him affirm, "I believe that Jesus Christ is the Son of God" (Acts 8:37), Increase reasoned that the church was entitled to ask its members "whether they have truly Repented of their Sins, and whether they truly Believe on Christ" and to restrict the Lord's Supper to those who, according to this testimony, were "Regenerate persons."[^003-note64]

Increase retreated from this argument the instant he had made it. Calling on the churches to use "tenderness and Charity," he conceded

<!-- p. 29 -->

(quoting John Cotton) that "it were better…to admit diverse Hypocrites then to keep out one Sincere Child of God" and spoke of the "Unregenerate" as qualifying for the sacrament because in "Outward appearance" they resembled the saints. Taking up the objection that his view of the church required ordinary Christians to achieve assurance of salvation, which they rarely did, he answered that assurance was not really necessary before someone ventured to the Lord's Table. Candidates needed only "a probable hope of Regeneration," a hope would-be saints could strengthen by participating in the sacrament. Mather's middle way allowed him to sanction admitting "the weakest Christians" so long as they were "Sincere." Notwithstanding these many qualifications, the two Mathers continued to insist that "Profane Persons" must not be allowed into the church, at least not as a matter of explicit policy.[^003-note65]

The two Mathers were aware that English Nonconformists had continued to debate these same issues. In general, English Presbyterians remained unsympathetic to the concept of the gathered church and therefore to any emphasis on limiting membership to the holy. Presbyterians viewed the church as "catholic visible," the church covenant as unnecessary, and membership as requiring only knowledge of doctrine and "moral sincerity." An important advocate for this point of view was Thomas Blake (1597?–1657), minister of Tarnworth, Staffordshire, who affiliated with the Presbyterian party during the period of the English Civil War. He entered the lists against two groups, the Baptists for denying infant baptism and any and all others (including English Independents and New England Congregationalists) who regarded the church covenant as restricted to the elect. Blake argued at great length in *Vindiciæ Fœderis; or, A Treatise of the Covenant* that since the covenant was unchanged in its scope from the Jewish to the Christian dispensation, the church under the New Testament was no less comprehensive than under the Old, when the "seed" of members were included in the covenant and the "unregenerate" were also welcome. Differentiating the external covenant from the internal, he insisted that the former encompassed unregenerate people. For him it did not matter that the church on earth contained many who were impure. The alternative, he reasoned, was complete paralysis: since no

<!-- p. 30 -->

one except Christ knew who was truly regenerate, a church that adopted such a rule could not admit or baptize anyone. Instead of imposing the conditions of faith and repentance prior to membership or baptism, Blake regarded them as consequent to these steps. Turning to the Bible, he interpreted the baptism of the three thousand as occurring *without* any knowledge on the part of Peter of repentance and faith. And these conditions did not figure in Philip's baptism of the eunuch or in the parables of the wedding feast (Matthew 22:2) and the wheat and tares. Blake made a further distinction between "dogmaticall" or "historical faith," which was the most that any church could require, and "justifying faith," which was known only to God. From his point of view the visible saint was someone quite likely to be unregenerate, though this same person had historical faith and wanted church membership for his or her seed.[^003-note66]

Richard Baxter, parish minister of Kidderminster and a man who refused to affiliate with any ecclesiastical party, did not fully agree. Like his near-contemporary Jonathan Mitchel, Baxter wanted a middle way between extremes. Though he favored limiting the church to "Regenerate Believers," he detested the Independents who unchurched so many English people and applied to their policy of restricted baptism a line of reasoning similar to Blake's: if in saying that "onely the Regenerate…are to be added to the Church…they mean onely such as are Really sanctified and sincere, or elect, then wee must admit none, becaus wee know not one man to bee such." When it came to admission to the Lord's Supper, Baxter shifted ground, however, and called for limiting that sacrament to regenerate believers. The trick was to define regenerate believers in a way that took account of sincerity and a "profession of true Christian saving faith," but that also acknowledged the likelihood of hypocrisy and the near-impossibility of achieving "full Assurance." Baxter resolved this problem by proposing that ministers and congregations accept the evidence of "Profession" and not seek to know what lies beyond a verbal statement.[^003-note67]

This assertion carried Baxter to the edge of a linguistic maze, the relation between a sign and what it signified. That relation had to concern everyone who relied on the evidence of a verbal profession or behavior or both in deciding whether a candidate for membership was

<!-- p. 31 -->

a visible saint. What did such outward actions signify of the inward heart or self? The ministers who asked these questions were quite aware that hypocrites could feign the real thing. Experience had taught them that verbal statements were deceptive, for candidates could repeat formulas learned from others. Moreover, a theological argument intruded: no one but God could know for sure "the heart of the Professor." For Baxter, the only way around these difficulties was to insist that in most cases, if not invariably, outward signs were sufficient evidence of inward circumstances:

> If they did by word of mouth say, that they believe with a saving Faith, these words are but signs of their minds; and whether counterfeit or not, the Church cannot tell.…Therefore the Church must not take the external Sacrament for a Nullity, every time a mans secret Intentions agree not with his signal Profession; for then we should not know whether ever we baptize any one.

Ever seeking compromise formations, Baxter asserted over and over again three points: we must demand evidence of grace; in doing so we are limited to signs; and we must regard signs, however outward, as signifying what they seem to be about.[^003-note68]

The debate between Baxter and Blake was representative of scores of such exchanges in the seventeenth century. In the course of these debates and discussions on both sides of the Atlantic the term "visible saint" became increasingly elastic. The same term could mean that visible saints (1) approximated being real saints or (2) were "morally sincere," though perhaps without saving grace, or (3) were often hypocrites even though the requirements for becoming a church member included the test of a relation. Logical and verbal precision foundered on the inevitable necessity of making distinctions, the fundamental impasse being the difference between visible and invisible, or the external and internal covenants. The drift of thinking in Nonconformist and New England circles was undoubtedly to grant more credence to a multitude of outward signs, some of them possibly denoting sanctification, without attempting to specify their relation to the inward workings of the Holy Spirit. The drift in practice was undoubtedly to broaden access to baptism while attempting to reserve the Lord's Supper for persons who (by whatever standard or evidence) were regarded as regenerate.

<!-- p. 32 -->

Well into the eighteenth century most of the New England clergy remained of several moods about the church. The interplay of these moods is revealed in a document originating in the Northampton controversy, a letter by Peter Clark, minister of Salem Village, to the laity of Northampton turning down their request that he answer the *Humble Inquiry*. Clark had been tempted to do so, for Edwards' scheme (which he knew about from rumors) seemed to "take away that commonly received and well-grounded distinction of the church into visible and invisible." It was "absurd" for anyone to suppose that he or she could discern "the state of men's hearts," and in any case the instituted church was designed to "consist of a mixture of good and bad, sound and unsound Christians, till the great day of discrimination." Yet Clark believed that members of the visible church should possess "visible saintship," and, in contrast to Solomon Stoddard, he required a "gospel profession" of those who wished to participate in the Lord's Supper. In the same breath he spoke as though he were Blake or Baxter, calling on his fellow ministers to accept "no higher evidence…of sincerity than such a profession" and warning that many who passed as visible saints "are really and in heart unconverted."[^003-note69] Moving first in one direction, then in another, Clark attempted to achieve a balance of conflicting values. In this regard he was representative of the Congregational tradition as it stabilized in the closing decades of the seventeenth century.

The voice of those who defended this tradition was often charged with equivocation, for they worried that formality and declension may have begun with their very decision to loosen the boundaries of the church covenant.[^003-note70] Privately, a handful of ministers continued to rhapsodize about the pure church.[^003-note71] But most of the clergy realized that the new system was a means of reconciling two contrary principles: a gathered church made up of living stones transformed by grace and the church as ordained means of grace (a school) that included hypocrites along with weak and doubtful Christians. We can characterize them as reluctant supporters of the gathered church-cum-halfway covenant: it was nothing glorious, but the alternatives were worse.

<!-- p. 33 -->

During these same decades of controversy and compromise, the clergy in England and New England were occupied with describing the work of grace, or how it was that election became "actual" in the lives of the saints. It is a truism (which happens to be true) that, from William Perkins onward, one wing of English Protestantism adopted a pietistic or "experimental" understanding of the doctrine of predestination. This way of thinking flowed from the premise that the saints would realize their election via certain forms of spiritual experiences. The basic model involved a three-stage process. The initial experience was achieving a "true sight of sin," or a recognition of one's utter worthlessness in the sight of God. This stage was commonly described as being accomplished by (or under) the "law." Then came a stage of affective response to Christ, a reaching out in faith to take hold of the promise of salvation he offered the repentant. Thereafter, the work of grace consisted of "evangelical" obedience to the law, or a heartfelt commitment to achieving holiness. The process of sanctification (to use the formal name for it) entailed a never-ending struggle against sin. Even as the saint progressed toward the eternal kingdom, he or she repeatedly experienced the cycle of repentance, cleansing, and renewal.

As the history of evangelical Calvinism amply displays, this model of the spiritual life was paradoxical in one key respect. The ministers who taught it, and the men and women who sought to live by its prescriptions, assumed that the saint was differentiated from the hypocrite or reprobate. The line between the two was absolute, and a veritable mountain of sermons and devotional manuals informed the reader (or listener) how to find out in which camp he or she stood—books that signaled in their very titles the radical difference between *The Sincere Convert* or *The Real Christian* and the hypocrite. Yet in practice, and even in theory, the difference became blurred. Evangelical ministers complained that people who merely pretended to be Christians were often taken for the real thing. Moreover, every theorist conceded that election was a mystery that would be resolved only at the end of time. Here on earth, as contrasted with the kingdom of God, the separation of the precious and the vile could never be complete or perfect.

The paradox of knowing and not knowing had a further dimension. Lay men and women expected to achieve assurance of salvation but instead were "often put to sad doubts of their own Estate." The sources suggest that such "weak believers," or those who failed to achieve "peace" and "comfort," became a major problem for the clergy. In

<!-- p. 34 -->

response, the ministers acknowledged that assurance could wax and wane and emphasized the possibility of gaining it from sanctification, or the practice of godly duties. This evidence was admittedly a sign of something else; it was consequent upon the work of grace and required reasoning along the lines of the "practical syllogism"—"he that repenteth and believeth the Gospel shall be saved; But I repent and believe the Gospel; Therefore I shall be saved"—that some theologians, including Calvin, found distasteful.[^003-note72] The problem of assurance thus opened up the possibility that the saints were not easily differentiated from hypocrites if the difference between them lay in outward signs or statements, for these could be convincingly imitated.

The nexus between church membership and spiritual experience added yet another layer of complications. That nexus was forged in New England in the 1630s when most of the clergy agreed to require candidates for church membership to make a relation of spiritual experience—in effect, to describe the work of grace and how it had transformed them into saints. Almost immediately, however, the ministers had to backtrack. We have traced how their commitment to infant baptism and the federal covenant forced them to acknowledge that church members were of two different kinds, some being of the elect and within the covenant of grace and others merely within the federal covenant. They arrived at more or less the same point via a different road, their critique of a radical spiritism, the "antinomianism" that emerged suddenly in Massachusetts in 1636 and 1637 and again in England in the 1640s. The antinomians grounded assurance of salvation on the direct "witness of the Holy Spirit," rejected the practical syllogism as tantamount to works-righteousness, and argued that the saints could infallibly differentiate the true believer from the hypocrite.[^003-note73] Opposing this purism, the ministers declared that the Holy Spirit worked through means or an objective order, insisted that the way to grace and assurance of salvation lay ordinarily through such means as the sacraments of the church and the duties of the Christian life, reasoned that everyone, elect or not, was summoned to make use of these means, and represented sanctification as providing reliable evidence of justification. No minister said that attendance on the

<!-- p. 35 -->

means guaranteed the reception of saving grace. But in contrast to antinomianism their way of thinking preserved a broad understanding of church membership and sustained the moral obligations of the Christian life as incumbent on everyone.[^003-note74]

Here then was the ultimate version of the paradox: on the one hand the doctrine of election and its practical corollary, that Christians underwent a work of grace which enabled them to know if they were saved; on the other, the imperative of baptism, entering into the disciplinary watch of the church and relying on a routinized holiness for assurance of salvation. The outcome was a kind of double speak among the clergy.[^003-note75] From the generation of Thomas Shepard and John Cotton to that of Jonathan Edwards and Solomon Williams, they summoned sinners and hypocrites to undergo conversion, lamented formality, and represented the church as the home of those who became living stones. In the same breath they extolled the benefits of duties, emphasized objective or external signs, and acknowledged that the church must always contain hypocrites who passed as visible saints.

This mixture of messages was vulnerable to criticism, and it left even those who made use of it feeling uneasy. Jonathan Edwards inherited this uneasiness, just as he also inherited the long-standing uneasiness about the halfway covenant. He had also to deal with antinomianism—not the 1630s variety but that which emerged out of the Great Awakening. Two other structures of thinking affected him. He had to reckon with popular religion, or the ways in which the laity of his congregation understood the nature of the church and its sacraments. What may have weighed as much upon him was the thinking of his predecessor in Northampton, Solomon Stoddard. Stoddard labored throughout his ministry to overcome the contradiction between piety and institutional practice. His grandson would seek to overcome these same contradictions, but by a different route.

#### Lay and Clerical Religion

Lay men and women in New England approached church membership and the two sacraments of baptism and the Lord's Supper in their own fashion, though how they acted and felt was substantially influenced

<!-- p. 36 -->
