by the ministers.[^003-note76] In those towns of which we have detailed knowledge of church membership, the main pattern seems to be that many people in the first generation became members—not at once when small groups of males participated in the founding of congregations, but soon thereafter.[^003-note77] In some communities, however, substantial numbers either did not come into the church or were kept from having their children baptized. By the third quarter of the century a series of compromises or shifts in policy—whether local variations on the halfway covenant or that policy itself—worked to make church membership more inclusive.[^003-note78] But as more people gained access to baptism, the number of members in "full communion" steadily decreased. Any generalization is hazardous, but at the time of the Great Awakening the ratio of baptized (or halfway) members to full members encompassed a range that, at one extreme, approached ten to one.[^003-note79] Another relevant pattern is the time of life that halfway members chose to renew their covenants or that persons outside the church asked for membership or that those in halfway membership advanced to full. In general these moments coincided with forming a family and beginning to have children. The layman Samuel Sewall was typical in waiting to apply for full membership (he was already in covenant as a child of the church) until he had married and his wife was expecting.[^003-note80]

<!-- p. 37 -->

These rhythms of affiliation and participation signify that lay people understood the two sacraments quite differently. Parents valued baptism for their children. They accepted the ministers' reasoning (or the ministers accepted theirs) that children within the covenant were better off because of being less threatened by the devil, more likely to obtain saving grace, and more apt to survive. Family preservation, the fundamental goal of the property inheritance system, was equally the goal of those who brought their newborn children to the church almost immediately. These people thought of the church as a place of nurture, a source of preservation and protection for the family. Yet the church was also a place where protection was intermingled with judgment and danger. Lay men and women regarded the Lord's Supper as encircled with this double message. Accordingly, they reasoned that they should not approach the sacrament unless they were assured of God's love for them.[^003-note81] On the eve of the Great Awakening, a minister confided in his diary that "the people…want to know they shall be sure they believe, that they love God, that they are in the right way."[^003-note82] Lacking such assurance, and too scrupulous to feign conversion,[^003-note83] such people harkened to the powerful warning of 1 Corinthians 11:27-28. "They have drunk in an opinion, that none but Converted Persons should come to that Ordinance, and so they neglect it," another minister observed in 1707.[^003-note84] He might have added that most of these people continued to value the ideal of the gathered church, though not at the expense of foregoing infant baptism.

For the most part, ministers in seventeenth- and eighteenth-century New England were unable to alter these patterns of behavior and the values from which they emerged. Year after year, decade after decade,

<!-- p. 38 -->

the ministers argued with their congregations and complained out loud about these attitudes. "The so general a neglect [^003-note85]…hath been both a wonder, and grief of heart to me, almost ever since I have been in the Ministry," Benjamin Wadsworth of Boston wrote in 1724.[^003-note86] It was not for want of trying that Wadsworth and others like him failed. Two strategies became common in the early decades of the eighteenth century, a milder, more generous reading of 1 Corinthians 11 and the argument that abstaining from the sacrament was more dangerous than partaking of it.[^003-note87] Yet the impasse lingered, for lay people continued to differentiate between baptism and the Lord's Supper. To be sure, the Great Awakening swept into full membership many who had hesitated for want of adequate assurance. But as was often noted in reports of local revivals, other people, "though brought to very hopeful dispositions…were through fear and darkness kept from entering into full communion."[^003-note88] Nothing seemed to alter this reluctance—not the revival or the encouraging gestures of the clergy and, as we will see, not even Stoddardeanism.

The behavior of lay people should make us wary of Sereno Dwight's hypothesis that in the decades after 1662 the churches were filling up with lax Christians. True, the structure of the gathered church was altered in response to the deeply felt need among lay men and women for access to baptism. Yet these same lay members continued to manifest a scrupulosity about coming to the Lord's Supper. They were like the ministers in bringing to the church a mixture of values. In their own fashion, they resolved the contradiction between scrupulosity and inclusiveness by differentiating between baptism and the Lord's Supper. This way of thinking and these patterns do not warrant being termed declension. Nor is this an epithet that applies to Solomon Stoddard and Stoddardeanism.

#### Solomon Stoddard and Stoddardeanism

Solomon Stoddard was the second minister in Northampton. Three years prior to his ordination in 1672, the congregation had voted to adopt the halfway covenant, though the first such members were admitted only after he began his ministry. Above all else, Stoddard was to

<!-- p. 39 -->

prove himself an evangelical preacher who regarded stringent preaching inversion as the one sure way of overcoming the formality that seemed to characterize so many of the colonists.[^003-note89]

Yet in his parish, as in so many others, the baptized adults were reluctant to advance to the Lord's Table. In this situation lay the origins of Stoddardeanism. Worrying over "his responsibilities to the unconverted in Northampton" and recognizing that "the half-way compromise had failed to meet their needs, he began to speak…for what he believed was a more workable solution."[^003-note90] Thinking further about lay religion, Stoddard came to feel that unnecessary scruples about assurance of salvation stood in the way of attendance at the Lord's Supper. He traced this scrupulosity to the requirement of a relation of the work of grace, a requirement, he declared in 1690, that "discourages many good Christians from seeking Full Communion." Moreover, he shared the perception of his fellow clergy that the prospect of participating in the Lord's Supper was torment to these people because they worried so intensely about 1 Corinthians 11:27-29. "This Scripture," he lamented in *An Appeal to the Learned*, "being a stumbling-block to many, it is meet it should be more fully considered." More generally, he understood that lay people were caught in the logical trap of expecting that they should possess a "certain knowledge of their spiritual state," even though this very knowledge lay beyond their reach. He started, therefore, from a pastoral situation, the scruples of his parishioners concerning a requirement (or an ethos) that "scared them out of Religion."[^003-note91]

Unrelentingly skeptical that the visible church could differentiate true saints from hypocrites, Stoddard called on the New England churches to eliminate regeneration, however understood or measured, as the threshold for admission to the sacraments. He knew that other ministers hoped to break the impasse by telling their congregations that the "smallest measure" or "probable hope" of saving faith would qualify them for coming to the Lord's Supper. The same ministers liked to argue that uncertainty of assurance was a sign of spiritual

<!-- p. 40 -->

health.[^003-note92] But from Stoddard's point of view it was false encouragement to tell people that a little bit of faith would do. Such advice got in the way of conversion.[^003-note93] As the historian E. Brooks Holifield was perhaps the first to realize, Stoddard was "criticizing the laxity, as well as the rigor, of prevailing New England practices."[^003-note94] Rather than welcome a weak degree of faith, as the Mathers did, he reasoned it was better to do away with the distinction between baptism and the Lord's Supper and allow everyone admitted to the first to participate in the second, whereupon the full message of evangelism could come home to them.

Stoddard's was a simple remedy to a messy theological and pastoral situation. He reasoned that the church contained but one kind of visible saint, that is, someone admitted to every duty, including both of the sacraments. Defending this conception of visible saint, Stoddard insisted that the church was unable to differentiate true saints from hypocrites; what "certain Rule," he asked, was there to use in making this distinction? Granted, congregations should exclude heathens and the profane and require moral sincerity of their members. But the church could go no further. Visible saints were simply those who "make a Solemn Profession of Faith, & Repentance, & are of Godly Conversation, having Knowledge to Examine themselves, & discern the Lords Body." If he reiterated familiar words, their meaning was different. For Stoddard, a "Profession of Faith" involved "Historical," not "Saving Faith" and was unrelated to the work of grace or assurance of salvation. The "visible" in "visible saints" was similarly disconnected from "Sanctifying grace," as was the term "sincere." It was important, Stoddard argued, not to exclude the "Unregenerate" so long as there was any hope of their being saints. He acknowledged, therefore, that many whom he was willing to term visible saints were unconverted or hypocrites.[^003-note95]

Stoddard presented some of these ideas at the Synod of 1679 and repeated them in sermons he delivered in Northampton in the 1680s. Not until the early eighteenth century did he publish his opinions in

<!-- p. 41 -->

three overlapping manifestos directed against the Mathers: *The Doctrine of Instituted Churches* (1700), *The Inexcusableness of Neglecting the Worship of God* (1708), and *An Appeal to the Learned* (1709). By this time he had a broader case to make against Congregational practices and principles. Critical of the Cambridge Platform, he asked for more authority for the ministry, including greater control over the procedure for admitting members. Historians have sometimes confused Stoddard's political agenda, which in essence was to make the New England church system more presbyterian, with his pastoral mission to ease the tensions that encircled the Lord's Table. But the two were largely unrelated. He did learn much from certain English Presbyterians and Erastians—Thomas Blake, William Prynne, John Humfrey, and John Timson.[^003-note96] The last three of these writers had advocated a sacramental understanding of the Lord's Supper, attributing to it the power of being a "converting ordinance" or means of grace in its own right. Though not fully acquiescing, Stoddard turned this sacramentalism into a further reason for admitting everyone to the sacrament. Blake played a role in persuading Stoddard that the doctrine of a "particular covenant," another of the root ideas of Congregationalism, was "unscriptural" (the Northampton minister complained that this doctrine was "the reason why many among us are shut out of the Church") and in supporting his conception of the instituted church as a place where the issue of election was irrelevant.[^003-note97]

Like every controversialist of the period, Stoddard invoked Scripture in defending his interpretation of visible saints and their privileges. He argued that the parable of the wedding garment referred to the final judgment and not to the Lord's Supper. Peter could not have inquired beforehand into the qualifications of the three thousand he baptized. Judas had participated in the Passover feast and then in the very first administration of the Lord's Supper; therefore Christ had not been concerned to search the hearts of those who were present. Stoddard denied that the word "examine" in 1 Corinthians 11:28 meant examine for the "truth of grace." The typological symmetry between the Old Testament and the New signified that the church should be national under the gospel.[^003-note98]

<!-- p. 42 -->

These expectations and policies spread to other congregations, some of which may have set aside or modified the requirement of a relation before Stoddard began to attack the practice. It is often suggested that Stoddard acted as a veritable pope in the Connecticut River valley and that other clergy were swayed by the force of his personality and perhaps by the example of his success as an evangelical minister to fall in with his way of thinking.[^003-note99] In point of fact few if any clergy appropriated the concept of the Lord's Supper as a converting ordinance. But by the 1720s many of the younger ministers in New England agreed with him that exclusionary policies regarding baptism and the Lord's Supper hindered the progress of evangelism. Like Stoddard, these clergy were Calvinist in their theology, evangelical in their preaching, and inclusive in their understanding of the church.

Central makers of the evangelical and Stoddardean program were the Williams clan: the brothers John Williams of Deerfield and William Williams of Hatfield and their four minister sons. These clergy joined with many others in favoring a more objective, sacerdotal, and inclusive church as policies that assisted their evangelism.[^003-note100] Facing a host of practical difficulties that included local Baptists and the persistent refusal of parishioners to attend the Lord's Supper, they embraced the argument that the federal or external covenant functioned as a means of grace to all who came within it. They buttressed this argument with the assumption, drawn from Blake and others, that the visible church under the dispensation of the gospel was continuous with the church of the Jews. In the one as in the other the condition of access to the covenant was profession, not repentance or true piety. And in both the seed of the covenant were fully entitled to the privileges of the church.[^003-note101]

William Williams, who made the case for the seed against the Baptists, knew from firsthand pastoral experience that people were avoiding the Lord's Supper. "Yet how many are there [^003-note102]," he told his

<!-- p. 43 -->

congregation in 1707, "who live from year to year in the neglect of it? Pretending a want of Preparation, and a fear of polluting and profaning it." He argued the benefits of a different understanding of the church in private reflections he penned in 1693 and again in 1727 in defending the doctrine of infant baptism. It is characteristic of his thinking that he read the parable of the wheat and the tares as signifying that the two were inevitably mingled in the visible church; reiterating the most important point in Stoddardeanism, he concluded from the parable that the visible church had no sure means of discerning the experience of conversion. It was crucial, moreover, that everyone participate in the Lord's Supper and that children be baptized, for the sacraments were means of grace.[^003-note103]

A historiography that equates Stoddardeanism with declension is a historiography that fails utterly to account for the record of the Williamses as evangelical promoters of heart-searching religion and as major actors in the Great Awakening. And that historiography does not acknowledge the origins and consequences of Solomon Stoddard's ecclesiastical program, much less his career as an evangelical Calvinist or the appeal of his thinking to persons who, like the Williamses and many others, were responding to a specific pastoral situation, a spiritual paralysis among lay people troubled by the intertwining of assurance and access to the Lord's Supper. In denying that persons in the church covenant must be "really and Savingly Holy," William Williams and his fellow Stoddardeans never imagined that this understanding of the church compromised their preaching for conversion.[^003-note104] And although this thought may have occurred to their younger colleague and relation, Jonathan Edwards, he also recognized his uncle's fervent evangelicalism. After William Williams' death in 1741, Edwards preached a commemorative sermon in which he described his uncle as "eminently an *evangelical* Preacher; evangelical Subjects seemed to be his Delight: CHRIST was the great Subject of his Preaching; and he much insisted on those Things that did nearly concern the *Essence and Power* of Religion."[^003-note105] It was left to critics in more recent centuries to draw a different conclusion.

<!-- p. 44 -->

Jonathan Edwards pursued the program of Stoddard and the Williamses in his Northampton ministry in part because he faced the same pastoral situation as his grandfather. Even after many years of hearing Stoddard invite them to the Lord's Supper, and after voting in 1710 to accept his policies, the church members in Northampton continued to exhibit the pattern of behavior I have termed "popular religion." The great majority of the townspeople had been baptized and therefore came within the church covenant. But some, possibly a significant percentage, resisted acting on Stoddard's interpretation of the Lord's Supper.[^003-note106] As events proved, they would take stronger action when Edwards challenged the customary mode of access to infant baptism.

The traditional reluctance to participate in the Lord's Supper accounts for a sermon Edwards preached on 1 Corinthians 11:29 in 1733, four years after his grandfather's death. The theme was the familiar one of urging people to hasten to the Lord's Table and not worry overmuch about the injunction to examine themselves. In another sermon from this general period, Edwards complained that his parishioners were "wholly neglecting…the sacrament of the Lord's Supper." Remarking that some of those who stayed away "pretend scruples of conscience," he urged upon the excessively scrupulous their duty to participate in a "positive institution." "Can sin excuse you from attending on a positive institution of Christ?" he asked his congregation.[^003-note107] These sermons indicate that Edwards found himself in the very same pastoral situation that drove Stoddard to articulate his distinctive understanding of the sacrament. Moreover, Edwards followed closely in the steps of his grandfather when he represented the church and its sacraments as instituted and participation as a duty.

Edwards carried on his search for a satisfying middle way in his private notebooks, or "Miscellanies." As early as 1728, he reflected in the "Miscellanies" that the church should "use all proper means to discriminate true Christians from others." But in the next breath Edwards cautioned against shutting out "multitudes…that are true Christians." The church, he was frank to say, had no good means of differentiating true Christians from those who were not, a situation to which the best response was generosity, or erring on the side of inclusion.

<!-- p. 45 -->

For this and other reasons he rejected the test of a relation and offered a generous reading of the parable of the wheat and the tares:

> We ben't directed to try them by an examination of their particular experiences, of their discoveries, illuminations, and affections; because such trials in multitudes of cases would leave us very uncertain and multitudes would be shut out that are real Christians; Matthew 13:19, "Lest while ye gather up the tares ye root up the wheat with them"—Christ is very careful that wheat is not excluded.

In the same entry, Edwards used Stoddardean language to define the criteria for admitting persons as visible saints: "The gospel rule seems to be, to receive those that make a profession of a hearty believing the truth of the gospel, and a walking in all the ordinances and according to the moral rules of the gospel."[^003-note108] Several entries later, Edwards defined visible Christians as "Christians in what is visible, or in what appears, or in what is outward." In a succeeding sentence he used the words "outward" and "visible" four times, always in contrast to "really" having "faith and holiness and obedience of heart." A "good report" of someone's outward behavior was sufficient to qualify that person for church membership. Edwards applied similar reasoning to the sacrament of baptism. In yet another entry from this general period he argued that since the apostles baptized "many adult persons that were hypocrites," so we in the visible church may admit infants whose parents are Christians "only visibly and not really."[^003-note109]

The numerous entries in the "Miscellanies" on baptism, covenant, and the church were not always this supportive of the middle way of Congregational tradition. Reflecting in "Miscellanies" no. 462 on visible saints, Edwards reasoned that access to "church privileges" belonged to those who "be Christians really…for only the righteous have any right to the privileges of the church.…And therefore, they must examine and prove themselves, whether or no they believe the gospel with all their hearts, or are heartily convinced of the truth of it." In the same entry he proposed certain tests as "evidential of sincerity" and concluded that "godly" persons who did not "experience a willingness to forsake all sin and…live universally in obedience to God's commands" should keep away from the Lord's Table.

<!-- p. 46 -->

Mixed in as it is with the warning that "a great number of truly upright ones would be excluded" if "positive" evidence were required this statement does not signal a repudiation of Stoddardeanism. A clearer glimpse of things to come is the argument he made in this entry that a stricter, more exclusionary practice of admission to the Lord's Supper *and to baptism* would give those not yet in the church (or not adequately so) a fresh incentive for seeking grace and observing the moral law:

> And their being denied all privileges…it would put them upon it to come, and being well instructed, that if they do come without forsaking their sins, they will eat and drink judgment to themselves, it will put them upon turning from all their sins and complying with the rules of Christianity and seeking sincerity therein.

The importance of this entry is twofold: not only did Edwards embrace 1 Corinthians 11:28, but he also reversed the logic of Stoddardeanism, for his grandfather had reasoned that evangelism was better advanced by separating access to the sacraments from self-examination and the issue of sincerity.[^003-note110]

Taken as a whole, the relevant entries in the "Miscellanies" reveal a minister who exalted the Lord's Supper and the church and who craved in his parishioners the same intensity of commitment he felt within himself. Almost in the same breath he differentiated the covenant of grace from the church covenant, described the church as a place of nurture where imperfect Christians gathered to benefit from the means of grace, and represented infant baptism as a helpful act.[^003-note111] The crux of these several-sided reflections was the meaning and significance of "profession," which Edwards treated both as outward and as an act that ought to be sincere.

The Great Awakening put this several-sided understanding of the church to the test. Edwards welcomed the awakenings that swept across New England between 1740 and 1742, for they vindicated orthodox preaching and restored a long-missing vitality to the practice of religion. Yet almost as soon as the revivals began, they precipitated separatist and antinomian tendencies he could not accept. The Great Awakening thus drew from him a series of statements in which he opposed a puristic understanding of the church and reaffirmed the compromises of the congregational system.

<!-- p. 47 -->

Under the influence of revivalism thousands of lay people, most of them church members, lamented having practiced "external duties" without, until this moment, experiencing the work of grace. Thus transformed, some of these lay people turned their newfound fervor against the halfway covenant, which they criticized for permitting unregenerate persons to enter the church. For the same reason they rejected the concept of the Lord's Supper as a converting ordinance. These New Lights (as they were termed by their opponents) urged that congregations resume the test of a relation. When, as often happened, the minister and other church members rejected this demand, separation sometimes followed. The Strict Congregationalists or Separates who withdrew went on to form new congregations of their own in which they implemented their understanding of the church.[^003-note112]

This action was rooted in discontents left over from the late seventeenth century, when a minority of the laity had opposed the introduction of the halfway covenant. Another source was a strain of spiritism that had been censored as enthusiasm ever since the Antinomian Controversy of 1636–38. In contrast to the orthodox position, the Separates tended to argue that believers achieved "full assurance." "All doubting in a believer," one such group in the mid-1740s declared, "is sinful, being contrary to the command of God, and hurtful to the soul." Full assurance followed from the premise that anyone who experienced the "new birth," or conversion, would recognize the event and know exactly when it occurred. "It is as easy for persons to know when they are converted," one New Light minister allegedly declared, "as it is to know noon daylight from midnight darkness." According to another New Light premise, the Holy Spirit provided true believers with a "key of knowledge" that enabled them to differentiate Christians from hypocrites. A leading minister among the Separates, Ebenezer Frothingham, declared that "a Saint of God having Divine Light shining into the Understanding, and the Love of God…ruling in the Soul, is also to know certainly that such and such Persons are true Converts, or the Saints of God."[^003-note113]

Asserting their ability to recognize the saints and angry at the churches for permitting hypocrites to come within the covenant, the Separates moved to alter the basis of church membership. In the words of one opponent, they argued that "it is the will of God to have a pure

<!-- p. 48 -->

church on earth, in this sense, that all the converted should be separated from the unconverted." When it came to setting up new congregations of their own, the Separates hoped and expected that they would admit only "real believers in Jesus Christ." The way of differentiating real from false was to depend on the Holy Spirit, albeit a Holy Spirit mediated through the "Fruits of…special sanctifying Grace."[^003-note114]

Edwards repudiated these consequences of the revival. We may judge the extent of his dismay by the fact that he likened the excesses of the New Lights to "the many wild enthusiasts that were in England in the days of Oliver Cromwell; and the followers of Mrs. Hutchinson, in New England," even though, in making this comparison, he reiterated the liberal Boston minister Charles Chauncy's critique of the revivals.[^003-note115] An important sign of his concern is the extraordinary effort he made in his own parish, and in person elsewhere in New England, to subdue the extremes of the Awakening. Thus he joined forces with his cousin Solomon Williams to preach against enthusiasm in New London, Connecticut, where the itinerant evangelist James Davenport had staged the most dramatic episode of communal repentance to occur in the revivals. Edwards and his allies defended the authority of the ordained ministry, denounced lay people who usurped this authority, and insisted that "the external fruits of holiness" were the only satisfactory evidence of conversion.[^003-note116]

The turmoil of these years led Edwards to address the nature of "true religion" in a series of publications: *Distinguishing Marks of a Work of the Spirit of God* (1741), *Some Thoughts Concerning the Revival* (1742), the *Treatise Concerning Religious Affections* (1746), and the *Life of David Brainerd* (1749). Together with a letter describing the revival in Northampton that he published in *The Christian History*, these texts constitute the major body of evidence about his understanding of the Great Awakening and the confusion it engendered about true religion. In these treatises he denounced deism and Arminianism and asserted the validity of Calvinist divinity. In them he set forth his understanding of

<!-- p. 49 -->

true religion as involving an infusion of supernatural grace that produced a "new sense" of the divine. But the main purpose of these publications was to criticize the New Lights, who had gone astray.[^003-note117]

The great error of the Separates concerned their understanding of conversion and its consequences. The New Lights celebrated a fluency in describing the work of grace that Edwards, never one to trust words alone, found distasteful because these people were not engaging in self-examination or relying on the evidence of "fruits." Any resting of assurance of salvation on the "immediate witness of the Holy Spirit" made him uneasy, as did Antinomian efforts to "cry down works." But he was especially disturbed by the premise that the regenerate could recognize who was truly a saint and who was not. Lamenting New Light outbursts against "unconverted" ministers, he also objected to their complaints against the unconverted who remained church members.[^003-note118]

Edwards rejected out of hand the possibility of purifying gathered churches of the unconverted. In doing so he reiterated some of his grandfather's arguments against the founders of New England Congregationalism. Espousing a policy of charity and insisting that mankind can never achieve absolute certainty, he cited the Christ who "acted the part of the minister of the visible church of God" in accepting Judas as co-worker. Similarly, he adduced episodes in Scripture in which "persons were suddenly admitted by baptism into the visible church…without strictness in their probation." And he drew on his wife's reaction to the New Lights, citing (though not by name) Sarah Edwards' "peculiar aversion to a judging others that were professing Christians in good standing in the visible church, that they were not converted, or with respect to their degrees of grace."[^003-note119]

He spoke out even more emphatically in the *Religious Affections*. There he denied that "converted and unconverted men" can "be certainly distinguished by the account they give of their experience," the reasons being that each could make "the same relation of experiences"

<!-- p. 50 -->

and that "many persons have given a fair account of a work of conversion, that have carried well in the eye of the world for several years, but have not proved well at last." It is notable that, in support of this argument, Edwards quoted his grandfather's *Appeal to the Learned*. Repeatedly he emphasized the difficulty of distinguishing, on the basis of "outward expressions and appearances," a "hypocrite and a true saint." It was, he lamented, an exhibition of an "indecent self-exaltation, and arrogance" for "poor fallible dark mortals, to pretend that they can determine and know, who are really sincere and upright before God, and who are not!"[^003-note120]

Throughout the 1740s Edwards reiterated two other traditional themes, that Christ was no "searcher of hearts" and that God had given men no "certain rule" to enable them to differentiate the converted from the unregenerate.[^003-note121] Similarly Stoddardean in tone is the following passage from *Distinguishing Marks*:

> To suppose that men have ability and right to determine the state of the souls of visible Christians, and so to make an open separation between saints and hypocrites, that true saints may be of one visible company and hypocrites of another, separated by a partition that men make, carries in it an inconsistency: for it supposes that God has given men power to make another visible church within his visible church; for by visible Christians, or those that are of God's visible church, can be understood nothing else than that company that are Christians or saints, *visibly so*; i.e. that have a right to be received as such in the eye of a public charity.[^003-note122]

Here as in "Miscellanies" no. 338, the word "visible" is conflated with "charity" and, by implication, with outward. Edwards also repeated an argument Thomas Blake and Richard Baxter had used in the middle of the seventeenth century, that in generating a church within a church purists ignored the legitimacy of the broader institution. And he appropriated Stoddard's exegesis of the parable of the wheat and the tares.[^003-note123]

Edwards the revivalist thus coexisted with Edwards the defender of the ordained ministry and instituted church against "enthusiastical

<!-- p. 51 -->

religion." Edwards the revivalist joined with his relatives the Williamses in welcoming the revivals as the answer to many years of prayer that God would intervene and awaken the New England churches from formality. However checkered, the process was moving the churches to a higher level; even though the revivals made him more aware than ever of hypocrisy and its manifold disguises, Edwards remained confident that the history of redemption was unfolding in these events.[^003-note124] Meanwhile he counseled patience in warning against the premise that, here on earth, the visible church should encompass only the regenerate, as judged by experience. So he argued not only on the eve of the Northampton controversy, but after it was under way, for he wanted to make absolutely clear the line between himself and "those wild people, who have lately appeared in New England, called Separatists." To this end he began the *Humble Inquiry* by citing his testimony against the Separates in the *Religious Affections* and the *Life of David Brainerd*, complaining anew of the "notion of a pure church by means of a spirit of discerning" and renouncing one more time the test of experience. He could not have been more explicit: his program was different from what the radical New Lights were demanding.[^003-note125]

#### Moving toward a Change of Mind

That Edwards had any reason to quarrel with Stoddardeanism may be the real surprise. He was not under pressure from a New Light faction in his congregation or from friends and colleagues in the ministry to purify the church; after having quelled the brief eruption of enthusiasm in Northampton, he was spared the turmoil that disrupted so many other parishes. Moreover, as a Stoddardean he had found that he could generate seasons of spiritual excitement while also practicing

<!-- p. 52 -->

a broad churchmanship.[^003-note126] By the close of the two revivals he experienced in Northampton, the little awakening of 1734–35 and the great of 1740–42, a high percentage of the adult population of Northampton were full church members and, according to the minister who participated in admitting them, visible saints. Edwards declared in *A Faithful Narrative of Surprising Conversions* that the three hundred or so townspeople he "received into our communion" in 1734–35 were to be considered true Christians; "I had very sufficient evidence of the conversion of their souls through divine grace," he asserted in the first printed version of *A Faithful Narrative*.[^003-note127] He was scarcely less emphatic in describing the consequences of the revivals of 1740–42. During this time he admitted at least one hundred others either to the Lord's Supper or to the church covenant. These figures mean that Edwards, not Stoddard, was responsible for the large enrollment of townspeople in the Northampton church; as Edwards noted in *Misrepresentations Corrected*, he had been "immediately concerned in the admission of more than three quarters" of the church's "present members." Those who voted to dismiss Edwards were not the leftovers from a lax admissions policy, but saints according to their pastor at the time that he admitted them.[^003-note128]

Nonetheless he changed his mind.[^003-note129] Why he did so and in what

<!-- p. 53 -->

manner are questions that can be answered only by keeping in view the fundamental elements of his situation: his defense of the compromises of the Congregational tradition in response to divisive enthusiasm; the uneasiness he shared with many others about the trade-off between purity and comprehensiveness; his confidence, inherited from evangelical Calvinism but newly reaffirmed, that true religion could be differentiated from hypocrisy; and the politics of his ministry in Northampton, especially as it had to do with the authority of his office and with popular religion.

The task of interpreting his change of mind would be easier if we knew exactly when he came to the conclusions he announced in early 1749. The evidence suggests that he had changed his mind by 1745, or when he began writing the *Religious Affections*. The evidence also suggests that he was in no hurry to inform his congregation.[^003-note130] During these years there is little to indicate that he was reading in the older literature on Congregationalism or reflecting on the nature of the church. Was it at his initiative that the Hampshire Association debated in 1745 "Whether an Unregenerate Person has a Right in the Sight of

<!-- p. 54 -->

God to the Lords Supper"? And what did he say when, two years later the Association discussed the situation that lay at the root of Stoddardeanism: "What is the Duty of a Church respecting those Members that absent themselves from the Lords Supper"?[^003-note132]

Only when we turn to the situation in Northampton itself are there signs of fresh difficulties. Some of these had to do with his salary. Of more significance, or at least more ominous in hindsight, was that by 1744 people had ceased to apply for church membership.[^003-note133] Then there was the "bad book affair" of early 1744, a mishandled case of church discipline that was cruelly revealing of the limitations on Edwards' authority. In the *Farewell Sermon* Edwards referred to this event as that "which gave so great offense, and by which I became so obnoxious," and Samuel Hopkins, who knew as much as anyone about the situation in Northampton leading up to the communion controversy, went back to 1744 and the bad book affair in narrating Edwards' dismissal.[^003-note134]

These troubles, together with the general cooling off of religious zeal, prompted a discontent in Edwards that he expressed in the judgment, asserted numerous times in the closing years of the decade, that "multitudes" of his parishioners remained "in a christless state" despite having entered the church.[^003-note135] That judgment energized a web of interrelated issues, for it broached the issue of true religion, which in turn touched on access to the sacraments of baptism and the Lord's Supper. Definitions of church membership and access to the sacraments of baptism and the Lord's Supper were intrinsically political; were a minister to defy popular religion, the outcome was certain to be a struggle. To make matters worse, the townspeople had a second grievance against Edwards. He was demanding that he have priority in examining candidates for church membership and, in keeping with this priority, the right to decide whether or not someone was suitable.[^003-note136]

<!-- p. 55 -->

But the laity were not about to grant an angry man this power—and that Edwards was angry at certain families in Northampton was no secret to anyone.

The deterioration of his ministry and the shape of his response to that deterioration can be glimpsed in the letter he published in *The Christian History* describing the revival in Northampton. Written in December 1743, it opens with a backward glance at the "little revival" and the "great abiding alteration" in "vice" that followed upon it. Edwards recalled in particular the good effects among young people "with respect to reveling, frolicking, profane and unclean conversation, and lewd songs." There had even been "a great alteration amongst both old and young with respect to tavern-haunting." True, there had also been a subsequent "decay of religious affections." But in general things were better.

There followed an account of the itinerant evangelist George Whitefield's visit to Northampton in 1740, the first wave of conversions, and the "very great revival of religion" that began under the leadership of Samuel Buell in early 1742 while Edwards was preaching elsewhere. As soon as he returned, Edwards had to deal with what he regarded as excessive emotionalism; "a great deal of caution and pains were found necessary," he told Thomas Prince, editor of *The Christian History*, "to keep the people, many of them, from running wild." It was at this moment that Edwards drew up a covenant and conducted everyone above the age of fourteen in the church (which is to say, practically the entire adult population of the town) through the ceremony of covenant renewal, a "vow to God" that they would "seek and serve" him in specific ways.

<!-- p. 56 -->

Any modern reader of this lengthy covenant, which fills four pages in a recent printing, must begin to feel, midway through, that it asks too much, that it defies common sense. Much is made of being honest in fulfilling neighborly obligations and foregoing private interest in public affairs. Other sections have to do with feelings of revenge and how the church members should "endeavor to their utmost to root it out." In a separate clause the youth pledged "never to allow ourselves in any youthful diversions or pastimes" to do anything that might hinder religious practice or feelings. Sex was another issue. Edwards had already noted that, in the aftermath of the revival of 1735, "instances of fornication have been very rare." Now he asked the young people to "avoid all freedoms and familiarities…tending either to stir up or gratify a lust of lasciviousness." The covenant concluded with a sweeping pledge to "devote our whole lives to be laboriously spent in the business of religion: ever making it our greatest business." And a note of realism intruded; acknowledging a "proneness to forget our most solemn vows," the church members pledged to examine themselves "especially before the sacrament of the Lord's Supper; and beg of God that he would…keep us from wickedly dissembling in these our solemn vows."

This final clause is crucial, for it contrasts sincerity (or practicing what you say) and a "dissembling in these our solemn vows" and links the two possibilities to participation in the Lord's Supper—that is, links them in the sense that persons who dissembled and who came to the Lord's Table were violating the sacramental rule of self-examination. From here the road lay open to the controversy that broke out in 1749. Were Edwards to conclude that the people of the church were dissembling hypocrites, he would have to find some means of dramatizing their unworthiness to participate in the Lord's Supper.[^003-note137]

Edwards started down that road in his letter to Prince. In a paragraph that began by alluding to the problem of New Light excesses, he spoke of judging "the goodness of a person's state" and affirmed that the basis for such judgments should be "the effect wrought on the temper of the soul…*and remaining afterwards*." How were his parishioners faring by this standard? In general, Edwards emphasized the "good effects" that lingered in the aftermath of the revival. But he also added a sentence that, in hindsight, has a different ring: "The temper

<!-- p. 57 -->

that some of them show, and the behavior they have been of…make me much afraid lest there be a considerable number that have woefully deceived themselves."[^003-note138]

The second thoughts he was having in December 1743, second thoughts implicit in the covenant of March 1742, had intensified by the time he wrote the *Religious Affections*. There he took up the question of sincerity as judged by "Christian practice" and the evangelical dictum that, despite the many difficulties in the way, the godly *could* be differentiated from the profane. Because the *Religious Affections* defends this distinction it deserves a place in the sequence of events that lead up to the *Humble Inquiry*.

The essential message of evangelical Calvinism was that grace and nature were utterly different. In the *Religious Affections* Edwards restated the case for the radical difference between grace and nature in terms of the objective "excellence" of God and, recasting older terminology, proposed that the Holy Spirit created a "new inward sense" in the regenerate that enabled them to perceive and participate in this excellence. These statements did not resolve the problem of knowing who was saved and who was not. What happened in the heart was invisible, and the hypocrite could *seem* to be transformed. Like so many of his predecessors Edwards turned, therefore, to "sanctification." The "great and distinguishing sign" of grace, and the only sure test of sincerity, was Christian practice.[^003-note139]

In the context of the controversy that erupted three years later, it is crucial to note that Edwards regarded practice as indissolubly connected to the affections. Asserting that Christ lives "in the heart," he went on to define the indwelling Christ as "an internal vital principle," the source of all actions in the world. The outer and the inner were one. What made them one was a common "activity, power, and efficacy." Echoing Paul's letter to the Ephesians, Edwards declared that "Christ is not in the heart of a saint, as in a sepulchre, or as a dead Savior, that does nothing; but as in his temple, one that is alive from the dead." "And thus it is," he concluded, "that holy affections have a governing power in the course of a man's life." By "course of…life" he meant the *full* length of someone's life, in contrast to ecstasies that lasted but a moment or some fleeting signs of Christian behavior.[^003-note140]

<!-- p. 58 -->

Yet how many lacked "holy affections" and consequently could not manifest the fruits of Christian practice! And how many who had once been deemed among the saints had failed the test of practice. A darker tone came over the *Religious Affections* as Edwards described the scope and depth of hypocrisy. "It has been a common thing in the church of God, for such bright professors, that are received as eminent saints among the saints, to fall away and come to nothing." There follows a series of descriptions that enforce the judgment about hypocrisy. Several of these descriptions seem rooted in his Northampton pastorate as when he condemned persons who, like the young men in the bad book affair, were contemptuous of the authority of those set over them; persons who went to taverns; and most lamentably of all, church members who made a "profession" but were insincere in doing so.[^003-note141]

A paragraph of the *Religious Affections*—a passage Edwards would cite in 1749 as signaling his change of mind—concerns this very situation:

> In order to a profession of Christianity being accepted to any purpose, there ought to be good reason, from the circumstances of the profession, to think that the professor don't make such a profession out of a mere customary compliance with a prescribed form, using words without any distinct meaning, or in a very lax and ambiguous manner, as confessions of faith are often subscribed; but that the professor understandingly and honestly signifies what he is conscious of in his own heart; otherwise his profession can be of no significance, and no more to be regarded than the sound of things without life.

Lax profession versus one that is honestly delivered—three years later, such would be the contrasting terms of the *Humble Inquiry*. In a further sign of things to come, Edwards cited the episodes of Peter and the three thousand and Philip and the eunuch in declaring that "repentance is a qualification that must be visible in order to baptism."[^003-note142]

The *Religious Affections* thus foreshadows the crucial argument of the *Humble Inquiry* in declaring that profession, properly understood, allows the church to judge adults seeking baptism for their children or access for themselves to the Lord's Supper.[^003-note143] Nothing in the *Affections*,

<!-- p. 59 -->

in the treatise of 1749, or in the "Miscellanies" that surround them indicates directly why Edwards finally allowed his animus against hypocrisy to overcome the policy of charity. Nowhere did he pause to acknowledge that certain passages in Scripture, like the parable of the wheat and the tares, had once meant something different to him. Yet the *Humble Inquiry* and its immediate companions, the *Farewell Sermon* of 1750 and the *Misrepresentations Corrected* of 1752, are remarkably explicit in two respects: in voicing the judgment that many of his parishioners were among the deceived; and in condemning as insincere the practice, crucial to the being of popular religion, of allowing parents readily to secure baptism for their children.

Some months after the *Humble Inquiry* appeared, Edwards made a revealing comment on the controversy in the course of a letter to Peter Clark, the minister of Salem Village. Here he spoke of popular religion and what he regarded as its corruptions. "The great thing which I have scrupled in the established method of this church's proceeding," he told Clark in May 1750,

> and which I dare no longer go on in, is their publicly assenting to the form of words rehearsed on occasion of their admission to the communion, without pretending thereby to mean any such thing as an hearty consent to the terms of the gospel covenant, or to mean any such faith or repentance as belong to the covenant of grace…: it being, at the same time that the words are used, their known and established principle, which they openly profess and proceed upon, that men may and ought to use these words, and mean no such thing, but something else of a nature far inferior.[^003-note144]

What else did the townspeople regard as a "known and established principle" that Edwards now condemned as hypocrisy? Nothing less than the central motif of popular religion, the expectation of lay men and women that their children would benefit from the sacrament of baptism. The relevant passages in the *Humble Inquiry* have gone unnoticed in spite of Edwards' bluntness. Why, he asked, did adult children of the church renew their covenants? Because they had gotten married and wanted their children to be baptized. Renewal of covenant had deteriorated into mere "form and ceremony," "it being visibly a prevailing custom for persons to neglect this, till they come to be

<!-- p. 60 -->

married, and then to do it for their credit's sake, and *that their children may be baptized*."[^003-note145] And why did churches like Northampton's practice the halfway covenant? Because such an "expedient" gives "ease to ancestors with respect to their posterity, in times of great declension and degeneracy." Accusing his parishioners of "presumptuous lying for the sake of the honor of being in the church, having children baptized, and voting in ecclesiastical affairs," he imposed the framework of declension on their patterns of religious observance.[^003-note146]

He shared this perspective with his nearby ministerial ally, Edward Billings, and with his friend and former student Joseph Bellamy. What these two had to say about the halfway covenant illuminates the situation in Northampton. In *A Dialogue about Sacraments* (written about 1752), Billings lashed out against the "many Churches in the Country" in which the baptism of infants signified nothing more than that "their Parents are married." Observing that "nothing induces a Man or Woman to join to the Church, like marrying; and there is scarcely a Child born whose Parents (one at least) did not join to the Church, just before the Birth of the Child," Billings denounced these practices as morally wrong.[^003-note147] In his *The Half-Way Covenant: A Dialogue* (1766), Bellamy dramatized the confrontation between a purist like himself and a parishioner who wanted a child baptized, a confrontation that ended with the minister refusing the request on the grounds that the parishioner was "graceless."[^003-note148]

We are now in a position to understand the rage of the church members and townspeople of Northampton. Edwards wished to abolish what for them was basic, the procedures that linked family structure and religion. So he acknowledged indirectly in the *Humble Inquiry* when he remarked that "parents are angry" and "complain that their children are denied the honor of having God's mark set upon them as

<!-- p. 61 -->

some of his."[^003-note149] And so he acknowledged openly in a letter to the Boston minister Thomas Foxcroft. "The greatest difficulty of all relating to my principles is here, respecting baptism," he wrote Foxcroft. Compromise seemed possible on the issue of access to the Lord's Supper. "But with respect to the other sacrament there is scarce any hope of it."[^003-note150]

In the aftermath of the little revival Edwards had described his congregation as beset by scrupulosity.[^003-note151] Now he described them as systematically insincere. Like so many others in the Congregational tradition he had tried to forge a ministry that accommodated these extremes. It was the failure of that ministry, a failure all too evident in the ineffectiveness of his preaching in Northampton by the mid-1740s, that led him to give up on Stoddardeanism and the middle way of tradition. The problem was not of his doing, he reasoned, but arose from the stubborn and intractable pride that expressed itself in popular religion. The one stratagem he could still pursue was the course of action he had imagined many years before in "Miscellanies" no. 462: do away with comprehensiveness, introduce the requirement of sincere profession, and force the hypocritical to obtain baptism for their children on terms that *he* defined.[^003-note152]

The *Humble Inquiry* is elusive, or perhaps purposefully vague, in specifying the actual procedures for becoming an adult member of the church and gaining access to its privileges. Historians of religion in early New England have frequently assumed that Edwards wanted to restore the requirement of a relation of spiritual experience. His contemporary critic Solomon Williams said as much in accusing his cousin of requiring an "account of experiences" of candidates for membership. But as Edwards strenuously insisted in his letter of May 1750 to Peter Clark, he did not specify the procedure of a relation. The *Humble Inquiry* is infused with a distrust of narratives of spiritual experience, a distrust rooted in his long-standing discontent with the traditional vocabulary of stages as well as in his disenchantment with the New Lights. He turned, therefore, to the traditional alternative, the act of profession. The two model professions he published in *Misrepresentations Corrected* seem remarkably benign. What they do not adequately convey are three crucial aspects of the process of admission: first,

<!-- p. 62 -->

Edwards' insistence, voiced at great length in these treatises, that candidates declare that they possess "true godliness"; second, and closely related, that anyone making a profession do so "heartily," which is to say, do so on the basis of an "inward assent" that saving grace alone made possible; and third, that those embarking on this process seek the counsel of a minister skilled in differentiating the sincere from the hypocritical. During that encounter, candidates were undoubtedly expected to describe the work of grace, for a young woman who came to Edwards privately in 1748 to request admission to the church gave him "a hopeful account of her religious experience and the operations of divine grace upon her mind." In effect, this scheme depended less on specific procedures than on the psychological consequences of calling upon candidates to acknowledge the absolute difference between real grace and its simulacres and to present themselves for admission only if they could profess "the real existence of…what lays a proper and good foundation" for such a statement.[^003-note153]

#### An Humble Inquiry

Edwards wrote *An Humble Inquiry* with great "rapidity" in March and April 1749.[^003-note154] His task was to prove Stoddard wrong for maintaining that the unregenerate or the morally sincere could be accepted into the church and to the Lord's Supper as visible saints. (The issue of the Lord's Supper as a converting ordinance was peripheral to the controversy, the reason being that this concept was secondary to, and consequent upon, the admitting of unregenerate persons to the ordinance.) Point by point, Edwards moved through the arguments advanced by Stoddard, Blake, and other seventeenth-century advocates of a moderate or comprehensive understanding of the church. Taking the contrary position, Edwards maintained that visible saints were those persons who met the conditions of the "covenant of grace." He regarded the visible and the real as qualities that were connected; for him, the "visibility of saintship" signified the reality of grace, or a "real" change of heart.

<!-- p. 63 -->

The central question Edwards posed at the outset and answered in the negative was this: "Whether, according to the rules of Christ, any ought to be admitted to the communion and privileges of members of the visible church of Christ in complete standing, but such as are in profession, and in the eye of the church's Christian judgment, godly or gracious persons?" He went on to clarify his terms, indicating, for example, that "complete standing" applied only to adults and not to infants.

Edwards next clarified the nature of an appropriate profession. Profession was visible, in contrast to the invisibility of "godliness itself." Instead of letting this distinction open out into Stoddardeanism, Edwards argued that profession had to be "explicit" and performed "sincerely." In this connection Edwards discussed appearance versus reality. And here he made a distinction (itself a commonplace within the Congregational tradition) between that which is made manifest to the church as over against that which motivates the candidate; between ecclesiastical right ("in *foro ecclesiæ*") and experiential foundation. "There is a difference between these." Thus, it is the profession of a belief and the visibility "to the eye of a Christian judgment" that give a person the right before the church, "but it is the real existence of these things, that is what lays a proper and good foundation for his making this profession, and so demanding these privileges."[^003-note155]

By "Christian judgment" Edwards did not mean a species of "negative charity" by which one forbears to censure because he does not know the truth for certain, but rather "a positive judgment, founded on some positive appearance, or visibility, some outward manifestations that ordinarily render the thing probable." He emphasized that probability was not the same as certainty. But for him it mattered that the church achieve the highest possible degree of probability with respect to true holiness in its members, while by no means implying the "pretense of any scheme, that shall be effectual to keep all hypocrites out of the church, and for the establishing in that sense a pure church."[^003-note156]

Having stated as clearly as possible his definition of the principal terms of the proposition, Edwards proceeded in the second and third sections of the book to defend his anti-Stoddardean position. His eleven reasons occupy more than half of the book. The great length of

<!-- p. 64 -->

this section is to be accounted for by Edwards' tendency to strive for an encyclopedic inclusiveness. In one sense, all eleven reasons for the negative are subdivisions of a single topic, namely, Edwards' interpretation of the biblical teaching on qualifications for full communion.

The first, second, and sixth reasons deal with the question of visible sainthood. Edwards began his discussion of the first reason by assuming "that none ought to be admitted as members of the visible church of Christ but visible saints and professing saints, or visible and professing Christians." Confronting, once again, Stoddard's understanding of visibility, he complained of the absurdity of a "visibility with regard to saintship or holiness" that "had no reference to the *reality*…as though by visible saints were not meant those who to appearance are real saints." He granted the difference between "real saints" in the "eye of God" and in the judgment of man. The church must rely on external signs and appearances. Even so, these signs must establish the probability of grace. Stoddardeanism violated this principle, for it allowed persons to invoke "words and signs" without "so much as making any pretense to the least degree of sanctifying grace." As Edwards went on to argue in his second reason, any equivocal use of language vitiates the essential nature of public covenanting. The person who enters into an explicit covenant is understood to be complying with it "internally and spiritually."[^003-note157]

The sixth reason continues the biblical doctrine of visible sainthood by emphasizing the "representations which Christ makes of his visible church." On the whole, according to Edwards, "all Christ's professing disciples…are such as profess a saving interest in him and relation to him." In the parable of the ten virgins, for example, the "lamps signify in general the appearance of grace or godliness." Similarly, in the parable of the "great supper," or (as Edwards calls it) "the marriage which the king made for his son" (Matthew 22 and Luke 14), the wedding garment stands for "true piety," which is the necessary qualification both for salvation and for visible sainthood and participation in the sacraments.[^003-note158]

Edwards' third reason employed a variation of an argument used by Increase Mather against Stoddard. Stoddard had maintained (and Edwards echoed him in denouncing the Separates) that since God has

<!-- p. 65 -->

given no "certain rule" by which the church can distinguish between true saints and hypocrites, all that may be expected of a prospective member is a historical knowledge of the doctrines of the gospel and a moral sincerity Mather pointed out that it was just as difficult to determine true belief of doctrine as to discriminate true from false professions of faith. Reversing the emphasis, Edwards saw "no good reason why" someone professing right belief could not also profess what was in the heart.[^003-note159]

Reasons seven and eight are based on an interpretation of the practice of the primitive Christian church. Edwards argued in the seventh reason that the early hearers of the apostles (as recounted in Acts) were first enjoined to repent, then to believe, and finally to profess their belief before being baptized and admitted to the church. He conceded that, in those extraordinary times, the church did not have to inquire so particularly into these matters "as may be expedient in a more ordinary state of things." The eighth reason extends the analysis to all other relevant books in the New Testament, and the conclusion reached is that "the apostles continually in their epistles speak to and of them as supposing and judging them to be gracious persons." This judgment was not "a kind of negative charity," but, insisted Edwards, "a positive judgment that" they were "gracious persons."[^003-note160]

The fourth, fifth, and ninth reasons add little to Edwards' argument. Number four shows that in the Bible visible saints who are not truly pious are dubbed counterfeits and deceivers. Number five is a brief commentary on Isaiah 56:1-8. Number nine deals with "Christian brotherly love," a theme of much importance to Edwards elsewhere but of incidental importance here.[^003-note161]

The tenth reason focuses on the significance of the actions of both parties in the administration of the Lord's Supper. The entire ceremony has to do with matters of the heart, with professing that which the parties have truly experienced and confirming and sealing what is reciprocally deemed a reality. Here too the theme of covenant enters, with Edwards arguing that an "explicit covenanting" must precede admission to the Supper. This act of covenanting is identical with the profession of religious faith that is the necessary qualification for full communion.[^003-note162]

<!-- p. 66 -->

The eleventh and final reason has to do with 1 Corinthians 11:28. Did the examination that the verse called for have to do with self-examination or with "discerning the nature of the ordinance," as Stoddard had argued? Edwards, of course, preferred the former interpretation and linked such self-examination to "a living faith" that must exist in the candidate.[^003-note163]

In the final part of the *Humble Inquiry* Edwards answered twenty objections to his scheme. Here he provided a massive review of his position from different perspectives, thereby clarifying, reemphasizing, and in some cases supplementing his presentation. These twenty objections may be classified into four major categories.

The objections in the first category arise from divergent interpretations of problematic passages of Scripture. This group comprises numbers one through seven. He took up the scriptural analogy of the church as a school, the typological interpretation of the nation of Israel, the Passover as type of the Lord's Supper, the multitudes that John the Baptist baptized (Matthew 3), the verse "many are called but few are chosen" (Matthew 22:14), the parable of the wheat and the tares, and the presence of Judas at Passover and the Lord's Supper. Respecting, this last, Edwards argued that Judas had left before the Lord's Supper was instituted; even if he remained, Jesus had not acted as "searcher of hearts."[^003-note164]

The second category of objections, numbers eight through ten, takes up the difference between "certainty" and "visibility." Edwards did not expect candidates for the sacrament—or the church in judging these candidates—to know for sure who were the regenerate; it was conscientious profession that mattered. The tenth objection concerns the pastoral consequences of heightened scrutiny. Here, in an echo of "Miscellanies" no. 462, Edwards argued that increasing the distress of "persons of a tender conscience" was not too high a price to pay if it helped overcome the "stupidity and hardness of heart" that characterized some who were admitted under the Stoddardean policy. He called for more, not less, self-examination, brushed aside the problem of perplexity, and insisted that assurance of salvation can be obtained.[^003-note165]

The third category of objections centers on qualifications, the purposes and effects of the sacraments, and the legitimacy of claims to

<!-- p. 67 -->

them. This category includes objections 11 through 13 and number 20. In numbers 13 and 20 Edwards addresses the argument that, because the Lord's Supper has a tendency to promote conversion, it was "appointed" for that purpose. In response, he differentiated what a sacrament may cause circumstantially from the purpose for which it was instituted.

The fourth category comprises objections 14 through 19, all of which are concerned with the nature of a profession. In these objections Edwards dealt with such problems as discriminating true from false profession, guarding against the exclusion of true saints because of overly stringent requirements, and avoiding infiltration of the church by hypocrites. Edwards granted what Stoddard had said so often, that hypocrites could not be excluded from the church. But was it "not better," he asked, "to have a few real living Christians kept back through darkness and scruples, than to open a door for the letting in such universal ruin" as admitting many who were unregenerate?[^003-note166]

This judgment leads into the answer to objection 19 about baptism. Edwards asserted that access to baptism depended on the same "profession of godliness" required of communicants in the Lord's Supper. He repudiated the distinction, formulated not by Stoddard but by the first-generation clergy, between the two sacraments. Edwards also complained of the connection between baptism and family religion. "Why should parents covet the external honor for their children," he exclaimed, "while they are so careless about the spiritual blessing!" Not explicitly, but by the logic of his argument, Edwards repudiated the halfway covenant. Yet he could not do away with all the contradictions that figured in the New England system, for he affirmed that baptized adults who, when they came of age, failed to make the proper profession of faith, ought "not to be cast out of the church or cease to be in any respect its members."[^003-note167]

The *Humble Inquiry* concludes with an *Appendix* credited to Thomas Foxcroft, the Boston minister who oversaw publication of the treatise. The *Appendix* summarizes what had been said by other ministers in the Reformed tradition in favor of limiting the Lord's Supper to visible saints. Three groups of ministers were featured: seventeenth- and eighteenth-century English Nonconformists, some of whom had written sacramental manuals advising communicants on how to approach

<!-- p. 68 -->

the Lord's Supper and others of whom had opposed the Presbyterians Thomas Blake, John Humfrey, and John Timson; the first and second generations of New England divines; and eighteenth-century Scottish Presbyterian ministers, some of them adherents of the Evangelical wing of that Church and others among the Seceders who left it over issues of evangelism and church and state.

Edwards played a part in composing the *Appendix*. We have to suppose, however, that Foxcroft played the larger role. In a brief note to him dated May 12, 1749, Edwards spoke of sending to the Boston minister "an abstract of your former letter to be added to my book as an appendix, if you please." In the absence of Foxcroft's original draft it cannot be determined what Edwards deleted, compressed, or added. He seems to have felt the limitations of his knowledge, for he referred to himself as "little read in church history." He may also have realized that Foxcroft, who enjoyed wide contacts with English and Scottish evangelicals, was better situated to amass the references that pile up in the *Appendix*. "You have vastly greater opportunities of full information concerning the present principles and practice in England and Scotland than I," Edwards wrote in May.[^003-note168]

The citations in the *Appendix* throw into relief an interesting characteristic of the *Humble Inquiry*, and one that is not accidental. Nowhere in the treatise did Edwards employ the Mathers' arguments against Stoddardeanism or follow them in lamenting apostasy from the principles of the Cambridge Platform and the Congregational tradition. This indifference to older debates has something to do with Edwards' determination to return to the Word of God, as he announced he was doing on the title page of the *Humble Inquiry*. But it also reminds us that, in contrast to the Separates, he was not seeking to retrieve the more democratic and puristic Congregationalism of the Cambridge Platform. The many citations in the *Appendix* mislead the reader in this respect, for Edwards was unable to invoke the past without equivocation.[^003-note169]

#### Critical Voices

The townspeople of Northampton looked for someone willing to rebut Edwards' arguments almost as soon as he informed the church

<!-- p. 69 -->

of his change of mind. None of the town's initiatives succeeded. Meanwhile, Elisha Williams began to prepare a response. Hearing of this possibility, Edwards wrote to Foxcroft asking him to do his best (using reasons Edwards had supplied) to dissuade Williams from the project.[^003-note170] In the event, the press of his career as a politician kept Elisha from continuing. He may have passed his notes or working draft to his cousin Solomon, the minister in Lebanon, though the more likely possibility is that Solomon had determined on his own to respond; so at least he indicated to Edwards in a letter of August 20, 1750, in which, having said frankly that he judged his cousin to be "on the Wrong Side of the Question," he reported that illness in his family had delayed the preparation of an answer—a delay occasioned also by the realization that Edwards "was so fixd" in his "Sentiments" that "it would probably be an Endless Controversy."[^003-note171] Nonetheless, Solomon went ahead and published *The True State of the Question Concerning the Qualifications Necessary to Lawful Communion in the Christian Sacraments* in May 1751. Another critique came from Jonathan Ashley, the minister of Deerfield. Two sermons he preached in Northampton in 1751 were published in Boston in 1753 as *An Humble Attempt to give a Clear Account from Scripture, how the Jewish and Christian Churches were Constituted, and what sort of Saintship is necessary in order to be a Communicant at the Lord's Table*.

Solomon Williams[^003-note172] took up Edwards' challenge to "attend the true state of the question" by subjecting the arguments of the *Humble Inquiry* to careful scrutiny on the basis of his own biblical exegesis and research among the standard authorities; responding to the citations heaped up in the *Appendix* to the *Humble Inquiry*, Williams countered with the names of Blake, Hudson, John Cotton, John Humfrey, and William Guthrie, among others, while insisting that Stoddardeanism was consistent with the "general Sense of Protestant Churches and

<!-- p. 70 -->

Divines."[^003-note173] The *True State* is formally divided into two main parts, but the actual substantive division overlaps this boundary. Most of part 1 is devoted to clarifying the question, defining the terms, and elaborating three general reasons that were fundamental to his position. The remainder of part 1 and all of part 2 consist of detailed responses to Edwards' views and reaffirmations of many of the objections posed in the third part of the *Humble Inquiry*. Here, Williams also noted which of these objections were Stoddard's own arguments.

Williams began by rejecting Edwards' statement of the question. The heart of the matter was not sincerity, as Edwards made it out to be, but whether "sanctifying grace is…necessary to the Lawful attending of the Lord's Supper." Williams quoted from the *Appeal to the Learned* to demonstrate that this had been the crucial issue for Stoddard. Another procedure against which he protested was the deliberate bracketing of all consideration of infants. Lamenting this subterfuge, Williams insisted that any discussion of policy is incomplete which ignored the problem of duly baptized infants who come of age without showing cause for excommunication; the church must determine the standing of persons baptized in infancy who attain maturity, possess doctrinal knowledge, lead nonscandalous lives, and evince a sincere desire to be godly. Reiterating the conclusions of the Synod of 1662, Williams granted such persons membership in the visible church. "At present," he insisted, the church cannot differentiate the unsanctified from those who are "professors of the Gospel of Christ." And he echoed Stoddard in arguing that admission to any one privilege or sacrament of the church was grounds for admission to them all, including the Lord's Supper: "I confess, I know of no Members of the Church, unless Persons under Censure, or scandalously ignorant, or immoral, but what the Church ought to admit to Communion & Privileges of Members in compleat Standing; if they are capable of receiving and enjoying them, and desire to do so." The question in debate is therefore the kind of evidence the church must expect "of the Saintship of those who are admitted to the outward Privileges of the Covenant of Grace."[^003-note174]

From this vantage, Williams construed Edwards to be saying that the church must require "the highest Evidence a Man can give of Sincerity." Edwards' scheme requires that candidates utter "words giving

<!-- p. 71 -->

an Account of their Experience of the sanctifying Work of God's Spirit on their Hearts." Picking up on the distinction Edwards had drawn between negative and positive judgment, Williams asserted that his opponent was expecting the church to make "a positive Judgment, that the man is a real Christian." But is the church equipped to go beyond the outward signs of sincerity? Consistent with what Stoddard had said, Williams declared that the church lacks the means of accomplishing a positive discrimination. Instead, the church must accept "the Profession & Engagement itself…taking it in the most favourable Sense that it can bear," a point he supported by emphasizing the distinction between the "External Exhibition" of the covenant of grace, which is "all that is visible in this world," and an inward or internal sense that remains hidden and mysterious.[^003-note175]

In support of his position, Williams offered three general reasons. The first proceeds from the fact that "Christ in his public visible Dealings with the Church" never acted as the "Searcher of Hearts." Accordingly, Williams held that the church is to found its judgment concerning church admission "only upon the visible Profession & Behaviour of Men." The church is to exercise a "rational Judgment of Charity." The second reason reinforces the first by canvasing biblical history to show that "Christ has in Fact always acted thus in his outward Dispensations toward his Church." Thus in Old Testament times, "God took all Israel into Covenant" without requiring any evidence of regeneration. Williams asserted as his third reason the psychological and theological premise that "true Desires of Grace are Grace." There will always be uncertainty about the "secret Working" of God's Spirit in "the hearts of other men." Hence he differentiates how the church made its judgments in "granting the Privileges of the visible Kingdom of Christ" from how the judgment is made of "the final State of Men." The Stoddardean conclusion from this line of reasoning is inescapable: "And since 'tis God's Will that his Church should admit all such visible Saints, it follows that the Lord's Supper is a converting Ordinance to such of them as are converted."[^003-note176]

Williams went on to defend Stoddard against the charge that his way of doing things allows (or indeed requires) the church to admit the very worst of sinners to the Lord's Table. Here, he argued, Edwards had misread his grandfather, who said only that the unsanctified

<!-- p. 72 -->

should not be excluded merely because of their "Want of sanctifying Grace."
