What is more, everyone who entered into covenant, whether sanctified or not, was making "a professed Subjection to Christ, and giving up themselves to be taught, ruled, & led by him in the Gospel way to Salvation."[^003-note177] Evangelical that he was, Williams did agree with Edwards that true piety is what communicants ought to bring to the Lord's Table, and, like Stoddard before him, he warned that it is "not visibly entring into Covenant with God, that will give Men just Ground of Hope of entring into Heaven." Members of the visible church who "rest in an outward Profession…without true Faith & sincere Repentance, will be dreadfully disappointed, when the trying Time shall come."[^003-note178] Yet it was wrong to impose the rule of sanctifying grace, for the judging of true faith and sincere repentance lies beyond the purview of the instituted church. Only the Separates think otherwise, and since Edwards declares that he has rejected the Separatist pretension of possessing a "Spirit of Discerning," he should either modify his position or acknowledge his inconsistency.

There is only one standpoint from which Edwards' scheme may appear tenable. Williams granted, as did Edwards and Stoddard, that assurance of salvation is attainable, "and where it is attained, and for so long as it is preserved," Edwards' scheme is practicable. But the major difficulty remains: "how to practice where it is not attained; and how Christians can act 'till they are free from Doubts." For the church in its present condition a less ideal but more realistic procedure has been established. God requires all who hear the gospel to believe, to repent, and to "attend on all the Ordinances which he hath appointed in his Word; and diligently to use all Means instituted for their Salvation…and engage to fulfil the Terms of the Covenant of Grace." The Holy Spirit will encourage some who do these things. Others who may feel that they lack the assistance of saving grace—who act on the basis of "Moral Sincerity"—are nonetheless fully entitled to "use and enjoy the Ordinances of Salvation" and are likely to benefit from them.[^003-note179]

Williams thus reaffirmed the reasoning that drove Stoddard to sever the connection between assurance of salvation and the Lord's Supper; where assurance is lacking, why make things worse by barring people from the means of grace? Williams predicted that a stricter system would intensify the distress of persons unsure of their salvation.

<!-- p. 73 -->

Like his father before him, he defended the connection between family and church privileges, arguing that

> All the Seed therefore of visible Believers who are baptized, are Seed sown by Christ in his Field the Church. When they grow up under the Education of the Church, and come for the Privilege and Seal of the Lord's Supper, I cannot find out why they have not as good a Right to it as their Fathers & Brethren that we call the Church.

Williams closed by hinting that the issue of admission to the Lord's Simper was really about power. If Edwards was proposing to decide all by himself who should be admitted, then this made him "like Nebuchadnezzer or a Popish priest."[^003-note180]

Jonathan Ashley based his critique of the *Humble Inquiry* on the traditional distinction between visible saintship and regeneration: "Men may be visible Saints, when we make no Judgment about the State of their Souls." For him, the category of visible saint comprehended "such who renounce Idolatry, and all heathenish Practices, who receive the Gospel, and are baptized." Beyond this the church was unable to proceed. The pastoral consequences of Edwards' scheme would be disastrous: "Who dare come, unless he is fully assured? If he has any the least Doubt, will he dare to approach the Lord's Table, lest the Lord command him to be bound Hand and Foot, and be cast into outer Darkness?" Further, Edwards' scheme did not take account of the need of "natural Men" to "attend upon the Duties of Religion." Ashley also challenged the uses of Scripture in the *Humble Inquiry*.[^003-note181]

#### Misrepresentations Corrected

Edwards was unwilling to allow someone else the last word.[^003-note182] In the spring of 1752, several months after he had moved to Stockbridge, Edwards responded to Solomon Williams in *Misrepresentations Corrected, and Truth Vindicated*. The treatise, which was published late that

<!-- p. 74 -->

year, is divided into three parts, the first treating concisely the "general misrepresentations" that Williams makes of the *Humble Inquiry*, the second providing a cogent examination of Williams' own scheme, and the third offering a series of remarks on his way of reasoning.

Edwards asserted in the first place that Williams had missed the point of the *Humble Inquiry*. The controversy in Northampton did not have to do with "the *degree of evidence*," as Williams said, but rather with "what was the thing to be made evident; whether *real godliness*, or *moral sincerity*?" Edwards also insisted that his intention was not to refute Stoddard but to defend himself in the controversy with Northampton.[^003-note183]

Edwards next considered ten related misrepresentations of "principles and tenets" expounded in the *Humble Inquiry*. He denied categorically the allegation that he was demanding the "highest evidence a man can give." To the contrary, he has asked for "some outward manifestation, that ordinarily rendered the thing probable," a view consistent with his repeated statement that the "point of difference was entirely the matter of profession, and the thing to be made visible; not the degree of evidence or visibility." Quoting a passage from a letter he had written to Peter Clark and citing two "drafts of the covenant, or forms of a public profession of religion" that he had been willing to accept, Edwards declared that these texts refute Williams' contention that he demanded the highest evidence.[^003-note184]

The next three misrepresentations involve language. Edwards complained that Williams misconstrued such phrases as "a positive judgment," a "probability of ten to one," and "singly taken," all of them used in the *Humble Inquiry* in connection with the status of the groups described in the New Testament as taken into communion together, and interpreted by Williams as indicating that Edwards demands assurance of salvation of everyone coming to the Lord's Table. The fifth misrepresentation is the suggestion that Edwards insists on "a certainty of others' regeneration," a view he expressly rejects. Misrepresentations six through nine deal with attempts on Williams' part to link Edwards with the excesses of enthusiasm and Separatism.

The remaining pages of *Misrepresentations Corrected* are devoted to an attack on Williams' scheme (part 2) and an expose of his fallacious reasoning (part 3). Edwards begins by constructing a threefold argument

<!-- p. 75 -->

based on Williams' "concessions," their "plain consequences," and their "inconsistence…with the lawfulness of unsanctified persons coming to the Lord's Supper." In the first step of the argument Edwards assembles a composite of more than a score of statements from *The True State of the Question* in which Williams appears to be on non-Stoddardean ground, as, for example, when he says that "none ought to be admitted, but such as openly profess and declare an hearty consent to the covenant of grace," and so forth. Next, Edwards shows that the necessary consequence is a contradiction, that persons would be required to look for "such a qualification in themselves…to determine whether they *may* come: when yet they may come whether they have it or no."[^003-note185] Would it be reasonable, Edwards asks, to imagine that God would give men without grace a lawful right to the Lord's Supper as a converting ordinance and at the same time insist that they exhibit evidence that they have grace?

The inconsistencies in Williams' scheme are traced to several mistaken assumptions. The most important of these is Williams' "notion of a public profession of godliness in terms of an indeterminate and double signification." Williams seems to allow consent to the covenant to be made in terms that do not allow anyone to know whether "the consent signified by the words is a gracious consent." Hence it becomes possible for Williams to affirm that "nothing should be expressed in the words of the profession, but what some unsanctified man may say, and speak true." This principle allows someone to use words in a double sense—to profess godliness, but in a way that signifies "two entirely distinct things, either moral sincerity, or real piety." And if someone should actually use words in this double way, Edwards charges him with being "guilty of deceitful equivocation."[^003-note186]

A second untenable assumption, closely akin to the ambiguity of profession, is the idea of a "visibility without apparent probability." Stoddard had maintained that, according to the rule established by God, "more unconverted persons will be admitted than converted." To Williams' defense of this statement Edwards replies, "That cannot be a *credible* visibility or appearance, which is not a *probable* appearance. To say, a thing is credible and not probable, is a contradiction."[^003-note187]

<!-- p. 76 -->

Edwards concludes his analysis of Williams' scheme by reiterating that the practice of explicitly owning the covenant is a divine institution. As Edwards points out, Williams himself has asserted that the ground of the public judgment includes "a hearty consent to the term of the covenant of grace, and engagement on the part of a person to fulfill it." This kind of statement becomes an additional instance of inconsistencies in the *True State*.

The third part of *Misrepresentations Corrected* contains comments on Williams' "exceptionable way of reasoning" and some final remarks on several issues. Edwards enumerates ten questionable "methods" that Williams employs and provides a near-exhaustive catalogue of examples. In the closing seven sections, Edwards gathers up a few loose ends, reiterates familiar points, and returns again to certain passages in Scripture.

An example is Judas' alleged partaking of the Lord's Supper. Edwards asserts that there can be no more argument "drawn from this to prove that it is lawful for men to partake of the Lord's Supper without sanctifying grace…than that it is lawful for them to partake without moral sincerity." And since Williams insists on moral sincerity as a basic requirement, the argument violates a "maxim of undoubted verity" that an argument "can avail nothing to the purpose it is brought for" if it contradicts both positions.[^003-note188] Here again, Edwards reiterates his objections to the Stoddardean conception of moral sincerity.

In the last four sections Edwards recapitulates and supplements arguments developed more fully in the *Humble Inquiry*. In section 14 he denies that children of visible saints, born in covenant, are ipso facto entitled to the privileges of the covenant. In 15, he deals with the Stoddardean argument about none coming except those who "know themselves to be converted"; the criterion of certainty worked as much against Williams, Edwards argues, as against his position. Section 16 is about assurance and confusion. Characteristically, Edwards asserts that it is the "negligence and sin" of believers that causes them to suffer "torment." Section 17 has to do with attending all "external covenant Duties." Edwards denies that his scheme required that God command and forbid the same thing at the same time.

At this point the text ends abruptly, to be followed by an "Appendix" in which Edwards addresses the Northampton congregation. He warns his former parishioners of the danger of being "led quite off

<!-- p. 77 -->

from" evangelical principles that Stoddard had affirmed. To follow Williams is to open the way to "Arminianism, and other loose notions in religion."[^003-note189]

#### Edwards' "Narrative"

The last of the documents in this volume is Jonathan Edwards' "Narrative"[^003-note190] of the Northampton controversy from its inception to the summoning of the council that met in June 1750. It details the negotiations that unfolded in the aftermath of the change of mind he announced to his congregation in February 1749. These negotiations were prompted by the intense and persisting hostility to his ministry among the great majority of church members and townspeople. Attempting to delay the rush to judgment that would end his career in Northampton, Edwards pleaded for a "fair hearing" of his ideas. He wanted everyone to read the *Humble Inquiry* and, this effort failing, to gain permission to preach the substance of the book. He urged the church to admit a handful of persons who were willing to satisfy the new condition of profession, and, after the members voted to cease celebrating the Lord's Supper, he asked that the sacrament be restored. The church members granted him none of these requests, but a council of ministers acknowledged his right to preach as he willed. In February and March 1750 he gave a series of lectures to an audience consisting mostly of "strangers" from outside the town.

Edwards had two other objectives. When it became inevitable that a council would be called to advise on the controversy, he insisted on the privilege not only of selecting a certain number of its members, but also of choosing them from outside Hampshire County. As he said frankly to the church and to a council called in December 1749 to advise on this very question, he was at odds with most of his ministerial neighbors and wanted persons on the council who were sympathetic to is person and point of view. He was finally accorded the privilege of acting two such delegations. The council that met in June 1750

<!-- p. 78 -->

consisted of five ministers and churches nominated by the church and five by Edwards; the church at Cold Spring, one of his five, refused, however, to send a lay delegate, leaving a council of nineteen persons that divided ten to nine on the issue of Edwards' immediate dismissal.[^003-note191]

Edwards' other objective was to redress his reputation. No sooner had he announced his change of mind than rumors began to spread that he had concealed his thinking from his congregation and was motivated in doing so by ill will and financial self-interest. The church and precinct conveyed some of these charges in a "set of arguments in writing" that was presented to the council of June 1750. This document does not survive, but it was later described as containing "some severe…imputations on Mr. Edwards." So too the majority of the council of June 1750 referred in its "result" to having "heard of some stories spread Abroad, reflecting upon Mr. Edwards' Sincerity, with Regard to the Change of his Sentiments about the qualifications for full Communion." We are left to infer the substance of the case against Edwards from his comment in the "Narrative" that he was suspected of rejecting a candidate for church membership "from personal prejudice, and that my alleging scruples was only to cloak my ill will"; from the glimpse we catch in the same document of Seth Pomeroy asserting in a church meeting that Edwards "regarded his own temporal interest more than the good of the church"; from depositions Edwards assembled for the council of June 1750 that deal with the timing and publicity of his change of mind;[^003-note192] and from passages in Samuel Hopkins' *Life and Character of the late Reverend Mr. Jonathan Edwards* (1765). For example, a long, apologetic paragraph in the *Life* has to do with Edwards' willingness to suffer financially from his decision, a response, it seems clear, to accusations that he hid his change of mind in order not to jeopardize his large salary. Acknowledging that "beggary as well as disgrace stared Edwards full in the face, if he persisted in his principles," Hopkins went on to say, using almost the very words of the townspeople, that Edwards "had the opportunity and the temptation to escape" these dire consequences "by concealing his principles." But in language that evoked the passion of Christ, Hopkins described his

<!-- p. 79 -->

mentor as someone who "counted the cost, and deliberately took up the cross…and in direct opposition to all worldly views and motives."[^003-note193]

The "Narrative" is thus a document shaped by the situation in Northampton and perhaps especially by the attacks on Edwards' reputation and his concern for any future "usefulness." In response, he was relentless in arguing that the church and precinct were unreasonable in refusing to debate the theological issue. He also asserted that church members "unlearned" in divinity should respect his authority. As for those members, they voted with virtual unanimity from the start that Edwards could no longer be their pastor unless he returned to his former way of thinking. Of the many signs of their mood, none is more revealing than their refusal to continue receiving the sacrament of the Lord's Supper from his hands. From time to time in New England church history, ministers (including Edwards' father, Timothy, in his East Windsor, Connecticut, parish) refused to administer the sacrament to a congregation or to certain members. Here, the tables were turned. In his *Farewell Sermon* Edwards turned the tables once again by imagining the fate of his congregation on the day of the Last Judgment.

Conflict over Edwards' reputation erupted anew in May 1751 when a small group of Northampton residents requested the advice of another council on whether they should form themselves into a congregation, with Edwards as the minister. Once again the town produced a "remonstrance" that was "everywhere larded with…sarcastical…insinuations" and that contained "divers direct, grievous and criminal charges."[^003-note194] Meanwhile the minority on the council of June 1750 had denounced the majority, which responded in kind. Edwards prepared to join in the fray with a public letter to his ally William Hobby, though he apparently decided against publishing it. His critics replied through the newspapers. The scales tipped in Edwards' direction when Joseph Hawley, Jr., a key figure in arguing the town's case before the councils of June 1750 and May 1751, sent him an apologetic letter in 1754. Hawley addressed a second letter of apology in 1760 to the Rev. David Hall of Sutton. Samuel Hopkins made this letter public in his *Life* of Edwards.[^003-note195]

<!-- p. 80 -->

#### "Backwards and Forwards": Edwards and the Boundaries of Tradition

Solomon Williams may have misread the *Humble Inquiry* when he interpreted "credibility" to mean the "highest degree of evidence" and implied that Edwards was akin to the Separates. Yet when other contemporaries read it in ways that departed from Edwards' preferred interpretation, we may suspect that the text contained ambiguities of which he was unaware or, more likely, that he wished to control on his own terms.

Even before the *Humble Inquiry* came off the press, Edwards was contending with the rumor (which reached Peter Clark in Salem Village) that he had thrown in his lot with the Separates or radical New Lights.[^003-note196] It was in the interests of his opponents in the ministry to encourage these rumors and to represent him as requiring "sanctifying grace" of candidates for church membership. So the majority of the council that met in 1750 declared in its published report, basing this judgment on a passage in the *Humble Inquiry*. Chester Williams, a member of the majority, supported this reading of the *Humble Inquiry* in a letter he published in the *Boston Gazette* of June 16, 1752. Williams "freely owned" that Edwards was not proposing that a candidate "say he was converted, or godly." Was it not the case, however, that Edwards' alternative to conversion, the "Profession of Godliness," amounted to very nearly the same thing? Williams adduced several pieces of evidence that sustained a reading of profession as signifying "real Sanctification": the passage in the *Religious Affections* in which Edwards described a profession of the "essentials of Christianity" as "the same as to profess that" someone "experiences those things"; the early pages of the *Humble Inquiry*, in which Edwards linked profession to "piety of heart"; and language from the May 1750 letter to Peter Clark. On the basis of these statements, Williams concluded that the majority of the council had not misspoken in characterizing the issue in the Northampton controversy.[^003-note197]

<!-- p. 81 -->

To another group of readers, the *Humble Inquiry* seemed appropriately radical. Certain Separates interpreted Edwards to be saying that "none have a Right to the Lord's Supper but real Saints, and that there is no half-way Covenant." A Separate Congregationalist-turned-Baptist, Isaac Backus, expressed his satisfaction that Edwards had affirmed the "capital article that the Separate churches were built upon," that baptism in the apostolic church was a "token of…being visibly regenerated." In the words of another leading Separate, Ebenezer Frothingham, the movement "highly esteemed" the *Humble Inquiry*, especially that passage in which Edwards described visible saintship as "even of that Sort of Saintship which the Saints in Heaven have." Was this not the same as what the Separates were maintaining? Yet it puzzled Frothingham that, having gone this far, Edwards reaffirmed the distinction between the visible and the real and, by doing so, split the category of saint into two. This was to repeat the error of allowing hypocrites into the church, the very error Separates accused traditional Congregationalists of making, and that Edwards himself had condemned in Stoddard. Voicing his confusion, Frothingham wondered if Edwards were someone who wrote "in a misterious Manner, backwards and forwards, about this Visibility"?[^003-note198]

A more moderate reading came from Peter Clark. He was relieved to learn from Edwards directly that he was not "designing to have a pure Church consisting only of true Converts." Once this misunderstanding was removed, and after Clark had read the *Humble Inquiry*, he told Edwards that he was "at a Loss to apprehend wherein the main ground of the Controversy, between you, and your people lies." He understood Edwards to be saying that the person making a profession could explicitly declare that "he did not think himself Converted," a

<!-- p. 82 -->

reading Clark based on a statement Edwards made at the outset of the *Humble Inquiry*, where he declared that persons coming to the sacrament "need not esteem themselves" as such. Were this the case, and were it also true that Edwards was not asking for "Evidence of a Work of Conversion in" candidates "even to their own assurance," Clark could then envisage an "accommodation" between pastor and people on more or less the customary ground of Congregational tradition.[^003-note199]

These diverse readings of the *Humble Inquiry* remind us that, no less than Peter Clark or Solomon Williams, Edwards was seeking a middle way between extremes. These readings also alert us to changes he was making in the boundaries of the path that tradition had beaten. His revised boundaries come into view when we ask, once again, whether Edwards expected candidates for communion to be real saints; and why he broke with his grandfather's thinking. The correct answer to the first of these involves a two-part statement. Edwards said that the visible church could never know for certain who was truly saved and who was not; because it could not discern an internal work of grace, it had to rely on profession. Yet he went on to declare that the persons making a profession had to "esteem themselves truly gracious." Profession rested on and made visible "the real existence" of what was professed; it had to be sincere, in the sense of testifying to something that was actually there. Edwards rejected out of hand any attempt to qualify the meaning of sincerity and visibility: "The thing which must be visible and probable, in order to *visible* saintship, must be saintship *itself*, or real grace and true holiness…and not mere moral sincerity." And he would allow no ambiguity about profession as a sign. His theory of the sign was effectively an antitheory, a rule of morals rather than a rule of language: it was morally right that the sign and what it signified be one and the same and morally wrong for profession or visibility to detach itself from what it signified. He acknowledged that profession differed from "godliness itself," which was "internal and out of sight." But he demanded that profession be explicit, and he insisted that candidates for church membership esteem themselves "gracious persons."[^003-note200]

To misread Edwards as requiring the "highest degree of evidence" and not "credibility," as he accused Solomon Williams of doing, is thus to misread him only slightly. His position must be differentiated from

<!-- p. 83 -->

that of the Separates in two respects: he never accepted the test of experience (and therefore, contrary to what some modern interpreters have too casually assumed, he never proposed restoring the procedure of a relation); and he rejected the claim that the spiritually enlightened could discern who was a saint. But his position must also be differentiated from the Congregational tradition. In the context of that tradition he was repudiating the customary explanation of the relation between church membership and the individual quest for saving grace. Most of his predecessors in New England understood this relation to be open-ended and inconclusive because of the difference between the external, or federal, covenant that included all the seed, and the internal covenant of grace. For nearly a century, the clergy in New England had used this distinction, together with the elastic catchwords "charity" and "profession," to justify broadening the basis of church membership. They had justified that process for a second reason, their diagnosis of the problem of "weak believers" who lacked assurance of salvation: better, they had argued, that the church include the lame and halting and serve as means of grace to the many than function only as the preserve of the few who achieved assurance of salvation.

Solomon Williams placed himself in this tradition when he quoted the Synod of 1662 on the difference between the highest evidence of sincerity, and the lowest.[^003-note201] Edwards stepped outside this tradition in manifesting a distaste for charity, in advocating a policy of strictness as the remedy for weak believers, and in limiting the range of meanings encompassed by the act of profession. And although he warded off the Separates and their criterion of experience by clinging to profession, he threw all of his intellectual weight into sharpening the boundary between grace and its simulacres. In so doing, he detached himself from the middle way that so many others had preferred and that, in broad outline, Calvin had articulated in the sixteenth century.

Should it be surprising that, hemmed in as he was, Edwards would seem to readers of the *Humble Inquiry* both daring and moderate?

Why did he change his mind about the nature of the church? The answer to this question may seem tantalizingly simple: the Great Awakening, or else the Arminian threat. Yet as we have seen, Edwards spent much of the 1740s reiterating a traditional ecclesiology against

<!-- p. 84 -->

the Separates. In and of itself the Awakening did not precipitate a change of mind. Neither was Arminianism the crucial factor; there is but a single direct reference to Arminianism in the whole of the *Religions Affections*, the term is peripheral to the *Humble Inquiry*, and there is no evidence to support his insinuation that Solomon Williams and the people of Northampton were tending toward that frame of mind.

The key lies in the situation in Northampton and in Edwards' life-long concern, which deepened in the aftermath of the Great Awakening, with the difference between true and false spirituality. As his ministry rapidly deteriorated in the aftermath of the bad book affair, Edwards came to think of most of his congregation as hypocrites. In reacting against his congregation, he was also reacting against the intermingling of the social and the religious that constituted popular religion. The intensity of his reaction against what he deemed hypocrisy is evidenced in the sentiment he expressed in the *Humble Inquiry*: reversing what he once had said, he argued that it were "better, to have a few real living Christians" kept out of the church than to admit any who might be false believers. Here again, he distanced himself from his more pastorally-minded predecessors in the Congregational tradition, the line that stretched back through Increase Mather to John Cotton.[^003-note202]

What Edwards did in the *Humble Inquiry* was to connect his reaction against the townspeople with the psychology of religion he laid out in the *Religious Affections*. A decade of experience and reflection had persuaded him anew of the evangelical premise that the saints were truly different from the unregenerate in their inner and outer lives. Convinced of the reality of difference, he wanted to restore the connections between this difference and the traditional practices of Congregationalism, the acts of professing the covenant and participating in the two sacraments. By the end of the 1740s he was blaming the collapse of the revival on the failure to maintain those connections—that is, the failure to force the issue between the "precious" and the "vile" against any counterforces, be these popular religion, pride, Arminianism, the pastoral issue of perplexity, or the Congregational tradition. So he declared in the preface he contributed to Joseph Bellamy's *True Religion Delineated* (1750),[^003-note203] and so he said repeatedly to his Scottish correspondents. Ever more disenchanted with "that bastard,

<!-- p. 85 -->

mischievous charity, by which Satan keeps men asleep,"[^003-note204] he turned to the instrument of explicit and sincere profession, profession that could flow only from the affective, willing, and sincere self. Thus he brought together what his grandfather had decided were better kept apart, the capacity to judge between true and false piety and admission to the church.

Edwards placed his decision in the context of an ever-threatening "triumph of the open enemies of religion."[^003-note205] Historians must step outside this rhetoric and reclaim the full spectrum of opinion among evangelicals in the 1740s, a spectrum that encompasses Elisha and Solomon Williams and the very many others who shared with them a different understanding of the visible church and how it should function. It is equally vital that historians step outside Edwards' hostile judgment of the people of Northampton. Stoddardeanism did not nun the townspeople into hypocrites; if anything, scrupulosity persisted in Northampton under Stoddard. Neither did they pass suddenly from sincerity to hypocrisy in the 1740s. The structures of popular religion were well in place before the revivals and outlasted them. Only if we adopt a wider understanding of religion, culture, and society in the eighteenth century do we grasp the nature of the politics that transformed the question of access to baptism into the controversy that cost Edwards his pulpit.

From start to finish the Northampton controversy unfolded within a relatively narrow range of terms and categories. We look in vain in the *Humble Inquiry* for a statement of Edwards' broader vision of the church. He explored the objective glory of God and the progress of the elect toward the kingdom in the "Miscellanies," in the sermons published long after his death as *The History of the Work of Redemption*, and in *An Humble Attempt to Promote Union in Prayer* (1748).[^003-note206] But the struggle in Northampton was rooted in circumstances peculiar to that town and church, to the revivals of the 1740s, and to the Congregational tradition as it had developed in New England. Edwards as a philosophical theologian transcended these circumstances. The treatises contained in this volume cannot but remind us that he was also a person of his time and place.

<!-- p. 86 -->

#### Legacies of the Northampton Controversy

The two treatises in which Edwards explained and defended his understanding of the church were not reprinted in America in the eighteenth century.[^003-note207] Copies of the *Humble Inquiry* were already hard to come by in 1750, or so Peter Clark complained to Edwards. In the initial decades their influence seems to have been as limited as their circulation, for Joseph Bellamy and Edward Billings were among the few who advanced the Edwardsean program. Thereafter, the pace of debate began to pick up.[^003-note208] How these debates played themselves out—in what ways Edwards was invoked, in what ways new issues were introduced—has yet to be charted by historians with any thoroughness. In particular, we know almost nothing of the politics and social sources of the movement to reject the halfway covenant, a movement that, by the early nineteenth century, had gained much ground within Congregationalism. But the triumph of the purists was short-lived, for the liberalism that came in with Horace Bushnell broke entirely with the issues of covenant, sincerity, and assurance that had dominated the Congregational tradition for two centuries. As the tide of strictness weakened and began to ebb, the treatises that some had once looked on as weapons against false religion slipped from view. In the first half of the twentieth century they were passed over by anthologists and ignored by those commentators bent on recovering Edwards as philosophical theologian.

#### Note on the Texts

The texts presented here are replicated from the first editions of *A Letter*, *Humble Inquiry*, and *Misrepresentations*. Lists of errata accompanying the original texts have been followed. The copy of *A Letter* in the collection of the Beinecke Rare Book and Manuscript Library, Yale University, is William Williams' presentation copy to Edward Wigglesworth. Errata in this copy corrected in pen by Williams have been incorporated into this edition. These three books were written, prepared,

<!-- p. 87 -->

and copy-edited by Edwards himself (in the latter stages of the final two assisted by his friend and literary agent, the Reverend Thomas Foxcroft of Boston). The text of Edwards' "Narrative," described below, presents its own set of problems quite distinct from these other works.

In addition to the editorial guidelines outlined at the beginning of this volume, an effort has been made in this edition to preserve original punctuation. However, certain emendations had to be made owing to the idiosyncrasies of eighteenth-century printing. Double punctuation is been eliminated. Some commas have been added, such as before and after page references, book titles, and dates as needed. Also, where the original uses brackets as parentheses, these have been changed to parentheses to avoid confusion with editorial insertions. Abbreviated names (for example, "Mr. B.," "Mr. W——ms," or "J.E.") are spelled out without comment to prevent the unnecessary proliferation of brackets.

There are several manuscript notebooks that contain notes and drafts for the *Humble Inquiry* and *Misrepresentations*. In the Edwards Papers at the Beinecke Library (f. 41.4) is a "working" notebook labeled by Edwards as "Sacrament Book I" that contains rough notes towards the *Inquiry*. It is a small quarto-sized book composed mostly of salvaged letter covers, stitched into a cover of stiff paper. There were at least four such books at one time, since in this remaining one he refers (p. 2) to "B. IV. p. 83." The pages are numbered 1, 40, 21, 6–7, 10–13, 20–25, 28–35, 38–47, and 70, reflecting Edwards' practice of tearing out pages that were no longer of any use to him. All of the entries in the book, which vary in length from just a few words to several pages, are deleted with a vertical line, or "use mark," a method Edwards employed to indicate he had either made use of an entry or had decided not to use it. The entries treat a variety of subjects, for example, public profession, observations on Old Testament practices, John the Baptist, the parables of the ten virgins and of the wedding garment, the covenant, rules for judging who is converted, and notes on objections to and the "method," or organization, of the treatise. There is even a list of transitional "Expressions" that Edwards records tor later use.

The preached version, most likely written from notes for the *Inquiry* either concurrent with or shortly after the completion of the treatise itself, is extant as a lengthy lecture series on Ezekiel 44:9. This discourse, in three booklets totaling 225 pages in length, is Edwards'

<!-- p. 88 -->

defense of his views that he delivered at Northampton from February 15 to March 22, 1750. The first booklet (42 pages) is located at the Beinecke Library, and the remaining ones are at the Franklin Trask Library, Andover Newton Theological School (f. ND5.9). Based on the same doctrine as the treatise, the lecture series is essentially the same as the printed work, though some points have been dropped or added, and there is necessarily some condensing. In addition, where the treatise downplays from a theoretical perspective the ability of saints to discern true faith in others, in the lecture Edwards seems to argue for that ability for practical reasons.

An advanced, possibly penultimate, draft of *Misrepresentations* is located at the Beinecke Library (f. 29); it is the only known complete draft of a treatise prepared for the press and published by Edwards in existence. Two quarto-sized books, bound in coarse brown paper and labeled by Edwards, "Answer to Williams—Printed," contain the draft. (A later owner of the manuscripts penciled the inscriptions "Bk. 3" and "Bk. 4" on the covers, but Edwards himself never identified them as such.) The first book, paginated 1–96 by Edwards, with many odd-sized scraps tipped in for additions, contains part I, 1 through part III, 1, and the second, numbered 1–84, has the remainder of the treatise as well as the appended letter to the Northampton church, and concludes with the preface. Comparisons of this draft with the printed work reveal that there are differences between the two, consisting of the reordering of passages as well as additions, deletions, and differences in wording.

Edwards' manuscript of his "Narrative" no longer exists, but a transcription of 136 quarto pages prepared by one of Sereno Dwight's amanuenses is in the Trask Library. Dwight printed what he called Edwards' "Journal" in the first volume of his edition of 1829 (pp. 313–98). The text used here is that of the Andover copyist, collated with Dwight's edition at the points where the copy has lacunae. Upon inspection, the copy is seen to preserve more aspects of Edwards' style, such as characteristic contractions, idioms, expressions, and mixing of past and present tenses and singular and plural subjects, whereas Dwight's text has evidence of free interpolation. Two fragments from the "Narrative" in Edwards' hand (Beinecke Library, f. 46) have been used at the appropriate places and indicated in the notes. Drafts of letters in Edwards' hand that he includes in the "Narrative" have also been used for verification where available.

Dwight did not have access to a number of documents that Edwards

<!-- p. 89 -->

meant to insert but did not at the time the "Narrative" was written. They include the result of the previous council, a letter by Edwards to Noah Cook and another to the Reverend Samuel Hopkins of West Springfield, letters from the Lower Hampshire Association to the Northampton church and to Edwards, and Peter Clark's letter to the Northampton church committee. The documents, printed here for the first time, are inserted at their proper places. Only one of the items Edwards intended to include—the recommendations of the council of February 7, 1750—has not been located.

[^003-note130]: JE told the Scottish minister John Erskine in May 1749 that, although he "formerly conformed to Stoddard's practice," he had had "difficulties with respect to it, which have been long increasing; till I dared no longer to proceed in the former way." Dwight ed., *1*, 276. He used very nearly the same words in the *Humble Inquiry* (below p. 169), in which he wrote that he was "formerly of his Stoddard's opinion…though never without some difficulties in my view, which I could not solve," and in the opening paragraph of his "Narrative" of the controversy. Important evidence comes from a deposition submitted to the council of 1750 by Sarah Edwards. She remembered conversations from 1746 in which JE spoke of his change of mind. But Sarah went on to quote him as still undecided: "He chose rather for the present to content Himself with giving some occasional Intimations of his opinion…and added, I am still looking & inquiring into this matter, and 'tis possible I may hereafter see otherwise." Iain H. Murray, *Jonathan Edwards, A New Biography* (Edinburgh, Banner of Truth Trust, 1987), p. 486. In another deposition dated June 13, 1750, Noah Parsons of Northampton reported that JE "manifested that He had thoughts of taking Pains and of making further inquery and talked of wrighting to divines beyond the seas about the matter But yet signified that He had alredy studied ye Point with great deligence and that He was greatly Established in it." These depositions, which echo JE's language (below pp. 169–70) that "by such means, after long searching, pondering, viewing and reading" he arrived at his position, were collected by JE in order to refute the townspeople's accusation that, out of self-interest, he concealed his change of mind. Three others that survive also refer to discussions in and around 1746. John Searle deposition (Hartford Seminary Foundation, Hartford, Connecticut); depositions by Joseph Bellamy and James Pierpont (Beinecke Library, Edwards Papers, f. 46). parenthetical

[^003-note136]: Ibid., *1*, 627, 629–30. JE had lost the "negative voice" (or veto) over congregational actions that Stoddard had exercised. Cf. ibid., *1*, 363. Tracy (*Jonathan Edwards, Pastor*, pp. 177–79) regards the issue of authority as stemming more from the fears of the congregation than from JE's position. See also Minkema, "Edwardses," chs. 3, 7. The problem of authority in JE's ministry was not simply a matter of ecclesiastical procedures. Early and late, he struggled to curb a temperamental impulse to judge and exclude others, an impulse he justified as essential to the life of the church and the work of the ministry. Perhaps because of the reactions this impulse provoked, he seems consistently to have imagined himself as surrounded by enemies and in ordination sermons of the mid-1740s likened ministers to the sintering Christ. But he could evoke the triumphant Christ and promise final victory to those who "maintained the exercise of discipline in the house of God" (*The true Excellency of a Minister of the Gospel* Boston, Rogers & Fowle for W. McAlpine, 1744, p. 22). In the *Farewell Sermon* he prophesied such a victory for himself at the day of judgment over the townspeople of Northampton. See also *Christ the great Example of Gospel Ministers* (Boston, T. Fleet, 1750); Dwight ed., *1*, 89; Tracy, *Jonathan Edwards, Pastor*, pp. 155–56. Even more remarkable is Sarah Edwards' sense (expressed in her narrative of spiritual experience) of "being chased from the town with the utmost contempt and malice, and of being left to perish with the cold." ## A Letter to the Author of the Pamphlet Called An Answer to the Hampshire Narrative

<!-- p. 91 -->

<!-- p. 93 -->

### The Preface

The publication of a pamphlet called *An Answer to the Hampshire Narrative*, having been the means to keep up the clamor that has been raised against us who disapproved of Mr. Breck's settlement at Springfield, we have for some months been silent, promising ourselves this advantage thereby, that those whose spirits have been heated, being by this time cooled, and prejudices on all sides much abated, everybody will be more ready to consider the matter with coolness and sedateness, and be under advantage to look on the case as it really is, and allow arguments their proper force. The author of the pamphlet which we endeavor to answer, having let us know by several passages in the book, viz. in page 53—56, etc. that he is a minister, was one of the council, and one that came from Boston, we have thought best, by directing a letter to him, to address ourselves to all the gentlemen who were concerned in the council with him.

<!-- p. 94 -->

### A Letter, Etc.

Reverend Sir,

We your brethren, in the calling of Jesus Christ, and ministry of his gospel, of the county of Hampshire, who from the beginning of your acting in the Springfield affair, have been looked upon, and treated by you, as especially, and above all others obnoxious: and in all your proceedings, from first to last, have been the butt of your resentment and obloquy, and especially in your book called *An Answer to the Hampshire Narrative*, have been treated with indignity and contempt, and represented with a great manifestation of disdain and insult as a set of wicked, contemptible men, looking upon it that you have gone out of the way of your duty, and acted much against the honor of Christ, and the interest of Christianity, and to the prejudice of the ministerial character, do think ourselves obliged, as we are your fellow Christians and brethren in the ministry, not only to vindicate ourselves, but to labor to lead you to a sense of your error, which though we have reason to fear, from the temper and prejudice you have discovered in your *Answer*, is not very likely to be successful; yet leaving the event with God, we think ourselves bound to endeavor. And would observe in general, that you have almost wholly overlooked the merits of the cause in dispute between us, and instead of that, have been pleased to divert your readers with such ludicrous and unfriendly reflections on our *Narrative* and conduct, as you have thought fit, for reasons best known to yourself. And therefore, for our own vindication and your conviction, we have thought it necessary to remark and reply to some of the exceptionable passages in it.

In pp. 1—2, where you distinguish those who disapproved of Mr. Breck's settlement at Springfield, and sent their protest against it, from those that were called to judge in the affair, speaking of the latter, you say, "Of which number were the eldest ministers in their own county," whereby 'tis insinuated, that the eldest ministers in the county acted, when you know that the true state of the case was thus, that the eldest minister of all in the county, and the eldest in the province but one, was one that disapproved and protested; the two next acted: the four next disapproved; and the next acted: which three

<!-- p. 95 -->

were all in the county that acted.[^004-note1] Now, sir, the case being thus, was not this that you gave an unfair representation: we appeal to all your readers that had their information only from your book, whether they han't been led by it, to apprehend the case quite different from what we have now represented. In the same place you blame us that we did not leave those eldest ministers that acted with others, to act according to their own light. And why, reverend sir, could not you, the ministers that come from Boston, leave them to act according to their own light, without taking such abundant pains in urging them to act against what they of themselves were inclined to, as you know you did the Rev. Mr. Chauncy, the eldest that acted, who has often declared, in the hearing of some of us, that had he not been exceedingly importuned, he would not have acted, and that he long resisted and opposed, but that you overcame him, at both times of the council's meeting. And the Rev. Mr. Devotion, before the council came up, did sufficiently declare in our hearing, his disinclination to act in the case; and there are many other concurring evidences, that he would not have acted had not you sent to him, urging him to it.

In p. 2, you boldly charge us with running this controversy into the public prints. Certainly you ought not thus to have declared this to the world before you knew it; and yet afterwards, before you get to the bottom of the page, you implicitly confess, that you don't know it; for you speak of the two letters in the *Boston Journal*,[^004-note2] as published by us, "or somebody that undertook our vindication": if it was only somebody that undertook our vindication, how does it thence follow, as you say, that we not being content that the matter should remain the subject of conversation only, run it into the public prints: and yet afterwards again, in the margin, you charge the publishing these letters at such a time, on us, as an instance of our unfair "way of managing"? Indeed, we none of us had any hand in publishing either of those

<!-- p. 96 -->

letters, and knew not that any such letters were published, or like to be published, or were in being, till we saw them in the public prints: and if they had been published by us, it would have been very injuriously said, that it was before anything was published on the other side: whereas you very well know, the complaint of Springfield Church to the General Assembly, was published in the *Boston Gazette*, and the letters referred to in your *Answer*, we suppose, were occasioned by that publication, and a stolen letter that was written on this affair, was before this exposed in the public prints, with ludicrous reflections, to render the author, and the cause he appeared in, ridiculous in the eyes of the world.[^004-note3]

Thus, sir, instead of our running our own writings first into print, those of your party stole 'em, and exposed 'em, and ridiculed 'em in the public prints. And then you write again, crying down both the ministers and magistrates of the county,[^004-note4] before ever we published anything at all: and this after you had, in a great measure filled the country with reproaches of us, and raised a general cry against us, as a set of ambitious, arbitrary, and unjust usurpers, in the principal part of the country, where we, by reason of our distance, have no other way to speak for ourselves but by the press: and then after all cry out of us for "running the matter into the public prints."

As to the things insisted on, pp. 3—5, we shall have occasion to speak afterwards. In pp. 5—6, after you had for two or three pages been ridiculing our Association, and its acts and pretensions, you say, "And when they" (i.e. associations) "come *ex officio*, to administer oaths, it seems also to entrench upon the authority of the civil magistrate"; and then in the margin you say to the world, "The form of an oath, or declaration taken by a particular minister, by order of an association, may be seen in the *Narrative*, p. 49, the first, we suppose, of the kind that has been given to the public, and therefore worthy of special notice." The thing referred to in the *Narrative*, is, that a particular minister in Connecticut took the evidence of certain persons, in order to be sent to Springfield, at the time of the sitting of the council there;[^004-note5]

<!-- p. 97 -->

and they in giving their evidence declared before God the searcher of all hearts, that their evidence was the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

Now, reverend sir, suppose this were indeed a proper oath, and this minister had been appointed to take it by the association to which he belonged, what is that to us that an association in Connecticut remote from us did so? As it is beside our intention to say anything in defense of the Association of the county of Windham, so we are well assured, that those gentlemen are well able to defend themselves, when it shall be needful for them to free themselves from apprehensions of the civil magistrate in their own colony, who have often heard of such kind of oaths or declarations, without any suspicion of the ministers entrenching upon their office. And we are very sorry that the reverend council have never heard of nor seen any such kind of oath or declaration in all the discipline of the Church of England, and of Scotland, or other Reformed churches abroad, which, if they had, it seems strange that they should think there was so much occasion to put the civil magistrate upon drawing his sword upon associations for presuming to do it.

In p. 9, after mentioning some things in the *Narrative* that you say are "low and trifling," you say, "Another pretty tale we are entertained with, in p. 63, there they tell us, 'that Mr. Breck, preaching from those words, "Many are the afflictions of the righteous" [Psalms 34:19], compared himself to David, Mordecai and other good men, and those who opposed him to Haman,' etc." Mayn't your reader have just ground to suspect that this is but a specimen of your way of judging and estimating things relating to Mr. Breck, in calling it a "pretty tale," and putting of it into the catalogue of things that you call "low and trifling," when it is related, that he that was so young, and not yet ordained, should in the pulpit, not only compare himself to David and Mordecai, and the neighboring ministers, that had been long settled and accepted in that work, and are old enough to be his fathers, to Haman? And may we not take it as a specimen of your impartiality? We would pray you, sir, to consider what you would think or say of any of us that are not so much younger than you, if we should in our pulpits, compare ourselves to Mordecai and you to Haman his cruel persecutor; would it be a pretty tale then? Would it not be horrid profaneness, and many other things as bad? And we would pray you also to consider how vehemently you have inveighed against us in your book for saying things of you that are far less than this. And though it be a low and trifling thing, not worthy to be mentioned for Mr. Breck to say this of his fathers in the pulpit, yet if they do but relate a testimony publicly

<!-- p. 98 -->

given by others, wherein there is something against Mr. Breck, how far is this from being a trifling matter? Instead of which they are ranked by you among those whose "tender mercies are cruelty"; and you cry out, "What can be more cruel, barbarous, more contrary to humanity as well as Christianity?" "What a spirit does this discover?" You say, in p. 10, this is not true, "and he did not make such a declaration as we speak of, and call God to witness that he was innocent of the things laid to his charge"; but though you positively deny it, yet Col. Dwight of Brookfield,[^004-note6] and several others that were present and heard him, have taken their oath to it before the justices of the county.

In p. 13, you say, that what we have written "discovers an evil and bitter, an uncharitable and unchristian temper and spirit." What occasion for this heaping of hard words? Was it from a Christian and charitable frame of spirit in you? Don't it savor of what you charge us with, p. 8, viz. a disposition "to lay on all the load that you could"? The first thing you mention as an evidence of our showing of such a spirit is, that we relate things that "don't enter into the merits of the cause"; and that therefore "the whole design of them must be only to fix, as far as we could do it, a mark of dishonor and disgrace where we would have it worn." Will you allow that, if this holds good, and is just arguing in our case, so it also is in your own in a like case? That if you insist on many things to our reproach, that don't in the least enter into the merits of the cause, that then we may justly argue, that it must be only to fix, as far as you could do it, a mark of dishonor and disgrace where you would have it worn? And that therefore it discovers in you an evil and bitter, an uncharitable and unchristian temper and spirit? And pray sir, consider how much it touched the merits of the cause, for you so much to insist upon the bulk of our book, with so much scoff and jeer; repeating it over and over so often, and declaring how it contained seven sheets (though yours contained no less) and that it was mounted to four shillings and six pence price (though yours was no less costly than ours) and how much did it concern the merits of the cause, for you, repeatedly and in a derisory manner, to mention it that we say in the title page of our book "Written by Themselves"? And how much does it concern the merits of the cause to insist, with so much ridicule, on our mean method of writing? That we "have thrust into the world a remarkable piece," and that we "don't appear to keep any

<!-- p. 99 -->

order or method throughout our whole book," that "things are oddly mixed and scattered," that "to trace our footsteps, by following us from page to page, would be little better than a goose chase," and that our book is "a large bundle of confusion," and that, we "repeat things in a manner that is perfectly troublesome and nauseous"; which observation you very often repeat, though we think there is no repetition that you mention but what may be vindicated from being impertinent, and that we also could show that there is no less of repetition in your book than in ours, were it worth the while to enter upon so trifling and childish a controversy.

Supposing it be so indeed, that we can't write so correctly and methodically as you can, or supposing you could make it manifest, that we did not know how to write well enough to appear in print, yet how does that alter the state of the argument, with regard to the merits of the cause? And what other end could you have in insisting on it, than to fix that mark of dishonor and disgrace upon us, that we have written in a weak and ridiculous manner?

You sarcastically say, p. 8, that our "repetitions are not vain, but serve mighty well to answer the very Christian design of our performance": we would pray you to consider what very Christian design you could have in these things. Is there anything in the manner of our saying these things, that you say don't enter into the merits of the cause, that shows that the whole design of them must be to fix a mark of dishonor and disgrace, and are from an evil and bitter spirit, etc.? And pray sir, let your own conscience speak, whether we said any of those things, in such a contemptuous manner, and in such bitter and opprobrious language, as you have said those things of us. And certainly, seeing you saw such a hatefulness and vileness in our doing as you say we did, and manifest such an abomination of it when you speak of it, you ought to have been so much further from it yourself.

In p. 14, after mentioning our pretenses of tenderness to Mr. Breck, you say, "Yet it seems they so far forgot their own cautions, that as soon as Mr. Breck left Springfield the first time, they let the papers from Connecticut go about the parish, when he was not there to make any answer for himself." In which you deal unjustly by us. Those papers from Connecticut were lodged in Mr. Hopkins' hands, and when the parish had chosen a committee to ask the advice of the ministers of the county, whether they should again make application to Mr. Breck, that committee went to Mr. Hopkins, and desired that they might have those papers to carry them to the ministers in the upper part of the

<!-- p. 100 -->

county (whose advice they intended first to ask) giving this as a reason for it, viz. that those gentlemen had heard the papers but once, and might be the better able to give advice, if they had a second view of them. Mr. Hopkins therefore (after cautioning them not to make any ill use of them) gave them the papers, and they being Mr. Breck's friends, he had no suspicion that they would use them to his damage, nor have we any reason to think they did: it is true they kept them much longer in their hands than was expected, and where they went we know not, but if they went about the parish to Mr. Breck's damage, Mr. Breck's friends are to blame for it, and not the ministers of the county: and we assure you that they never went about the parish any time, except while they were in the keeping of his friends of that parish.

And then you proceed, in pp. 14—17, to raise an exceeding outcry against us, as cruel, barbarous, unchristian and inhumane, and those whose tender mercies are cruelty, for publishing Mr. Clap's testimony, in which he declared wherein he supposed Mr. Breck had been wanting to the truth, in denying his stealing books in college, because herein is contained a mention of that crime, that he was then guilty of when he was so young, etc. Though herein you represent us as a most vile parcel of men, and worthy of the utmost detestation, yet we pray you with a little seriousness to consider whether or no your treatment of us, with respect to that matter, be right in the sight of God, and whether it han't been, on the contrary, exceeding unjust: what is it that we did, that we should be thus set forth as so exceeding black and vile? Our professed design in writing our book was to give the world a narrative or history of our proceedings in Mr. Breck's affair; being, as we thought, obliged thereto by the clamor that the country was filled with against us, as having been intolerably injurious in that affair: and in order to this, we gave an account of and recite at large, that information or testimony that we received from the Rev. Mr. Clap that was the occasion and main foundation of those our proceedings: and how was it possible for us to give the world a narrative of our proceedings, and not give an account of that? For all our proceedings were upon those testimonies that were sent: how can any judicature, or any that act publicly in a cause, when they are complained of for maladministration or injustice, vindicate themselves without giving an account of those informations or testimonies on which they proceeded; and when they do so in their own necessary vindication, is it just to cry out of them as the most monstrous and barbarous wretches for so doing?

<!-- p. 101 -->

The Association, while the affair was in their hands, never had proceeded any further than only to insist on a particular hearing of the case, Mr. Breck and the witnesses being face to face, in order to our concurring in his settlement at Springfield: and this you know is what we were especially cried out against for, that we would not accept of his vindication, or account of himself in an examination without this. We judged that the information we had had against his principles and morals rendered such a particular inquiry necessary, and this we were concerned to show to the world for our vindication, and how could we possibly do it without letting the world know what these informations or testimonies were? It was necessary that we should relate those testimonies as they were; if we had published only a part and concealed a part, should we not have given a handle to those who stand ready to reproach us? Could we have expected any other from yourself, who are so ready to take all advantages against us, than that you would cry out that our testimonies, on which we proceeded, were such as we durst not let the world see? And it was especially necessary that that part of the information that respected his veracity should be declared, for it was particularly on the account of this that we think ourselves to be vindicated, for not accepting what he should say of himself without hearing him and the witnesses face to face, which was the thing we were especially condemned for: and we were brought to this necessity of giving this narrative very much by Mr. Breck's own reproaches and revilings of us, of which his comparing us to Haman in the pulpit, which you call a "pretty tale," is a specimen: this we think would have justified us in publishing that testimony, though this matter, which one thing testified has a reference to, had been of that nature as would have greatly wronged his reputation; but you yourself seem to speak as though it had very little of that tendency– that we must by no means be allowed to speak of Mr. Breck's former faults, or so much as give an account of testimonies that contain a reference to them, though laid under never so great necessity by him himself, by his reproaches of us, and though our names never so much suffered in the country by them, and though these faults being published tend very little to his discredit (as by your own arguing they do), [which] comes to this, that we ought to be vastly more tender of Mr. Breck's credit than our own, even to that degree that we are obliged to yield up our reputation a sacrifice to his revilings, and to be at his mercy rather than vindicate ourselves in the least to the wrong of his reputation. What we do is barely to recite Mr. Clap's testimony, wherein Mr. Breck's stealing books is referred to,

<!-- p. 102 -->

without one reflection on that particular, or any hint as though we made any use of that crime, or anything said about it throughout the whole book, nor was that thing ever insisted upon by us, among ourselves, or even mentioned by us, as any article against him, in this controversy; and the only reason why it appeared in our book, was because Mr. Clap's information, which contained a reference to it could not be published without it: and yet you charge us, ourselves with fastening this charge upon him: is our giving an historical account of another's testimony, wherein he had occasional reference to a fault committed, without saying a word before or after about it, our fastening a charge of that fault upon him? Yea, you charge us with being the contrivers of it, and tell the world for what end we contrived it, in saying that "for fear the truth of the story should be questioned," we take care to direct all that desire to be confirmed "to inquire of such and such persons." Please, sir, to suffer your own conscience to make its own reflections upon this.

In pp. 16—17, you cast some reflections upon Mr. Clap, upon this account; and say, "Perhaps it may be said Mr. Clap made the inquiry with a charitable hope the story was not true, and a kind design to contradict it, when he heard it mentioned." And then you add, "Whether it was just or not, there is some reason to doubt, when he could write to a minister in Boston, to desire him to make inquiry into Mr. Breck's conduct," etc.

The reason of Mr. Clap's informing Mr. Breck of that story, was because he was often inquired of by the people of Windham, and he knowing nothing about it thought it proper to give Mr. Breck an opportunity to vindicate himself. And when he had absolutely denied the truth of the story, many suspected his veracity; and others, who pretended to be his peculiar friends, supposed that the story was absolutely false and scandalous, and therefore earnestly solicited Mr. Clap to write a letter to some gentleman, who was acquainted with him, to know the truth of the story; that so if he were innocent he might be vindicated, or if otherwise he might be made sensible of his fault in denying of it. And accordingly Mr. Clap was prevailed upon to write a letter for that end. And, sir, what color is there for any reflection upon Mr. Clap on this account? Will you say it was an unchristian or impertinent thing in Mr. Clap, to act such a Christian part, as to inform a gentleman of an ill report which there was about him, that so he might have opportunity to vindicate himself, and that *he* might be in a better capacity of vindicating of him, and to comply with the importunity of

<!-- p. 103 -->

his friends to write a letter for that end? Or if Mr. Clap began afterwards to suspect that the story was true, and so that Mr. Breck was not a man of truth in denying of it, must it then be a fault in Mr. Clap, to desire to be satisfied in that point, when there was some probability that he might be settled over part of his church.

In p. 18, you charge Mr. Williams of Longmeadow with being the means that the contents of the Rev. Dr. Colman's letter, was spread about Springfield before it reached where it was directed.[^004-note7] How did you know that it was before it had reached where it was directed? Have you not ventured positively to assert this before the world on mere conjecture? For what is asserted is contrary to fact, for the letter was sent from Brookfield to the Rev. Mr. Williams of Hatfield, to whom it was directed, by his daughter, and reached to him the same day that Mr. Williams of Longmeadow got home himself.

Again, 'tis there represented as though the author of that letter had written to Mr. Williams, manifesting his dislike of letting the contents of that letter be known; which is quite wrong. The words of the doctor's letter are these, "Mr. Cooper tells me of my letter's being put into the hands of a mean person, I think a shoemaker, who carried it from house to house."[^004-note8] The reverend doctor never blamed Mr. Williams for letting the contents of the letter be known, nor did Mr. Williams go about to excuse himself for so doing; but to let the doctor know that the report was not true which the Rev. Mr. Cooper had told him, of his doing so ungentlemanly a thing, as to put a letter of his, that was committed to his care, into the hands of a shoemaker, to be carried from house to house.

At the bottom of the same page, you tell the world, that our book "abounds with misrepresentations and untruths"; and elsewhere are often charging us with vile and "willful misrepresentations"; yea, you represent us as persons so guilty in this matter, that our word is of no significancy, or is not to be taken; your words, are, p. 58, "And how

<!-- p. 104 -->

should such men be credited in their representations of other matters."

Mr. Cooper, in his letter to Mr. Hopkins, which he wrote to him after our book had been published so long that we may well conclude he had seen it, expresses charity for us all with respect to our veracity: his words are these, "I thank God, my charity is not so shocked, with respect to brother Hopkins, or any of the ministers of Hampshire, as to suspect them, after all the stories I have heard, to be guilty of willful departure from truth and fact." Mr. Cooper knows whether he had any hand in writing this book;[^004-note9] if he had, and believed in his heart, as he says to Mr. Hopkins, certainly it was very injurious in him, so abundantly to represent to the world, as if we so abounded in lying, as that there was no trust to be put in our words, so publicly to wound our reputation, contrary to what he thought in his own heart, or at the same time, that he believed that we were men of truth, so as not so much as to suspect that we were otherwise, and to thank God that he had so much charity for us.

The first instance you mention of a misrepresentation, wherein you say, "our haste and warmth probably carried us beyond our evidence" [p. 13], is in saying that the ministers that came from Boston "had joined in giving Mr. Breck a certificate of his orthodoxy, when but one of them had signed it": and though you find this mistake corrected in the end of the book, yet you say it was done by a gentleman in Boston, that looked over that half sheet: you repeat this matter again, p. 36, you say if you mistake not it was so; but why, reverend sir, will you thus treat your brethren in the ministry, to publish such a thing to disparage us, and render us vile in the sight of the world on a mere conjecture; when indeed your guess is entirely wrong, for the error was corrected by the same person that made it, and 'tis mentioned as an *erratum* in the end of the book, in his own words, as he sent them down in a letter to the printer; and if you don't believe it we desire you would inquire of the printer.

Certainly, sir, when you was blaming us for going beyond our evidence, it did not become you in the very same instance you produce to prove it, to do the same thing! We leave it with you to consider what decency or ingenuity there is in thus insisting on a thing that comes corrected, repeating it in different parts of your book, only on a

<!-- p. 105 -->

groundless guess, that not we, but somebody else corrected it: don't this again show that you endeavored to lay on all the load you possibly could, and that you was greedy of instances of untruth and misrepresentation in us; otherwise why would not such a multitude of other instances, that you pretend you have found, that ben't mentioned as *errata*, suffice you?

In answer to our first argument to prove that those that sat at Springfield, and took upon them to sit there as judges of that case, were not regularly called thereto, viz. "because the prevailing part of them were not of neighboring churches, but fetched from remote parts of the country, in neglect of the churches of the neighborhood, and in opposition to the body of neighboring ministers," you say, first, that it was because one of the churches of the neighborhood that was sent for would not come, that it was so that the prevailing part was of remote churches: and if you had told the whole truth, would you not have said too that but one of the churches of the county would have come, if you that came from Boston had let them alone?[^004-note10] You speak of the Rev. Mr. Williams of Hatfield, his refusing to come, as a thing that strengthened your warrant to act; but it seems to us, that considering his age, and that he was the principal person of all that Springfield applied to, his refusing to come, as discountenancing the method of proceeding, should have rather made you more slow in acting, especially when he not only refused to come, but entered his solemn protest against your proceedings.

Then you proceed to reply to what we produce from the Platform: and in the first place, you declare to the world, that we said that which we never did say: your words are, "Are churches in the calling of councils limited to the vicinity, so that it is an irregularity and offense to them if they don't take the next neighboring churches, and no other? This is what those gentlemen assert; and they deliver it not only as their own opinion, but say it was evidently the mind of the composers of the Platform." Our words are, "It appears evidently reasonable in itself, that churches that are by providence planted together, and must dwell together, so as necessarily, above all others, to be concerned in each other's affairs, and will be continually and unavoidably in the way of mutual intercourse, and mutually interested in each other's welfare, should be jointly concerned in their religious affairs, and not be neglected or set aside one by another, wherein other churches are to have

<!-- p. 106 -->

influence in their affairs, but should principally be regarded; so this was evidently the mind of the composers of the Platform." Why, sir would you so abuse us, and strain the matter so much higher than we had done, and express a thing that is so diverse from our words, and opposite to the plain import of them, and then say that this is what we assert? And again, lower down the same page, you cite our words wrong, and represent us as saying what we never said, that you may have opportunity to ridicule us: your words are, "If they had, they never would have asserted that" (and then the following words are in another character, as being cited from us) "*as often* as it directs to a particular church to apply to other churches, it specifies neighbor churches." Our words are, "They, when they direct to, or mention any application to be made by a particular church to other churches, *from time to time* specify neighbor churches." Perhaps you will say this is the same sense, though not the same words; but if it be the very same sense, why did you not mention the same words, seeing you plainly mention them as a citation? But we apprehend there is indeed a great difference in the sense: can't the Platform from time to time specify neighbor churches, when they mention any application to be made to other churches, and yet not do it every time? Our words, as we conceive, imply thus much, and no more, viz. that when the Platform directs a church to apply to other churches, it does from time to time specify what churches should be applied to, and that wherever it does so, it specifies neighbor churches, and that it never specifies any other; of which the world have good evidence from this, that you can find no other *specified* in it, who have doubtless thoroughly searched the Platform to this end.[^004-note11]

And to what purpose is that passage that you cite from the Platform, wherein it says, "*That all churches* ought to preserve communion one with another"?[^004-note12] We can conceive of nothing that you can intend by it, unless it be this, viz. that because the Platform says, that all churches ought to hold communion, that therefore they ought to exercise that communion in everything that is an act of communion; but if this be what you mean, then it will follow, that all the churches in the world

<!-- p. 107 -->

ought to be consociated; for the Synod in 1662 mentions consociation of churches as one way of exercising the communion of churches; however, they have expressly limited that exercise of communion to churches in a "convenient vicinity":[^004-note13] or else you must mean, that because the Platform says all churches should hold communion, and one way of communion there mentioned is to consult other churches, that therefore a particular church ought to consult all other churches. But 'tis ridiculous to infer any other from what the Platform says, than this, viz. that every church ought to be ready to exercise communion with all other churches in all those ways, as the disposals of providence, in the circumstances and occasions of churches shall open a door for it and call to it. And to what purpose are those other passages that you cite, where the Platform says a particular church ought to consult "*other churches*"? Which you seem to think should be taken so much notice of, and observe that it is said "other churches at large"; does it thence follow, that the Platform neither does, nor can design that churches should be especially limited to neighbor churches?[^004-note14] What sort of arguing is this: The Platform says, churches should consult other churches, therefore it nowhere especially limits them to neighbor churches! Can't the Platform tell us that we must consult *other churches*, and then afterwards tell us *what other churches*? Can't a parent advise a child under difficulties to consult others, and then in the same discourse tell him who? And after he has told him, must the child, because his father first said others, still look upon himself no more directed by his father to one than another? The Platform does indeed sometimes say other churches, but then in other places, from time to time, both before and after, tells what churches, viz. neighbor churches; it specifies them without any conjunction; and therefore for any to suppose that the composers of the Platform did not by this intend to direct churches where to go when they consulted other churches, is to reflect upon them as though they were ignorant of the nature of language, and did not understand what they said.
