They have brought an application to this Association for advice, and lodged it with {Rev. Williams}; and at their desire, and at the advice of some of our brethren in the ministry, I have written to the ministers, to desire them to meet at my house on Thursday, early in the morning. I hope you will come, for you cannot easily think what posture they are in. And unless we do concert some measures, we are in danger of being overrun, and Northampton will proceed to extreme measures, being conducted by some gentlemen not over-tender of ministers of churches; which may prove of pernicious consequence to us and all our churches. I have the promise of some gentlemen to come, and hope you will not fail. From your brother, etc. Chester Williams. Hadley, Feb. 20, 1750.

<!-- p. 600 -->

Six of the ministers came together on this notification, viz. Mr. Partridge of East Hadley, Mr. Billings of Cold Spring, Mr. Ashley of Sunderland, Mr. Ashley of Deerfield, Mr. Woodbridge of Hatfield and Mr. Williams of Hadley. That day, being Thursday, Feb. 22, I had my second lecture, which was also thinly attended by my own people, but by a great number of strangers: as it appeared to me, more than half of the congregation being strangers.

In the evening, three of the forementioned ministers came to my house, viz. Mr. Partridge, Mr. Billings and Mr. Woodbridge, and showed me the paper which had been lodged with Mr. Williams, directed to the Association, subscribed by a number of members of this church; and also showed me a vote which they had passed among themselves, that they would proceed to give some advice to the people of Northampton, as they desired. I informed them that there was a great misrepresentation in the paper sent to them, representing me to have declared that I utterly refused to have any hand in calling any council, unless I might choose *half* of the members out of the county: whereas all that I said was that I would have no hand in calling any council, unless I might choose *some* of the members out of the county, and that I had no thought of insisting on half when the deacons were here; but all I had thoughts of was only choosing a minor part, agreeably to the private advice of the members of the late council. After much more conversation with them on our affairs, the next morning these gentlemen returned to their brethren at Hadley; and after long consideration, they broke up and did nothing.

March 5, the precinct met again, according to adjournment. This being also the day of the town meeting for choosing town officers, the precinct meeting was adjourned to the next day. The next day, they met and adjourned themselves until half after four o'clock p. m. That was the day of my fourth lecture on the subject in controversy, which being the last I intended but one, and the public fast being appointed on the Thursday following, which would put by my lecture a week longer, I sent the people word at this meeting that if they insisted on my calling a church meeting in order to my calling a decisive council before my last lecture was past, I would warn one the next Monday; though I chose, if they were willing, that it should be deferred until my last lecture. Accordingly they consented that it should be so deferred, and appointed Deac. Cook to come to me and desire me to call a church meeting the week after my last lecture, and then adjourned themselves to March 22, at half after four o'clock, the day of my

<!-- p. 601 -->

last lecture; when they met, and adjourned themselves to April 2, 1750.

On the nextLacuna in copy; text taken from Dwight ed., *1*, 392. sabbath, March 25, I warned a church meeting for the next day, at one o'clock, to see if pastor and people could not agree upon a council to advise under our difficulties and, if they thought fit, to bring our controversy to a speedy issue.

Accordingly the nextReturn to Andover copy. day, March 26, the church met and, at the request of some of the brethren, I desired that those who were of the same principles on which the church had proceeded in their former practice in the admission of members to full communion in the church, would manifest it by holding up their hands; and it appeared that there was a great majority still of these principles.

We next proceeded to consider the business on which a council should be called, and I proposed the following draft of a vote for consideration: "That a council be called to give us their best advice for a remedy [from the calamities],As in Dwight ed., *1*, 392. arising from the present un[settled], broken state of the church, by reason of the controversy here subsisting concerning the qualifications for full communion in the church. And if, upon the whole of what they see and find in our circumstances, they judge it best that pastor and people be immediately separated, that they proceed to dissolve the relation between them."

There was much discourse concerning this draft. It was read publicly and distinctly, three or four times, and it was desired that each particular passage of it might be considered and scanned.

It was offered to such as desired to view and examine it, and handed from one to another. Some amendments were proposed, but the amendments did not seemAndover copy: "seemed." to be liked as well as the first draft. It was then put to vote, and it was questioned whether it was a vote. Then it was desired that all might sit down and hold up their hands for some considerable time, and then it appeared plainly to be a vote, and was generally acknowledged to be so by such as had appeared most to oppose it, and was not questioned by more than one or two. And one of them, viz. Maj. Pomeroy, said it was generally allowed to be a vote, and therefore intimated it to be his mind that it should pass as such, and that we should proceed to other business.

Then I declared to the church what I should insist on with regard to

<!-- p. 602 -->

the council that should be chosen, viz. to choose half of the members of the council; and to choose three ministers or churches without the bounds of the county, and should not insist on more than three, unless the whole council consisted of more than *fourteen*. I also told them that I should insist on a provisional choice of some others out of the county, to come in case any of the three first pitched upon should fail, so that I might indeedAndover copy: "indeed <to>." have three from other parts of the land.

It was then strongly insisted on by the church that I ought not to be allowed to choose *any* out of the county, so that the consideration of the *number* to be chosen out of the county was for the present laid aside; and the matter debated was whether I should be allowed to bring *any at all* from without the bounds of the county. After much talk, it was put to vote in the following words: "Whether or not you do consent, that in choosing the council now under consideration, I, in my choice, should go out of this county for any part of the council? Let those, who do consent, manifest it by holding up their hands." It was not voted. Upon which I told the church that the business of the meeting was come to an end, as it was apparent that pastor and people could act in nothing together in calling a council. After some discourse, I told them that I stood ready to yield to have but two of the council from abroad, unless the council consisted of more than ten; but should insist on three, if the whole was more than ten, and on more, if the council was above *fourteen*. It being moved by some of the brethren that the meeting should be adjourned for farther consideration, it was accordingly adjourned to the next day, at one o'clock.

Accordingly the next day we met again, and the last subject of consideration, concerning my going out of the county for any part of the council, was proposed again; and supposing they now had sufficient consideration of the matter, I was about to put it to vote again. But then it was desired by some that there might be a reconsideration of the first vote which had passed the day before, concerning the business of the council; and suggested that, if some alteration were made in that vote, there was a probability that the latter vote, concerning my going out of the county, might pass without difficulty. Then Maj. Pomeroy declared that a number of brethren had met together and drawn up something determining the business of the council: which draft he read, which was to this purpose, viz. that the council should come and propose terms of accommodation between pastor and people;

<!-- p. 603 -->

to which, if the people did not consent, the council should proceed immediately to dissolve the relation between pastor and people. I objected much against setting aside what had been already voted, to make way for any new projections, as only tending to open a door for new contests and difficulties, and greatly to entangle and lengthen out our affairs; and also because there was nothing in what had been already voted but what was essential, what the nature of things and the state of our affairs did necessarily require, and therefore what I must insist upon. And I particularly [objected] to what Maj. Pomeroy proposed, as limiting the council without referring anything to their judgment or advice, and not so much as suffering them to act their own judgment in determining whether it was best immediately to proceed to separate between pastor and people. The same things were strongly objected by some others, and on the whole I manifested that I should wholly decline putting it to vote; on which, after much earnest talk, I put the other matter to vote, viz. whether I should be allowed to go out of the county for any members of the council, which again passed in the negative.

Upon this I informed the church that I was not against their having farther time for consideration, if they desired it, and farther conference with them, or with a committee they might choose; but it would not be worth the while to make any farther attempt to act in concert, if they were fixed and resolved in these two things: not to leave it to the discretion of the council whether to separate; and not to allow me to choose any members of the council out of the county. Some of them declared they were fixed in these things. Upon which I asked if any had anything to object against my dissolving the meeting, seeing we were come at present to a stop as to acting in anything together; and told them withal that, if afterwards, on farther consideration, a church meeting was desired to reconsider these matters, I would not refuse warning one. On this occasion, there was much earnest talk about the power of the church to act without me and to call a council themselves.

Finally, some of the brethren thought I had best dissolve the meeting, and accordingly I dissolved it; and immediately after which, as the people began to move in order to go out of the meeting house, some individuals called out very earnestly for them to stay and proceed to act without me, and see if they could not have Maj. Pomeroy's draft (aforementioned) put to vote. I then came away, and the people that

<!-- p. 604 -->

stayed behind, differing among themselves, gradually dispersed and did nothing.

The next Friday, March 30, 1750, I sent to Deac. Cook the following declaration:The following document was not available to Dwight and is printed here for the first time. The Edwards Papers in the Beinecke Library contain two versions: f. 39, a draft, and Scattergood Deposit, #1, a fair copy, the latter of which has been used here.

> To Deac. Cook of Northampton. Dear Brother, I now make the following declaration, which I am willing you should show to any of the members of this church whom you please, as you have opportunity. I declare I have no disposition to continue in the pastoral relation to this church, they retaining their present settled aversion to it after such a council as I have insisted on have had fair opportunity, on a view of our calamitous state, to judge whether it don't admit of some other remedy, and to give their own judgment and advice, and use their own means (if they shall think fit to use any) in order to a reconciliation, and in order to your consenting to continue longer under my ministry: I say, if after this you appear still fixed in an aversion to my being any longer your minister, my private inclination and judgment is that you should be gratified by an immediate separation. Though, at the same time, I don't think it proper to bind myself by any promises or come to any absolute determination before I have had the advice of a council in so great and important an affair; because for either of us to do thus, and then send for a council to advise us, would be preposterous and inconsistent. I declare that as the above-mentioned is at present my private inclination and judgment, so I fully expect that it will be the judgment and advice of the council when they come, provided such a council be called as I insist on. I declare I have no scheme or secret design in view, in any step I take, to bring the church into any snare, so that they should at last be obliged to continue under my ministry, contrary to what shall finally appear to be their fixed inclination after any means the council may think proper to be used. And if the council advise to any such thing, it will not be in the least owing to any design or contrivance of mine, and will be altogether unexpected to me: that

<!-- p. 605 -->

  is, it will be unexpected to me if they advise to my finally continuing, contrary to the church's fixed inclination, etc. I declare that I do not decline setting aside the vote passed the last Monday because it was my own draft, or because I desire to get my will or obtain any victory over others, or because I am fond of those very words or phrases; but because I insist on the things therein contained, they being only essential things I studied, when I drew the vote, barely to express such things as the nature of the case absolutely requires the judgment and advice of a council in. And I think to set aside the vote, when passed, after its being so fully and particularly debated and considered, unless it be with a view to some material alteration, would be to open a door for the lengthening out our controversy with frivolous jangling and strife. I declare that I have no desire that the time should be lengthened out before a council is called, in order to bringing our matters to some issue: but on the contrary, I desire that the calling such a council may be hastened. And whereas many of the church have expressed a fear or suspicion that, if the council should have so large a liberty of judging and advising as is expressed in the forementioned vote, they would persuade me to comply so far with the church as to go on to admit members into the church in our former manner, though not fully brought off from my opinion; and some (one at least) intimated a suspicion that I expected it myself and had long acted with this view: I now declare that I have never taken one step with this view or expectation, and that I have not, and never had, any such expectation; and that it is not because I would make a reserve for such an event that I insist on such liberty of judgment and advice in the council as is expressed in the forementioned vote, and oppose their being limited, as is proposed in Maj. Pomeroy's draft, but because I am not willing to have any hand in what I judge to be in its own nature unfit and preposterous; for which I am satisfied I should be much blamed abroad as laying myself under disadvantages, and should not be able to vindicate myself; and also because I doubt whether members of a council will be willing to come from a distance, if tied up in such a manner from giving advice and acting their own judgment. As I declared things to the same purpose with these above before in the church meeting, so I now renew the declaration, and know of nothing further I can do at present to convince my brethren that

<!-- p. 606 -->

  these things are true, than by declaring that I speak uprightly and in the simplicity of my heart. If there remains a fixed resolution, either that the council called shall not have liberty of giving advice for a remedy of our calamities according to their own judgment (not that I desire the church to bind themselves to stand to their advice), and judging for themselves whether an immediate separation be best, or to confine me wholly to this county in my choice, I don't think it will be to any purpose to call another church meeting, unless it be to prolong fruitless wrangling and strife. But if it be thought there is a disposition further to consider of these matters, I stand ready to call the church together to that end at any time I shall be desired. Jonathan Edwards. Northampton, March 30, 1750.Return to Andover copy.

The Monday following, being April 2, the precinct met according to adjournment. It was a very thin meeting, consisting of about 44 persons. It was proposed by some that the precinct should send a messenger to the Association of the lower part of the county, who were to sit that week at Springfield Mountains,Wilbraham, Massachusetts. for their advice whether they had best to consent to what I insisted on with regard to my going out of the county or not; and it was put to vote whether they should send such a messenger, but they were not able to determine whether it was a vote or not until they divided, when it appeared to be voted by a majority of 26 against 18. Accordingly Maj. Pomeroy, Sr. and Mr. Joseph Hawley were appointed a committee to write to the Association in behalf of the precinct, and Josiah Pomeroy was appointed the messenger to carry the letter and bring the return. The meeting was then adjourned until Tuesday, April 10. Accordingly the committee wrote and sent to the same Association. On this occasion, the day before the Association met, I sent the following letter to Mr. Hopkins of Springfield.Samuel Hopkins (1693—1755), minister of West Springfield. The letter was not available to Dwight; a draft is printed here for the first time (Beinecke Library, Edwards Papers, f. 39).

> To Mr. Hopkins at Springfield. Dear Brother, I understand that our people had on yesterday a precinct meeting for the managing our ecclesiastical affairs (as they have had a great many such the fall and winter past). And that at this meeting a

<!-- p. 607 -->

  committee was chosen to write to the Association in the lower part of the county to desire their judgment and advice in some things concerning the controversy subsisting between me and this church, and have appointed a messenger to carry the letter. The whole meeting, as I was informed, consisted of 44 persons; and the majority that voted this was 26, as I was informed by one that counted 'em. They gave me no notice of the meeting or their design in it, so that I had no opportunity either to concur or remonstrate. They have given me no notice of what they have done or what particulars they intend to ask the judgment of the Association in. It was proposed by one in the meeting, as I was informed, that I should be notified of what they had determined, that I might have opportunity to send also if I thought fit. But the motion was rejected with much dislike. Why they chose to send to your Association rather than our own, I don't know. Only, as I am informed, that Maj. Pomeroy, Jr. said he had conversed with several of the ministers and by their conversation he was persuaded that Association would take cognizance of their affairs. I conjecture that one main thing that they would have your judgment in is a controversy between me and the church, whether I ought not to allowed to choose, without the bound of this county, two of the members in ten of the council that shall have power to issue our affairs. I am persuaded that if you knew all circumstances, you would be fully satisfied we needed no previous council to decide this controversy, or any further advice than we have had, or, if we did, that it was proper I should have some hand in this previous council in calling them and representing things before [them]. And that 'tis especially needless for them, if they will have this controversy judged by a council in which they only have a hand, to have this Association to go to yours. But if you judged these things were proper, yet I am persuaded you would not think this offer properly brought to you when referred only by about 26 of the precinct at a precinct meeting, instead of being referred by the church, which consists of about 300 male members. But if you would allow 'em all those forementioned things proposed,"Proposed" is a conjectural reading where the word is rubbed away at the bottom of the MS page. yet doubtless you would not think it proper to undertake to judge this matter, or anything else that has been matter of controversy between me and the church concerning our mutual rights, only as being the representations of one side. It would be impossible

<!-- p. 608 -->

  you should have a just view of our affairs, so as to put you into a proper capacity to judge or advise in matters relating to our controversy, without a very long rehearsal. To be sure, some expect a just view of 'em only on the representation of one side. The church and pastor have already by mutual choice called a council of churches chiefly to decide this very point in controversy between us, viz. whether I had a right to go out of the county for a part of the council that shall have power to issue our affairs, who were so far from thinking that there was no need of hearing both parties in order to decide it, that they at their first sitting spent about two days in hearing and considering what each had to say. And then, being at a loss what to determine, adjourned themselves for about six weeks to take time to consider of it. And at their second meeting, spent another day in further hearing each party and in deliberation and finally were at a loss, being equally divided as to [the] question whether I had a proper right to go out of the county, which was all they had power to judge of as a council; but as its being prudential, that I should be allowed to go out for a minor part, they did (to all appearance with a concurring) judge and did advise that it should be allowed. About 50 of my people did lately subscribe a request to the ministers of our Association to come together to give 'em advice what they should do under present circumstances, and in their draft made such a representation as moved the ministers that they met at Hadley and actually passed a vote that they would give advice. But some of them thought it necessary to hear my representation of things before they proceeded to act and accordingly came over hither, and having heard my representations, altered their minds and determined that it was best to act nothing, and accordingly they broke up and did nothing. But I believe, sir, I need say no more (and probably needed not to have said anything) to make you sensible how far you are from having a proper call at present to judge of any matters in controversy between me and this church. I am your loving brother, Jonathan Edwards. Northampton, April 3, 1750.Return to Andover copy.

<!-- p. 609 -->

The Association, on account of the message sent to them and my letter to Mr. Hopkins, sent a letter to me and another to the committee, which are as follows:The documents were not available to Dwight; they are printed here for the first time (Beinecke Library, Edwards Papers, f. 39, #38 and #39).

> Springfield, April 5, 1750 Rev. and Dear Sir, We have received a letter from a committee, chosen at Northampton on the 2nd instant, desiring our advice whether the church there should agree with yourself in your desire or resolution to go out of the county for two or three churches or ministers of a council to decide your laboring affairs. We have returned them an answer, a copy of which we enclose to you, as of this also to them. We are heartily concerned at the unhappy situation of your affairs, and should gladly contribute to your help. We looked upon ourselves in duty bound to answer their letter, and you there see our sentiments as we have offered them to your people. We would also propose to yourself that you will use condescendency and Christian methods, that the question in debate may be resolved, that thereby the way may be opened to a decisive council as soon as may be, which we understand you yourself and the people are very desirous of. The Rev. Mr. Hopkins has communicated to us the letter you wrote to him of the 2nd instant, and we are fully of the mind that you ought to have opportunity to give your reasons why you should go out of the county to those who have the consideration of the case. And we hope, sir, that you, with the church, will in a friendly manner agree upon some method for the resolution of that laboring question. And we need not say to you that the more of a Christian condescension is used on both sides, the nearer you will come to the obligations you lie under as Christians, and the more likely to obtain a happy issue. Wishing the divine direction and blessing to you and your people, We are your brethren and fellow servants, Stephen Williams,Stephen Williams (1693—1782), minister of Longmeadow and JE's cousin. Moderator, in the name and by order of the Association.

<!-- p. 610 -->

To the Rev. Mr. Jonathan Edwards at Northampton.

Springfield, April 5, 1750

Gentlemen,

We have yours by Mr. Pomeroy, are heartily grieved at the unhappy situation of your affairs, and would gladly contribute anything in our power for the bettering your state.

Your question to us is whether you shall agree to what the Rev. Mr. Edwards insists upon, of choosing two or three ministers or churches out of the county or no?

We are sensible that Northampton church, in the Rev. Mr. Stoddard's days, voted "that what difficulties might arise among them, should be issued by a council of churches within the county," or to that purpose. We see no reason for your departing from that vote, except in some special case in which there may be weighty reasons why you should recede from it.

We are not acquainted with the reasons your reverend pastor may have to offer why you should go out of the county: perhaps, therefore, we should be too rash if we should advise you not to agree with him; and on the other hand, no less rash if we should advise you to agree with him in the case. We are indeed too much unacquainted with your state, and what may be said *pro* and *con* in your case, to be positive in our advice.

We understand that a council, to which the Rev. Mr. Edwards and the church referred the question, were equally divided upon it; but, gentlemen, cannot there be further steps taken to determine that matter, either by adding some other churches to the council, or by referring of it to one or both the Associations of the county, or in some other method, that your reverend pastor and the church may agree upon in a friendly manner? And we should heartily desire you to act jointly in the affair, if possible, and advise you to put on all Christian condescension; but if this cannot be obtained by any means, we don't know but you will be reduced to a necessity of calling in the assistance and advice of the churches of the county. Wishing to you and your reverend pastor the divine direction and blessing, we are your hearty friends,

Stephen Williams, Moderator, in the name and by order of the Association.

<!-- p. 611 -->

A true copy, John Ballantine, Scribe.John Ballantine (1716—76), minister of Westfield. Andover copy resumes.

Tuesday, April 10, the precinct met again according to adjournment. It was a thin meeting of about 41 members. The Moderator read my declaration, aforementioned, sent to Deac. Cook, and also the letters of the Lower Association to me and to the committee; and after some discourse it was voted to desire me to call a church meeting the next Monday, in order to some farther attempts for an agreement between pastor and people on some measures for bringing these affairs to an issue, or [to] that purpose. Then the meeting was adjourned to the next Tuesday, April 17.

Accordingly the next sabbath, April 15, I warned a meeting of the church for the next day at three o'clock, p. m. Agreeably to this warning, the church met on Monday, April 16. After the meeting was opened by prayer, Maj. Pomeroy read the letter which the committee of the precinct had received from the Lower Association of this county. After this ensued some new disputes concerning the reasonableness of my being allowed to go out of the countyAndover copy: "Committee." for some of the council which should have power to issue our controversy. I also read the forementioned declaration which I had sent to Deac. Cook, of March 30. I then told the church, if they had anything to propose concerning another previous council, agreeably to the advice they had received, I stood ready to hear it and consider of it; and told them, if there appeared a disposition to call another previous council to determine whether it was not reasonable that I should be allowed to go out of the county in the choice of a decisive council, I would take the matter into consideration, and would ask the advice of my friends. But from what was said, there did not appear to be any prevailing inclination to it, but the contrary.

Then it was put to vote again whether they were willing I should go out of the county for any members of the council which should have power to issue our controversy; and the church dividing upon it, there were about 109 against it and 56 for it.

After this, I put it to vote whether the church were willing that another previous council should be called, in some way mutually chosen, in order to determine whether I might be allowed to go out of the county for some members of a decisive council; and whether, in that case, they did consent that I should take time to consider of this matter,

<!-- p. 612 -->

and ask advice of my friends: and I saw but three or four hands up for it. So the meeting was dismissed.

The next day, April 17, I went a journey down the country. The same day, after I was gone, the precinct met again according to adjournment; when was read the following letter from the Rev. Mr. Clark of Salem Village, directed to Maj. Pomeroy, to be communicated to the precinct:The document was not available to Dwight; in lieu of the original, the text (printed here for the first time [Beinecke Library, Edwards Papers, f. 39, #3]) is from Timothy Dwight's transcript, who wrote at the end: "Tuesday, April 17, 1750, I read the original, of which this is a true copy throughout, in a precinct meeting in Northampton. Timothy Dwight, Sr." The use JE made of this letter and the relationship between JE and Peter Clark are described in the Introduction, p. 59

> Honored Sir, Yours of the 12th of last March came to my hand on the 25th, wherein you repeat your request to me, at the motion or by a vote of your precinct, about my writing an answer to Mr. Edwards his late book: which was a little surprising to me, considering what I had written in a former letter, which I thought might have induced you to lay aside all further expectation of my being engaged in that affair; and indeed, sir, I must confess it unhappily falls out that I am in no better capacity of returning a more satisfactory answer to your request than when you wrote your first letter, for want of a sight of that book, which I have not as yet been able to obtain: having been under bodily indisposition the latter part of the last winter, I have gone but little abroad. Yet I have taken some considerable pains in making inquiry after the book among my neighbor ministers and others whom I thought it most likely to meet with it, but find it very scarce in our parts. None that I have discoursed with about it in Salem or Marblehead, either before or since the receipt of your last letter, having as yet seen it, the contents and design of which book have been differently represented to me, so that being left to conjecture I could not hitherto, you may be sure, form any distinct thoughts upon it; nor can I easily recollect what the expressions were that occurred in my letter which might give encouragement to my good friends in your parts to expect that I might be prevailed with to answer that piece of Mr. Edwards', unless it were my saying that, as Mr. Edwards his opinion was represented to me, it was easily answered by being reduced to an absurdity. But this (as I remember I signified to you) was said upon

<!-- p. 613 -->

  a general representation of it in private conversation, and that some considerable time before the book came out of the press. The common report then was to this effect, as I remember: that Mr. Edwards was about new-modeling of his church, designing to have a pure church consisting only of true converts, and that he had written and was about printing in defense of his opinion. Now there needs not many words or any long controversy to show the absurdity of such an opinion or purpose in any man, for it takes away that commonly received and well-grounded distinction of the church into visible and invisible: it supposes a thing contrary to the declaration of our Lord in several of his parables, that his church in the world, according to the instituted course of its administration being committed to fallible men, would consist of a mixture of good and bad, sound and unsound Christians, till the great day of discrimination; it supposes those that have the power of admitting members into the church to be infallible discerners of the state of mens' hearts, to judge of their sincerity, all which are openly absurd. But I have always esteemed Mr. Edwards a gentleman of more sense and modesty and piety than to make such pretensions, and therefore can scarce persuade myself that that is the subject and scope of his book. However, you see, sir, how much at a loss I am, and how unprepared to engage in a controversy on a subject I have so little certain and distinct knowledge of; and possibly, upon the sight and perusal of that book, I may not have the same apprehensions with your people of the necessity or expediency of an answer to it; and to deal plainly and ingenuously with you, I must so far declare my opinion about the qualifications of church members as to let you know that, though I think it not necessary to constitute the visible church of Christ [so] that all the members of it should be sincere converts, but that a visible saintship or, in other words, a credible profession of faith and repentance (I call that a credible profession which is founded on a competent measure of Christian knowledge, together with a good conversation joined to a serious and solemn consent to the covenant of the gospel) gives a gospel right to all sacred ordinances in the church, in which all that have power of admitting members into its communion ought, by the gospel rule of charity, to acquiesce and leave the judgments of the state of their hearts to God alone, to whom it belongs. Yet I cannot in all points fall in with the sentiments of [the] venerable Mr. Stoddard, your

<!-- p. 614 -->

  former worthy pastor, though I pay a great deference to his judgment and can easily apprehend in what sense his opinion upon this subject, wherein he differed from others, may in the main be reconciled to that of those with whom he had a controversy in his day; setting aside a few tolerable differences, particularly I have no clearness to give my assent to that position which he has maintained, that the sacrament of the Lord's Supper (or indeed any other sacrament which, as seals of the covenant, presuppose conversion, especially in the adult) is a converting ordinance, and some other points depending thereon, for reasons not here to be mentioned or insisted on. Though I agree it is the duty of unconverted professors to come to the Lord's Table– but in a right manner, i.e. with the gospel qualifications of repentance and faith in Christ– it is equally their duty to repent and pray (Acts 8:22), and so to repent and partake of the sacrament, or attend any other divine institution; but that the latter is not to be urged without the former, and it is a gospel profession of this, as I have explained it, that must satisfy ministers and churches in order to their admission, and warrants them to receive such as make this profession and carry it toward them as true converts, as saints and brethren in Christ, though at the same time it be granted that many who pass under this character are really and in heart unconverted, known only to God and to their own consciences. But ministers and Christians being but fallible men, and keeping within the bounds of their own faculties, are in reality (whatever may be pretended) capable of no higher evidence of their sincerity than such a profession, taken in its proper latitude, includes in it. How far my principles relating to this subject (which I have thus briefly opened) agree or disagree to those which Mr. Edwards has maintained in his late book, I know not; but by them perhaps you may be able to judge whether or how far I shall be obliged by the principles I have laid down to oppose any tenets advanced in the said book. But forasmuch as I perceive a speedy answer is thought necessary and generally desired among you and the premises considered, you will see how remote I am at present from being in a capacity to gratify such a desire. I must therefore entreat my Christian friends and brethren of your precinct to dismiss all further expectations of my writing an answer to the said book; and I can't but think there are gentlemen in your parts of the country, or much nearer to you, who have had time to digest their thoughts upon the

<!-- p. 615 -->

  subject and may have greater leisure and capacity for that undertaking, if that be found advisable and necessary, as it seems it is. I am greatly obliged to you, sir, and to the rest of the good brethren of the precinct, for your respect to me, as also to the reverend gentlemen, the ministers in your neighborhood, for the good opinion they have conceived of my abilities and influence in such a case, which is far higher than what I dare assume to myself; yea, which humbles and shames me, when I consider how little I am able to make it good, who best knows my own infirmity. Writing is tedious to me, more than what is common, and [I] have no inclination to controversy further than plain duty makes it necessary. However, if upon reading the book (when it shall fall into my hands) I think it proper and advisable, and if it shall please God to give leisure and ability, I may write my thoughts upon it and send them to you (which you will not understand as a promise especially of any such thing as an answer); but this may require a considerable space of time, considering the stated duty of my charge, attended with too frequent [and] necessary avocations. I am sorry to hear of the threatening aspect of the present controversy upon your church and town. I heartily wish you may be led into healing methods, or to the proper means of preventing the evils feared. And though it be very desirable that both minister and people should be of the same mind and judgment, yet it may deserve the serious consideration of yourselves and of your reverend pastor whether, retaining your several sentiments in the present case, you may not, consistently therewith, accord and unite in affection and practice and in all the holy administrations of the house of God, as has been usual? Especially considering what an eminent branch of gospel holiness that charity is which is directed to express itself in a condescension to the infirmities of the weak and in a mutual forbearance in love, under different apprehensions among Christians, against the mischievous consequences whereof there is no remedy but this charity; and how earnestly it is recommended in the evangelical writings as a means to prevent the violation of unity in Christian churches, Romans 14:1-5 and Romans 15:1-3; Ephesians 4:1-3, 15-16; Colossians 3:12-15; Philippians 3:15-16; John 13:34-35 and John 17:21. Though most of you are strangers to me, yet not only the bonds of our common Christianity oblige, but Christian charity also teaches and inclines me to desire your welfare and prosperity, and to stand ready to serve you and the cause of truth, holiness and peace

<!-- p. 616 -->

  among you, so far as God shall call and enable me, and to lament the present difficulty and temptations you are under, which call for much prayer and watchfulness, humiliation and dependence on God to overrule them for good and prevent the unhappy effects of them. So, beseeching almighty God, the Father of Lights, to afford you direction and assistance in all your difficulties and to pour out a spirit of light and love, of holiness and peace on your pastor and all the members of the flock, and commending you with them to the care and influence of the great Shepherd of the sheep, I remain, honored sir, your sincere and affectionate friend and servant in the gospel, Peter Clark. Salem Village, April 4, 1750. To the honored Ebenezer Pomeroy in Northampton, to be communicated. P. S. I had no prospect of an opportunity of sending before now, else I should have written sooner.The inserted document ends, and here begins a lengthy lacuna in the Andover copy, which has been supplied from the Dwight ed., *1*, 396—97.

At this meeting it was determined that the brethren of the church should be called together by the warning of the deacons the next Friday, and the precinct meeting was adjourned to Wednesday, May 2.

Accordingly on Friday, April 20, there was a meeting of many brethren of the church in the meetinghouse, in my absence. Maj. Pomeroy was chosen moderator of the meeting, and then they proceeded to take into consideration the propriety and expediency of the brethren proceeding to act separately, i.e. without their pastor, in calling a council. After some discourse, Mr. Joseph Hawley offered some proposals in writing, which, for substance, were, that a number of gentlemen, not exceeding seven, ministers or laymen, or both, should be mutually chosen from any part of the country, to come, not as sent by their churches or as an ecclesiastical council, but as a number of advisers, to see if they could devise some way in which the pastor and church might consist together, notwithstanding their difference in opinion. And to know the minds of the meeting, a vote was proposed by some; but others objected, and thought it better for the church to choose a committee to consider of the proposals and, if they saw needful, to amend it and present it to the pastor, and see if he would agree to it, and, if he

<!-- p. 617 -->

did, then to present it for their approbation. Upon this it was objected, since the proposal took its rise from the church, that it was improper that they should present it to the pastor for his approbation before it was known whether the church would consent to it or not, if the pastor should. Hence it was urged that a vote should be put whether the church would consent to it, or the substance of it. The vote accordingly was put, and in passed in the affirmative by a great majority, as the moderator declared, and then the brethren present chose a committee, viz. Maj. Pomeroy, Col. Dwight, Mr. Joseph Hawley, Deac. Pomroy and Ebenezer Hunt, to consider what circumstantial alterations might the made in the proposal; and then the meeting was adjourned to the next Friday. The committee met, but could not agree as to their business for which they were appointed, whether it was to consider of the proposal not only as to circumstantials, but also as to substance; and three of the committee thought it not best for the church to act any further on the aforesaid proposal, but that it was better for the church to comply with what the pastor had insisted on, of choosing some of the members of the council without the limits of the county.

Friday, April 27, the brethren met again according to their adjournment, and voted by a great majority to comply with what I had insisted on, as to choosing some members of the council without the bounds of the county, and appointed Deac. Pomroy to come to me to desire me to call a church meeting to prosecute that affair. Accordingly, the next sabbath I warned a church meeting to be the next Thursday, May 3, at three o'clock, in order to another trial whether pastor and people could not agree on measures tending to bring our controversy to an issue.

Wednesday, May 2, the precinct met again according to adjournment and adjourned themselves further to the next day, at the meetinghouse, to be held there after the church meeting.

Thursday, May 3, the church met according to my appointment, andReturn to Andover copy. the former vote respecting the business of the council, which passed at the church meeting, March 26, was read. Then I proposed that a vote should be put again, respecting my going out of the county for two ministers or churches of the council; and it was insisted that there should be a saving clause added, intimating that it was not proposed that this vote should be used as a precedent for the future. Then

<!-- p. 618 -->

I put the vote to the brethren thus: "Do you consent that, in choosing the council to transact the forementioned business, I in my choice should choose two ministers or churches without the bounds of the county, not intending that this shall hereafter have the force of a precedent?" It passed in the affirmative. Then I desired that I might make a provisional choice of two more, who might be applied to in case those I might first choose should fail, or could not be obtained. This also was voted.

Then it was proposed whether the council should be a council of *ministers* or *churches*; and it was determined by a vote that it should be a council of churches. And then, with respect to the number of *churches* of which the council should consist, it was voted that it should consist of *ten* churches.

Then we proceeded to a nomination and choice of particular ministers and churches, of which the council should consist. And I first proposed Mr. Billings and the church of Cold Springs, which were voted.

Then it was moved that a committee of the brethren should be chosen to go aside, to consider whom to nominate to the church to be chosen on their part. Accordingly a committee was chosen, viz. Maj. Pomeroy, Mr. Joseph Hawley, Lieut. Wright, Deac. Pomeroy and Deac. Cook; and after they returned, we went on with the choice. On the whole, of those whom I nominated were chosen the following ministers, with their churches:

Mr. Williams of Longmeadow, | } | with their churches.Those ministers not previously identified are Peter Reynolds (1700—68); Robert Abercrombie (1712—80); Ebenezer Parkman (1703—82); Samuel Wigglesworth (1688—1768); William Hobby (1707—65); Jonathan Hubbard (1703—65); and Joseph Ashley (1709—97). Hubbard was selected as moderator of the council. The Result of the Council was supported by Hubbard, Breck, Ashley, Woodbridge, and Chester Williams, together with the lay delegates from their churches; voting against it were Reynolds, Abercrombie, Billings, Hobby, and David Hall (1705—89) of Sutton, joined with one exception by lay delegates. Three of the churches selected by JE failed to send ministers and delegates. |

Then it was voted that the day for the opening of the council should be the 19th of June next. Then the brethren proceeded to choose a committee to be their agents, to represent them and manage their cause before the council; and the persons chosen were Maj. Pomeroy, Lieut. Wright and Mr. Joseph Hawley. Then the church meeting was dismissed, and the precinct meeting was opened, who determined to defray the charge of entertaining the council; and desired the committee of the church to procure some person, either a minister or a layman, to act as an advocate for the brethren and plead their cause before the council.
